article_title: Grade One: Math Computation. Case Study #1
citation: Powell, S. R., & Seethaler, P. M. (2007). Grade One: Math Computation (Math Case Study #1). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Peer tutoring as a primary-prevention evidence-based practice in first-grade math
description: At primary prevention, the classroom teacher supplements the district curriculum with a peer-tutoring program run "3 times per week for 30 minutes each session." Each session opens with teacher-led introduction or review, then higher-performing students are paired with lower-performing students to work on the lesson. Topics include number concepts, comparing numbers, addition and subtraction concepts, place value, double-digit addition and subtraction, and missing addends.
requirements: Cross-ability pairing of students, a structured session opening with teacher-led review, and topic materials such as worksheets (e.g., drawing tens and ones for place value)
target_learners: All first-grade students in the general education classroom
target_learning_goals: Number concepts, place value, and addition and subtraction computation
examples: The case study includes a sample peer-tutoring worksheet focusing on place value by asking students to draw tens and ones
key_sources: Powell, S. R., & Seethaler, P. M. (2007). Grade One: Math Computation (Math Case Study #1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED502453

article_title: EveryDay Intervention (Formerly InClass Today and EveryDay Labs)
citation: EveryDay Intervention (formerly InClassToday) Absence Reports Intervention — Evidence Summary. (2018). https://www.everydaylabs.com
title: Deliver personalized attendance information directly to parents as a low-burden absenteeism intervention
description: The article's program model is that mailing parents "actionable, personalized information about their student's attendance" can change attendance behavior without instructional changes at school. Implementation burden is minimal: staffing is "one district staff member to support program implementation (approximately 30 min/week)" plus a data staff member, with no professional development, training, or technology required.
requirements: Secure receipt of attendance data from the district
One district staff member (~30 min/week) and one district-level data staff member (< 3 hrs total)
constraints: No professional development or training required beyond the stated staffing; no technology required
target_learners: Students at risk of chronic absenteeism and their parents/guardians
target_learning_goals: Reducing absences so students attend and benefit from instruction
examples: In both randomized evaluations, at-risk students' families received mailed, personalized Absence Reports while control families did not.
key_sources: EveryDay Intervention (formerly InClassToday) Absence Reports Intervention — Evidence Summary. (2018). https://www.everydaylabs.com

article_title: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs — Family Engagement
citation: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs™. (2025). Evidence review summary. https://www.justrightreader.com
title: Personalized, relevant decodable texts with named students and meaningful storylines to foster ownership and reading identity
description: Each pack is personalized with the student's name and includes books featuring relevant characters and meaningful storylines, along with writing pages that strengthen the connection between reading and writing. The article states "This personalized and relevant design fosters ownership, increases engagement and confidence, and supports the development of strong reading identities."
requirements: Books must be matched to each student's phonics skill level and personalized with the student's name.
target_learning_goals: reading engagement
reading confidence
reading identity
phonics practice
examples: Packs include writing pages that connect reading and writing practice.
key_sources: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs™. (2025). Evidence review summary. https://www.justrightreader.com

article_title: Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief)
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez. (2017). Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Use personalized messages added to existing communications to encourage student participation in advanced coursework
description: The brief presents personalized messages as a low-cost behavioral-science nudge: a small change in how information is presented—a personalized message added to a test score report—can substantially change students' decisions to participate in a program. It reports that "Personalized messages can be a cost-effective way to encourage students," grounded in the finding that message recipients were 49 percentage points more likely to participate in AP classes.
requirements: The message must be personalized to the student's potential to succeed in the coursework
An effort to call attention to the messages should accompany delivery
constraints: The brief notes the messages "might only work when combined with an effort to call attention to the messages"
target_learners: high school students considering Advanced Placement coursework
target_learning_goals: increasing participation in advanced coursework and AP exam taking
examples: A personalized message about a student's potential to succeed in AP coursework was added to a test score report
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez. (2017). Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/small-changes-make-a-big-difference-how-behavioral-science-improved-participation-in-advanced

article_title: Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP Growth Tests
citation: Wei He. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP® Growth™ Tests. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Update achievement norms periodically with recent data and combine normative information with other evidence for high-stakes decisions
description: The report argues that because the educational ecosystem constantly changes and can exert impacts on student achievements, norms "need to be periodically updated, typically utilizing more recent test event data" so they reflect changes in student achievement in a timely manner. It also cautions that placement or instructional decisions relying solely on normative performance are likely to be less accurate, so normative information should be combined with other evidence about student performance or growth for major decisions.
requirements: A schedule for re-norming using recent test event data (the report describes three-year rolling user norms updated every other fall)
constraints: Placement or instructional decisions that solely rely on the normative performance of students are likely to be less accurate
target_learners: Students in Grades 6–12 taking course-specific assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement and growth scores for placement and instructional decisions
examples: NWEA updated the Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 norms using 2019/20–2021/22 test events and plans three-year rolling norms released every other fall
key_sources: Wei He. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP® Growth™ Tests. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/achievement-and-growth-norms-for-course-specific-map-growth-tests/

article_title: Collaborative Argumentation for Learning
citation: Schank, P., Barth, C., Crawford, V., and Fusco, J. (2025, May). Collaborative Argumentation for Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/251
title: Use peer review of arguments to improve learning while reducing teacher workload
description: The primer recommends peer review as a strategy that accounts for teachers' limited time: "Through a powerful approach called peer review, students review and assess each other's arguments, serving to both improve student learning and reduce teacher workload". It works especially well when teachers use role-playing games, prompts, and other scaffolds to seed peer reviewing of discussions as students practice argumentation skills (Clark et al., 2009).
requirements: Scaffolds such as role-playing games and prompts to seed peer reviewing of discussions
constraints: The primer notes teachers do not want to be the sole source of feedback, and a trust-based classroom culture supports students giving and receiving critical feedback
target_learners: Middle school and secondary STEM students
target_learning_goals: Argumentation skills
Learning from evaluating peers' arguments
examples: The primer's recommendation of peer review as one of the promising strategies that take teachers' available time into account
key_sources: Schank, P., Barth, C., Crawford, V., and Fusco, J. (2025, May). Collaborative Argumentation for Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/251

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Design in tools and opportunities for peer-to-peer interaction among adult learners
description: The brief's fifth principle rests on research that students learn from peers as well as teachers, particularly peers of different abilities and backgrounds. Working with others increases the social-emotional memories of a learning experience and thus the learning, and for adult learners these connections also build confidence because they learn with others managing the same adult responsibilities. Digital tools such as wikis, discussion threads, and video and text chats can be built into products as places for peer work.
requirements: Products must include built-in spaces for peer interaction such as wikis, discussion threads, and chats
Instruction should be peppered with peer discussion, peer-review writing, and group project opportunities
target_learning_goals: deepening learning through peer input and models
building a peer support system for managing learning
examples: Online courses use discussions with peers, peer-review writing activities, and group projects as peer-to-peer collaboration practices
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: The Growing Diversity in Today’s Classroom
citation: Making Learning Personal for All: The Growing Diversity in Today's Classroom. (2016). https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Personalize learning by connecting it to each individual's development, background, interests, and experiences
description: The paper defines personalized learning as "learning that is connected to each individual's development, background, interests, and experiences," an approach it says broadly and equitably supports educators' efforts to empower learners as individuals. It argues personalization means engaging, motivating, and inspiring learners with the right resources at the right time, in the right medium, and at the right pace, and warns that current overly simplistic personalization models risk leaving diverse learners behind.
requirements: Structured supports: curriculum, pedagogy, tools, and resources specifically designed to support personalization strategies
Knowledge about the individual learner, since personalization can only be based on what is known about the learner
constraints: The paper states current models that drive personalization remain overly simplistic and are rarely based on research
target_learners: Diverse K-12 learners, including students in poverty, English language learners, students with disabilities, and gifted students
target_learning_goals: Equitable support of diverse learners' academic success and engagement
examples: The paper cites adaptive working memory training and individualized phonological awareness and reading instruction as personalization approaches grounded in research
key_sources: Making Learning Personal for All: The Growing Diversity in Today's Classroom. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/7acc6442-9c20-42ff-b4b2-21645832493e

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Avoid overly automated personalization; preserve meaningful learner choice
description: The report supports personalization that tailors content, pacing, and assessment, but states that 'personalization alone is not sufficient to design for agency.' Personalization promotes agency when learners make meaningful choices about how, where, and what learning produces. The authors explicitly 'do not recommend personalized learning experiences that are overly automated, because providing learners limited opportunities to make informed decisions can detract from agency.'
requirements: Customizations must give learners freedom to engage in learning experiences that feel valuable and meaningful to them
target_learners: learners across ages and abilities, including those served by adaptive tools
target_learning_goals: learner agency, ownership of learning, engagement
examples: Mentu's AI suggests evidence-based strategies but educators remain final decision-makers, with explanations of why each strategy was selected
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Merging Cognitive Science and Curriculum to Strengthen Middle School Math
citation: Merging Cognitive Science and Curriculum to Strengthen Middle School Math. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://www.wested.org
title: Test students periodically with targeted feedback so they practice retrieving knowledge and learn from mistakes
description: The fourth design principle states that testing students periodically, accompanied by targeted feedback, gives students opportunities to practice retrieving knowledge and to learn from their mistakes. Like spacing, Davenport traces this principle to basic psychological concepts documented more than a hundred years ago.
requirements: Tests must be accompanied by targeted feedback
target_learning_goals: knowledge retrieval practice
learning from mistakes
key_sources: Merging Cognitive Science and Curriculum to Strengthen Middle School Math. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559573

article_title: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors
citation: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://www.wested.org
title: Structure peer networking among isolated district leaders so they can compare notes and build lasting support networks
description: Because district-level special education leaders lack regular contact with professional peers, the Academy deliberately builds peer connection into its structure, since "what they learn from each other is particularly valuable." Graduates report establishing support networks that continue after the program ends, supported by a maintained email list for communication among participants.
requirements: A structured setting with time for participants to interact and share successful projects and effective materials
A communication mechanism (e.g., an email list) to sustain connections between sessions
constraints: Addresses isolation in a role the article describes as lacking regular contact with professional peers
target_learners: District special education directors and administrators
target_learning_goals: Sharing strategies and materials with peers who understand the job
Reducing professional isolation and burnout
examples: A graduate notes that when a question stumps her, she puts it to peers met at the Academy and a good portion will respond.
key_sources: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559625

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Persuasion across Time and Space: five-week CCSS-aligned ELA unit on persuasive text and media messages
description: A five-week, Common Core State Standards-aligned English language arts unit on persuasive text and media messages, targeting middle school English learners at an intermediate level of proficiency. It shows teachers how to help students build English language mastery in tandem with conceptual understanding of text, using texts from television commercials to the Gettysburg Address and Civil Rights Movement speeches, with tools such as Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos for evaluating arguments. The unit is available online with downloadable teacher and student materials.
requirements: Teachers learn how to differentiate instruction for ELL students and help them draw on background knowledge rather than simplifying text
target_learners: middle school English learners at intermediate English proficiency
target_learning_goals: reading, interpreting, critically analyzing, and creating persuasive texts
academic practices and the language required to express them
examples: Six school districts affiliated with the Council of the Great City Schools field tested the unit during the past year, and teachers in several other large districts reviewed and critiqued it.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: Strategies for Trauma-Informed Distance Learning
citation: Pate, C. (2020). Strategies for trauma-informed distance learning. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Perry's 3 Rs framework (Regulate, Relate, Reason) sequences trauma-informed intervention from regulation to reasoning
description: The brief adopts neuroscientist Bruce Perry's "3 Rs" approach as its organizing framework for trauma-informed education. Educators are told to "closely follow the process of how to reach the 'learning brain' — beginning from the back of the brain and moving to the front": first ensure students are regulated in their hindbrain, feeling "physically and emotionally calm and settled"; then related in the midbrain through safe, supportive relationships; and finally able to reason in the forebrain, ready for formal instruction. The brief argues a child who is unsettled is unlikely to connect with others or have the cognitive capacity for higher-level learning processes.
requirements: Educators must address regulation and relational safety before expecting engagement with formal academic instruction
constraints: The framework is presented as applying to all children but is described as particularly critical for students experiencing adversity and in distance learning contexts
target_learners: K-12 students learning remotely, especially those experiencing adversity or trauma
target_learning_goals: Emotional regulation
social connection
readiness for academic learning
examples: The brief organizes all of its distance-learning strategies under the three headings Regulate, Relate, and Reason
key_sources: Pate, C. (2020). Strategies for trauma-informed distance learning. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606091

article_title: Moving toward Instructional Coherence: How Four Popular Student-Centered Approaches Deepen Identity, Agency, Equity, and Community
citation: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Personalized learning as learner-centered variation of place, pace, content, and strategies guided by ongoing evidence
description: The paper defines personalized learning as 'a philosophy or broad orientation to learning that places the individual learner at the center of the learning process so that resources, strategies, and content are varied to meet the individual's learning needs and preferences.' Teachers act in a facilitative role, using multiple sources of data, learning progressions, and success criteria to scaffold learning opportunities. The approach prioritizes student voice and choice and adaptive teaching, and it is explicitly technology agnostic—blended and digital learning are common strategies but not required.
requirements: Teachers rely on multiple sources of data and information to understand individual and group learning progress
Teachers scaffold learning opportunities to guide and prompt students to progress
constraints: Personalized learning is technology agnostic and does not require or rely on digital resources or instruction
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Active engagement
academic success
student motivation
preparation for postsecondary opportunities
examples: Place, pace, content, and strategies may vary depending on student learning goals and needs
key_sources: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655925

article_title: Educating the Whole Child: Improving School Climate to Support Student Success
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child
title: Personalize supports to each child's unique developmental path rather than designing learning around a mythical average
description: Because variability in human development is the norm, the report holds that effective teachers personalize supports and intervention for different children rather than assuming all children respond equally to the same teaching approaches. It warns that "when educators try to force all children to fit one sequence or pacing guide, they miss the opportunity to nurture the individual potential of each child," and can cause children and teachers to adopt counterproductive views about learning potential that undermine progress. Supportive schools avoid attaching labels to children or designing learning experiences around a mythical average.
requirements: Teachers need the capacity to personalize supports and intervention for different children
target_learners: K-12 students with diverse developmental pace and profile
target_learning_goals: Individual learning potential
Positive learning self-concept
examples: The report's principle that variability is the norm notes children of precisely the same age are at different developmental levels in different domains.
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Performance Assessment Resource Bank of reviewed curriculum-embedded tasks
description: The Performance Assessment Resource Bank is a nationwide bank of curriculum-embedded performance tasks "developed by the Council for Chief State School Officers (CCSSO) in collaboration with the Stanford Center for Assessment, Learning, and Equity (SCALE) and the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education (SCOPE)". Tasks are "reviewed for quality by a team of assessment experts and, frequently, piloted and revised", and are presented with their embedded units, rubrics, and scored samples of student work. The bank includes "tools and protocols for training educators to develop, review, revise, and score tasks with consistency".
requirements: Tasks are reviewed and validated before sharing; educators use the bank's tools and protocols for training in task development and scoring
target_learners: K-12 students whose teachers draw on the bank's tasks
target_learning_goals: application of concepts to real-world contexts, data collection and analysis, and communication of findings
examples: The Rising Cost of a College Education mathematics task, in which students collect and analyze data, develop equations and graphs, and write an article; New Hampshire, Colorado, and Kentucky are drawing on the bank while developing their own task banks
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Design Principles for Teacher Preparation: Enacting the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854
title: Align pedagogy across coursework and clinical work so candidates experience the teaching they are expected to use
description: The report identifies pedagogical alignment in both coursework and clinical work around a coherent vision of whole child development, learning, and teaching as a critical program strategy. New teachers should experience the very kinds of teaching strategies they are expected to develop for their pupils. Instructors, supervisors, and cooperating teachers should enact and unpack the approaches they expect candidates to use, integrating theory and practice around SoLD-aligned principles through close partnerships between programs, schools, and districts.
requirements: Close partnerships between programs, schools, and districts
Coherence of strategies across coursework and clinical site contexts
target_learning_goals: Whole child development-focused teaching
Implementing holistic models of learning
examples: In classroom management, strategies like community circles, design of classroom responsibilities, and restorative practices are used in both coursework and clinical site contexts
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: Persona progression model: a four-stage AI-instructor persona (Guide→Collaborator→Peer→Launcher) operationalizing the Gradual Release of Responsibility framework for AI-mediated instruction
description: The persona progression model ties the AI instructor's tone and scaffolding depth to the learner's position in the module sequence across four stages: Guide (patient teacher, explains every concept), Collaborator (working partner, asks before telling), Peer (senior colleague, terse and direct), and Launcher (states the goal and steps back). The article states that "The curriculum defines four personas, each specified as a prompt engineering directive in every module file", mapping 1:1 to GRR's four phases, with "I do it" reinterpreted so the learner is always hands-on. Persona boundaries are set at onboarding from three experience-level schedules (4/3/2/1, 3/3/3/1, 1/3/5/1) and can shift at module boundaries via the adaptive system. Implementation uses descriptive prompt directives alone, without fine-tuning, RLHF, or RAG.
requirements: Each module file must contain an explicit persona directive metadata line consumed by Claude Code when reading the module
constraints: The article notes a static tone either underwhelms beginners or patronizes experts, motivating stage-dependent personas; the adaptation is validated only for structural consistency, not instructional effectiveness
target_learners: professional software engineers learning an agentic AI coding tool, at beginner, intermediate, or advanced experience levels
target_learning_goals: compositional mastery of an agentic AI coding tool's features, from setup through multi-agent orchestration
examples: Module 1–3 use the Guide persona; the intermediate schedule assigns Guide to modules 1–3, Collaborator to 4–6, Peer to 7–9, and Launcher to module 10
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success
citation: Andrew Howard Nichols. (2015). The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org/resource/pellgradrates
title: Pell Grant Graduation Rate Database and Institution Profile tool
description: A publicly accessible database built by The Education Trust from a yearlong collection effort using four sources: state higher education systems, colleges and universities, U.S. News and World Report, and IPEDS. It covers "graduation rates for Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients at nearly 1,150 institutions, the percentage of Pell Grant recipients attending each school, the cost for each, and much, much, more." The report states this is the first time such information is widely available to the general public.
requirements: Institutions must report six-year graduation rates for first-time, full-time Pell recipients in their IPEDS graduation-rate cohorts, as defined in the report's Appendix A
constraints: For-profit and non-specialized colleges were excluded
Private institutions are underrepresented, and participating institutions tended to be slightly larger and more selective than the surveyed population
For some colleges the gap was calculated by combining U.S. News Pell data with IPEDS overall rates, which the authors note could produce small discrepancies
target_learners: prospective low-income and working-class college students
target_learning_goals: informed college choice by low-income students
institutional accountability for low-income student completion
examples: The report's Table 1 lists 36 standout institutions meeting criteria including Pell graduation rates at or above the national Pell rate of 50 percent and gaps at or below 3 percentage points
key_sources: Andrew Howard Nichols. (2015). The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org/resource/pellgradrates

article_title: AI Agents Can Now Navigate and Complete LMS Tasks: A Call for Pedagogical Innovation
citation: Hadjisolomou, S. P., & El-Haddad, R. W. (2026). AI Agents Can Now Navigate and Complete LMS Tasks: A Call for Pedagogical Innovation. Intersection: A Journal at the Intersection of Assessment and Learning, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.61669/001c.169225
title: Because AI agents can now navigate and complete LMS tasks, assessment practice calls for pedagogical innovation
description: The article's subtitle issues 'A Call for Pedagogical Innovation' in response to AI agents that can navigate and complete LMS tasks. Its keywords scope the innovation to assessment design, assessment validity, and academic integrity within learning management systems, positioning assessment redesign as the recommended response in higher education.
requirements: Assessment practices delivered through a learning management system, where AI agents can navigate and complete tasks
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of student learning
academic integrity
key_sources: Hadjisolomou, S. P., & El-Haddad, R. W. (2026). AI Agents Can Now Navigate and Complete LMS Tasks: A Call for Pedagogical Innovation. Intersection: A Journal at the Intersection of Assessment and Learning, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.61669/001c.169225

article_title: AI-Driven Educational Reform: Enhancing Talent Cultivation in Computer-Related Majors for the Digital Era
citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: Performance indicator design pattern translating competencies into scored, industry-adjusted assessment standards
description: The reform uses Performance Indicators as the assessment layer of the competency map. As printed, "Performance Indicators (PIs) serve as critical tools for translating abstract learning goals into measurable and actionable assessment standards." Each PI is defined as a specific observable action with clear scoring rubrics and paired assessment tools such as programming assignments, project reports, and peer reviews; standards are reviewed regularly using student, industry-expert, and faculty feedback, and are tested through interdisciplinary projects.
requirements: Each PI must be aligned with core and sub-competencies, defined as quantifiable skills and behaviors, and accompanied by explicit scoring rubrics and evaluation tools
constraints: PIs are reviewed and adjusted regularly (e.g., every semester) to remain aligned with technological developments and industry requirements
target_learning_goals: measurable assessment of technical and teamwork competencies
examples: For one indicator, students' code quality, model accuracy, experimental design, and problem-solving capacity are quantified on a 10-point scale where code quality accounts for 4 points, model accuracy for 3 points, and problem-solving for 3 points
key_sources: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916

article_title: Designing Needs- and Attention-Aware AI Learning Tools for Engineering Education: Insights from Psychological Outcomes
citation: Kevin Zhongyang Shao, Denise Wilson, Yale Quan, Sep Makhsous. (2026). Designing Needs- and Attention-Aware AI Learning Tools for Engineering Education: Insights from Psychological Outcomes. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26338
title: Personal agency as an empirically merged self-efficacy/self-regulated learning factor in AI-use motivation modeling
description: In this study's measurement model, exploratory factor analysis of adapted self-regulated learning and self-efficacy items produced a single combined factor rather than two separate constructs. The authors "labeled personal agency to reflect a combined sense of being able and ready to act on academic demands", capturing confidence in handling challenges, planning, and integrating new knowledge. This factor then served as a baseline latent predictor in the SEM of perceived AI outcomes, where it negatively predicted perceived relief from competence frustration. The interpretation aligns with prior work treating self-efficacy and SRL as conceptually distinct but closely related.
requirements: Adapted Likert-scale items measuring self-regulated learning and self-efficacy must be factor-analyzed in the target sample before treating them as one construct
constraints: The merge is an empirical result of this sample's EFA, not assumed a priori; one help-seeking item (SR4) was removed for weak and conceptually inconsistent loading
target_learning_goals: motivation and psychological need fulfillment in AI-supported learning
examples: EFA on baseline items (KMO = .862) suggested a four-factor structure in which SRL and self-efficacy items loaded on a common factor

article_title: When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills
citation: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700
title: Persona-skill pipeline risk formulation: risk concentration, impact amplification, and defense degradation
description: The article formulates persona-skill safety along a trace-skill-agent pipeline, where a distillation function processes personal traces into a reusable person-grounded artifact that is then equipped to an agent. It identifies three distinctive risks: "Risk concentration", since distillation consolidates fragmented information into artifacts that are easier to inspect, transfer, and misuse; "Impact amplification", since portable artifacts can be deployed across agents without modifying the underlying model; and "Defense degradation", since cross-trace distillation weakens record-level anonymization and retrieval filtering. Risks are operationalized at two levels: skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level impersonation risk.
requirements: A threat model with adversaries acting at either the skill-inspection stage or the agent-interaction stage of the pipeline
constraints: The defender can only intervene on the trace side before distillation, and does not modify the distillation function, the agent, or the deployed skill-use interface
target_learners: LLM-based agent systems and their developers
target_learning_goals: Understanding how personal traces become exposed when distilled into executable persona skills
examples: Skill distillation and skill-equipped generation form the process Tu -> su -> y, with skill-level leakage during distillation and impersonation risk downstream
key_sources: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700

article_title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
citation: Yearim Kim, Injun Baek, and Nojun Kwak. 2026. When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation. In Proceedings of Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education (CHI '26 Workshop). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19812
title: PedaCo: a dual gatekeeping human-AI video co-creation system
description: PedaCo (Pedagogical Co-creation) is a human-AI collaborative system that "integrates two complementary gatekeeping mechanisms: reviewing scripts through CTML-informed criteria, and an automated metric evaluating finished videos against computationally measurable CTML dimensions." Layer 1 intervenes before rendering: an LLM generates an initial script, an AI reviewer produces principle-organized feedback identifying potential violations, and the educator decides what to accept, revise, or regenerate. Layer 2 performs post-synthesis evaluation, automating five dimensions: coherence, redundancy, temporal contiguity, modality, and image quality.
requirements: The educator inputs learning content and configures which CTML principles the system should enforce before script generation
constraints: The article states dimensions like Personalization (tone) "require a deep understanding of curricular structures and learner psychology that currently remains the sole domain of the human expert", so only algorithmically feasible dimensions are automated
target_learning_goals: instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization in AI-generated videos
examples: The interface visualizes automated metrics at the video level, allowing users to assess alignment between the final video and the learning content

In Proceedings of Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education (CHI '26 Workshop). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19812

article_title: When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
citation: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958
title: Design AI tutors for pedagogical structure first; humanlike modality is an engagement lever, not a learning lever
description: The article's headline design recommendation is that what makes an AI tutor educational is its pedagogical structure — attempt-first questioning, scaffolding, and production demands — not how humanlike its delivery channel feels. As the authors put it, "Pedagogical structure shapes what students practice, and modality shapes how they interact with the tutor. Making an AI more humanlike does not by itself make it more educational." Voice roughly doubled conversational interaction and was increasingly preferred, yet produced weekly mastery statistically equivalent to text at 2.8× the cost, so programs should treat modality as a purchasable engagement and adoption lever and invest their design effort in the guardrailed tutoring pedagogy that the offloading evidence identifies as protective.
requirements: A structured tutoring prompt that diagnoses before explaining and requires student production on every turn
Assessment instrumentation (engaged-time metering, transcripts, cost accounting) to verify that engagement gains are not mistaken for learning gains
constraints: Voice carried a 2.8× cost premium for equivalent measured mastery in this quantitative, problem-set-driven graduate setting
The modality null is identified within students in one course; the authors note task–technology-fit reasons text may suit stepwise analytical work
target_learners: Working professionals in asynchronous online graduate programs
target_learning_goals: Authentic learning (unassisted exam performance and SOLO-scored reasoning depth) rather than assisted performance
examples: The experiment randomized tutor access against a no-AI holdout and alternated voice and text weekly within AI-arm students, holding pedagogy, model, and knowledge base constant across channels
key_sources: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958

article_title: Benchmarking the Pedagogical Knowledge of Large Language Models
citation: Lelièvre, M., Waldock, A., Liu, M., Valdes Aspillaga, N., Mackintosh, A., Ogando Portela, M. J., Lee, J., Atherton, P., Ince, R. A. A., & Garrod, O. G. B. (2025). Benchmarking the Pedagogical Knowledge of Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18710v3
title: The Pedagogy Benchmark: 1143 curated MCQs of pedagogical knowledge from Chilean teacher exams (920 CDPK + 223 SEND)
description: The Pedagogy Benchmark is a publicly released dataset of multiple-choice questions testing LLMs' pedagogical knowledge, built from the Chilean Ministry of Education's ECEP teacher exams administered 2017–2023. Questions were extracted, de-duplicated, translated, and manually curated by a pedagogy expert, yielding "1143 high-quality, annotated MCQs". The 920 general questions form the CDPK benchmark and 223 form a separate SEND benchmark, each tagged with education level, subject, and pedagogical subdomain.
requirements: Questions must be de-duplicated, translated, and reviewed by a pedagogy expert for relevance, clarity, and context-agnosticism before use
constraints: Questions come from a single source, the Chilean Ministry of Education, so the pedagogical principles valued may differ from other cultural contexts; all questions were translated from Spanish into English
target_learners: large language model developers and education technology developers
target_learning_goals: evaluating models' cross-domain pedagogical knowledge and special educational needs and disability pedagogical knowledge
examples: Example questions include a pre-primary science question on evaluating a learning objective about natural environment exploration and a secondary general question on Bowlby's theory of attachment

article_title: Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks
citation: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590v1
title: Per-draw robust linking: solving a response-count-weighted robust Haebara criterion separately for each posterior draw propagates linking uncertainty into the linked posteriors
description: The linking step maps each independently calibrated period to a common reference metric by minimizing a response-count-weighted pseudo-Huber (robust Haebara) discrepancy between expected-score curves on anchor items. Following Baldwin (2011), the criterion is minimized separately for each posterior draw rather than once at the posterior mean; the article states that "Applying it draw-wise propagates the linking uncertainty, together with its dependence on the item parameters, into the linked posteriors." Weighting anchors by response count lets better-estimated items contribute more to the link, approximating concurrent calibration.
requirements: An anchor set of common items that is invariant in aggregate
A designated reference period defining the metric
Anchor screening by potential scale reduction factor (R-hat at most 1.05) and iterative purification removing top-decile residual anchors
constraints: Each period's fit identifies the latent metric only up to a linear transformation, so linking is required before aggregation
Robust variants suit a partial-invariance context in which a minority of anchor items function differently
target_learners: language-assessment examinees in adaptive testing programs
target_learning_goals: accurate cross-period item calibration with propagated linking uncertainty
examples: In the evaluation, the robust per-draw criterion with the R-hat-and-purification anchor screen was solved for 200 draws of each non-reference period
key_sources: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590

article_title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: Taxonomy of pedagogical sycophancy: frame abandonment distinguished from factual error via CS-SYC, AUTH-SYC, FACE-SYC, and DIR-SYC subtypes
description: The paper defines pedagogical sycophancy as pressure-contingent validation of a misconception after the tutor is pushed to agree, distinguishing it from ordinary factual error. Its core organizing concept is "frame abandonment-a tutoring-specific failure where agreeableness collapses the corrective friction needed for conceptual change". The taxonomy decomposes this into channels: CS-SYC (context-switch frame attack, where a student invokes valid but instructionally inappropriate jargon), AUTH-SYC (deference to notes, textbooks, or instructors), FACE-SYC (social-affective face-saving that overrides corrective duty), and DIR-SYC (direct endorsement), with EVADE as a sixth judge label. A rubric operationalizes the labels for automated judging.
requirements: Judging requires the full four-turn dialogue for context but labels only the post-pressure response T2, using a shared rubric with structured JSON outputs
constraints: The three pressure modes are intended as core tutoring-relevant channels rather than an exhaustive ontology of all possible pedagogical failures
target_learners: students interacting with LLM tutors in math, physics, economics, chemistry, biology, and computer science
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptual understanding resistant to misconception reinforcement under social-epistemic pressure
examples: Figure 2 depicts a student pressure turn inducing misconception validation via the three channels, with the label determined from the tutor's post-pressure response
key_sources: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604

article_title: Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision
citation: Shi Shi, Lingyun Chen, Zitao Zhang, Amanda R. Draper, and Eli Blevis. 2026. Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision. The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18598
title: Perceptual-reference-during-action account of embodied accessibility
description: The article proposes that in embodied skill domains, accessibility is not only about accessing instructions or representations but about accessing ongoing perceptual reference during action. String technique states such as bow path, grip tension, and wrist alignment are conventionally monitored through vision, so learners with BLV must reconfigure technique learning "from seeing to inferring" via proprioception, auditory feedback, kinesthetic memory, and teacher mediation. This account frames the study's breakdown findings and motivates designs that externalize invisible technique states into non-visual, practice-compatible cues.
requirements: Applies to embodied skill domains where technique states are conventionally taught and corrected through visual demonstration or mirror-based self-monitoring.
constraints: Derived from a qualitative study of four upper-string musicians with BLV; the authors note violin and viola offer fewer stable external reference points than floor-anchored instruments.
target_learners: Musicians with blindness and low-vision learning bowed string instruments
target_learning_goals: Embodied instrumental technique such as bow control, hand-arm alignment, and intonation
examples: The study triangulated practice videos, lesson observations, and interviews, identifying breakdowns in right-hand bow control, left-hand coordination, and score-related practice.
key_sources: Shi Shi, Lingyun Chen, Zitao Zhang, Amanda R. Draper, and Eli Blevis. 2026. Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision. article_title: Distinguishing performance gains from learning when using generative AI
citation: Yan, L., Greiff, S., Lodge, J. M., & Gašević, D. (2025). Distinguishing performance gains from learning when using generative AI. Nature Reviews Psychology, 4, 435–436. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-025-00467-5
title: Performance versus learning distinction: performance during task execution does not imply durable learning
description: The article organizes its argument around a fundamental distinction between performance and learning. Performance refers to observable behaviours during task execution, often influenced by external supports, whereas learning involves enduring changes in knowledge or behaviour characterized by the ability to independently retain and transfer skills. The article applies this distinction to critique generative-AI research that measures only immediate task success.
requirements: Assessment must capture independent retention and transfer, not just in-task performance, for the distinction to be observable
constraints: The article notes the distinction is underexamined in emerging research on generative AI in education
target_learning_goals: durable knowledge retention
transfer of skills
examples: The article illustrates the distinction with cramming: a student may achieve high test performance after massed practice yet fail to retain or apply the knowledge later

article_title: Suitability of Artificial Intelligence Supported Lesson Plans from the Perspective of Science Education Experts
citation: Karaismailoglu, F., Surmeli, H., & Yildirim, M. (2026). Suitability of Artificial Intelligence Supported Lesson Plans from the Perspective of Science Education Experts. Journal of Science Education and Technology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-026-10342-4
title: Build pedagogical models and learning-science principles into educational AI systems, since domain-specific training improves instructional output quality
description: The article argues that AI developers should integrate established pedagogical models such as EDBL into system design, enabling more coherent and process-oriented instructional outputs. The education-focused platform's stronger performance in supporting EDBL's iterative stages suggests that "pedagogical training in AI systems can yield meaningful improvements, regardless of subject matter or grade level." Developers are advised to prioritize deeper integration of learning science principles and pedagogical models into AI architectures.
requirements: Integration of established pedagogical models such as EDBL into AI system design
constraints: Both platforms still scored lowest in engineering skills, indicating a persistent challenge in simulating complex, process-oriented learning tasks
target_learners: Teachers and students using AI-supported lesson planning in science education
target_learning_goals: Process-oriented, iterative instructional outputs aligned with pedagogical frameworks
examples: The education-focused platform (Teacher's Buddy) outperformed the general-purpose ChatGPT-4 on iterative EDBL stages and on most overall quality criteria in expert ratings.

article_title: Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective
citation: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453
title: PETSP-ML: a four-stage classroom process model for explanatory thinking in machine learning, adapted from CRISP-DM
description: PETSP-ML (Promotion of Explanatory Thinking Standard Process for Machine Learning) is a process model the authors developed "to promote explanatory thinking in a structured manner", adapted from the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM). It reorganizes CRISP-DM's six phases into four classroom-aligned stages: Task Understanding, Data Phase (merging data understanding and preparation), Model Understanding, and Model Training and Evaluation, with an iterative structure encouraging students to revisit earlier stages. Its deliberate departure from professional practice is making model understanding a distinct, prerequisite stage before model training and shifting focus away from performance metrics.
requirements: Model Understanding is treated as a distinct, prerequisite stage before model training, reflecting the pedagogical priority of building conceptual foundations before procedural skills
constraints: CRISP-DM's original formulation is not directly suited to educational settings, where objectives, constraints, and prior knowledge differ substantially from industrial projects
target_learning_goals: explanatory thinking about how and why ML systems behave as they do
understanding of training data, algorithmic mechanisms, evaluation metrics, and sources of error or bias
examples: In the Data Phase students collect, inspect, and prepare data while engaging critically with data quality, representativeness, labeling accuracy, and potential biases

article_title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
citation: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429
title: Pedagogical instruction following: conditioning model behavior on system-level pedagogy instructions
description: The report's central framework recasts injecting pedagogy into generative AI not as fixing one definition of good tutoring but as instruction following for pedagogical System Instructions. The authors "cast our work aspedagogical instruction following, meaning that we contextualize training and evaluation examples with system-level instructions that describe desired pedagogical behavior." This lets teachers or developers specify desired behavior, avoids conflicts of persona or style when mixing pedagogical data into Gemini's training mixture, and treats pedagogy as hard constraints (e.g. "do not reveal the answer") plus soft guidelines (e.g. "use a motivating tone").
requirements: Training and evaluation conversations must each begin with a specific System Instruction describing the pedagogical behavior present in that conversation; vague instructions are counterproductive because the model learns to ignore them.
constraints: The authors note pedagogy is "prohibitively difficult to define" across grade levels, subjects, languages, cultures and philosophies, so the framework deliberately avoids committing to any particular definition of pedagogy.
target_learners: learners across grade levels and subjects interacting with AI tutors
independent EdTech users and classroom students
target_learning_goals: tutoring and teaching interactions guided by teacher- or developer-specified pedagogical behavior
examples: LearnLM conversations were seeded with pedagogically focused System Instructions, and human preference raters labeled model samples on adherence to those instructions to train reward models for RLHF.
key_sources: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429

article_title: LearnMate^2: Design and Evaluation of an LLM-powered Personalized and Adaptive Support System for Online Learning
citation: Xinyu Jessica Wang, Christine P Lee, and Bilge Mutlu. 2026. LearnMate2: Design and Evaluation of an LLM-powered Personalized and Adaptive Support System for Online Learning. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), June 13–17, 2026, Singapore, Singapore. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3812972
title: Design AI-driven educational tools by conceptualizing personalization as a continuous learning workflow with course-grounded, in-situ support and mixed-initiative adaptation
description: The authors present design implications for AI-driven educational tools that "conceptualize personalization as a continuous learning workflow, emphasize course-grounded and in-situ support, and enable mixed-initiative, learner-steerable adaptation." This principle holds that personalization should not be implemented as isolated features but as an integrated workflow where planning, studying, and adaptation continuously inform one another. Support should be grounded in the specific course materials being studied rather than generic, and learners should be able to steer how the system adapts to their needs.
requirements: Integration of planning, in-session support, and adaptation components into a coordinated workflow
Course materials must be available for grounding AI responses
Learners must have mechanisms to initiate and steer adaptations
constraints: Demonstrated in online learning contexts with self-directed learners

adaptive learning support
learner autonomy

citation: Minsun Kim, S. Moonwara A. Monisha, Zihan Wu, David H. Smith IV. (2026). Exploring the Design Space of LLM-Based Programming Support in CS Education: A Scoping Review through the Lens of Assistance Governance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21257
title: PEA: a three-dimensional analytic lens of Policy, Enforcement, and Authority for assistance governance in LLM-based programming support
description: PEA organizes assistance governance around three design questions: what forms of assistance are allowed or restricted (Policy), how those boundaries are implemented (Enforcement), and who can control them during use (Authority). The authors state: "This What–How–Who structure was initially informed by the 5W1H design heuristic". The three dimensions were specified before corpus coding, while subcategories and decision rules were refined iteratively from the 90-system corpus. PEA is offered as a vocabulary for comparing and designing learner-facing LLM programming support systems.

constraints: The authors use PEA as a corpus-grounded analytic lens rather than a complete or externally validated theory of governance

target_learning_goals: Programming learning supported by governed LLM assistance
examples: Applied to code and analyze 90 peer-reviewed learner-facing LLM-based programming support systems published January 2023 through March 2026

citation: Martinez-Roig, R., Aragonés-González, M., & Cazorla, M. (2026). Exploring the implementation of the Pepper social robot in formal education: a scoping review. Journal of New Approaches in Educational Research, 15, 22. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44322-026-00072-1
title: Pedagogical mediation as the determining factor in social robots' educational implementation
description: The review's central explanatory account: the educational value of a social robot such as Pepper depends less on its physical presence or multimodal interaction than on the pedagogical conditions surrounding its use. The review concludes that "its contribution depends on instructional design, the purpose of the activity, student profile, technical stability and teacher mediation", positioning the robot as a supportive pedagogical resource rather than a teacher substitute. Benefits are interpreted as products of the relationship between pedagogical objectives, student profile, teacher role and technical conditions of use.

Curriculum learning in mathematics, language and STEM

citation: Martinez-Roig, R., Aragonés-González, M., & Cazorla, M. (2026). Exploring the implementation of the Pepper social robot in formal education: a scoping review. Journal of New Approaches in Educational Research, 15, 22. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44322-026-00072-1

Motivation and engagement

article_title: Using the Pepper Robot to Support Sign Language Communication
citation: Giulia Boaa, Marco Boaa, Cristina Gena, Alessandro Mazzei, Massimo Donini, and Alberto Lillo. (2025). Using the Pepper Robot to Support Sign Language Communication. https://github.com/CodeCruncher63/ISCR2025
title: Pepper robot with 52 co-designed LIS signs and four SOV-order signed sentences
description: The element is the Pepper social robot configured as a LIS signing agent: the authors co-designed and implemented "a total of 52 LIS signs" spanning school-related terms, common actions and nouns, and work-related vocabulary, plus four short sentences following LIS Subject–Object–Verb word order. Signs were built with the Pepper SDK Animation Editor and a MATLAB inverse-kinematics toolchain, with videos released on GitHub. It was evaluated for intelligibility with 12 LIS-proficient participants.

Constrained wrist and elbow mobility limits faithful reproduction of LIS handshapes

article_title: Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing
citation: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598
title: Pedagogical friction: reflection-gated feedback architecture in which cognitive effort precedes support
description: The article introduces pedagogical friction as a first-class architectural primitive: revision suggestions are gated behind an intelligent reflection gate that assesses the student's written defense for substance and, if thin, coaches rather than answers. The two-phase API design (/challenge → /unlock) ensures that "genuine cognitive effort—not merely a keystroke—precedes the delivery of revision support." The gate uses a deterministic assessment layer (length floor, reasoning markers, topical relevance) followed by a model-side status check, and after two coached attempts a genuine effort is released to a scaffolded hint.
requirements: A written student defense must be captured and assessed before any revision suggestion is released
A deterministic assessment layer checking length, reasoning markers, and question-specific relevance
constraints: The architecture supports only up to two coaching turns per question, not open-ended multi-turn dialogue
If an unlocked suggestion is misaligned, there is no mechanism for iteratively refining the defense–suggestion exchange
target_learners: K–12 students developing argumentative writing skills
students preparing for standardized assessments such as AP English Language and GRE Analytical Writing
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing quality
metacognitive reflection and self-explanation
examples: In the deployed system, a defense failing the deterministic layer receives a targeted coaching nudge such as adding a because-style reasoning link, and only a defense clearing both gate layers reaches the model-side unlock
key_sources: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598

article_title: Penny: Transition Network Analysis of Learner-Chatbot Interactions in Scaffolded EFL Writing
citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Yuko Toyokawa and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Penny: Transition Network Analysis of Learner-Chatbot Interactions in Scaffolded EFL Writing. Preprint, accepted at the 1st Workshop on Transition Network Analysis (TNA) at LAK '26.
title: Penny: an LLM-powered EFL writing support chatbot with structured feedback guidelines
description: Penny is a generative AI chatbot powered by GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024–08–06) that scaffolds English writing practice three to four times per week with daily prompts. Learners must write at least 100 characters before requesting feedback, and feedback is given in English or Japanese. Its system prompt directs it to "Adapt to the student's level", review grammar and syntax, enhance vocabulary, encourage and support, limit responses to 50 words, and keep the student on topic.
requirements: Learners must write a minimum of 100 characters before the Check my writing button becomes active
The system prompt supplies the student's name, proficiency level, chat language and the day's writing prompt
constraints: Learners could not engage with future writing prompts past the present day
The writing textbox only accepted English characters
target_learners: Japanese junior high school EFL learners aged 14–16
target_learning_goals: English as a Foreign Language writing accuracy and engagement with written corrective feedback
examples: Used by three EFL classes (n = 119) at a high performing public school in Japan over four months

article_title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning
citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: PersonaPath benchmark for Knowledge-Centric learning path planning
description: PersonaPath is a benchmark that "pairs 2,000 fine-grained learner personas with a hierarchical knowledge graph of 347 textbooks, 1,751 units, and 4,092 concepts across 77 subjects" connected by prerequisite dependencies. Given a learner profile, mastery state, and target unit, a model must generate a prerequisite-respecting path that adapts to prior knowledge and reaches the goal. Personas are stratified into Low-, Average-, and High-performing archetypes in an approximate 1:3:1 ratio, and paths are scored on Validity, Adaptivity, and Efficiency with a joint Final Pass criterion.
requirements: Explicit learner goals, a prerequisite knowledge structure, and learner-specific mastery states are the three inputs the pipeline is designed around
constraints: The benchmark is grounded in Chinese textbooks and curricula; learner states and mastery updates are synthetic
target_learners: learners from primary school to higher education in the Chinese curriculum
target_learning_goals: goal-directed, prerequisite-aware selection and ordering of knowledge toward a target unit
examples: Two educators independently rated 100 sampled personas on a 5-point Likert scale, with mean ratings from 4.11 to 4.68 and ICC(2,2) from 0.74 to 0.85
key_sources: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861

article_title: Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs
citation: Jeongmin Rhee, Changhee Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Kiroong Choe, Bohyoung Kim, Sungahn Ko, and Jinwook Seo. 2026. Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19870
title: Penquiry V2: in-situ pen-based Q&A system with Content Snapping and Question Autocompletion
description: Penquiry V2 is an in-situ question-and-answer system that lets learners query an LLM directly on digital study materials using a pen. It introduces Content Snapping, which "maps the sketch to nearby character-level PDF text elements and redraws it" to confirm referential targets, and Question Autocompletion, which generates "four autocomplete question candidates" from minimal ink keywords, categorized by question-content type, while retaining free-form questioning. It was evaluated in a within-subjects study against V1.
requirements: Requires pen-based digital devices with stylus input and PDF study materials with character-level text elements for snapping
Relies on GPT-4o across a multi-stage autocompletion, refinement and answering pipeline
constraints: Generated candidate questions may anchor learners to system-framed perspectives or narrow considered alternatives
Utility of autocompletion scales with domain expertise and can interfere when learners already have a specific question
target_learners: university undergraduate and graduate students studying textbook materials
target_learning_goals: concept clarification and inquiry during self-directed pen-based study
examples: In Study 2, 74.9% of submitted queries used autocompletion and the system achieved an average SUS score of 84.9, rated "Excellent"
key_sources: Jeongmin Rhee, Changhee Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Kiroong Choe, Bohyoung Kim, Sungahn Ko, and Jinwook Seo. 2026. Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19870

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: Six-component pedagogically grounded instructional storyboard structure
description: The framework's instructional planning stage produces a storyboard whose components are "grounded in educational the-ory, each serving a clear pedagogical purpose": Learning Objectives, Prerequisite Activation, Concept Explanations, Visual Representation Plans, Worked Examples, and Diagnostic Assessment Probes. Each component is tied to an educational-theory rationale (e.g., Bloom's taxonomy for objectives, cognitive load for prerequisite activation, multimedia learning principles for visual plans, worked-example research for examples, formative assessment for probes). The storyboard serves as the semantic backbone for downstream code generation, narration, assessment, and verification.
requirements: Storyboard must progress from prerequisite knowledge to core concepts, then to examples and assessment
Each shot should focus on one local learning goal
Narration should explain why the concept works, not only describe what appears on screen
target_learners: STEM learners in high-school and university settings
target_learning_goals: Structured conceptual understanding of a specified STEM topic
Early detection of misconceptions via diagnostic probes
examples: The generated Bubble Sort storyboard defines the objective of understanding adjacent comparisons and swaps, activates prior knowledge of arrays and loops, and includes an assessment probe targeting the misconception that the smallest element is fixed first

article_title: Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach
citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Persona-based, person-centered framework for understanding GenAI chatbot adoption in higher education
description: The article introduces a persona-based framework that moves beyond aggregate, variable-centered adoption models such as TAM and UTAUT by identifying latent user segments. It argues that variable-centered models "rely on the assumption of user homogeneity, estimating average structural relationships across entire populations", which obscures meaningful variation. Using unsupervised clustering on validated adoption constructs, the framework yields personas grounded in "psychographic and behavioral clustering" rather than demographic segmentation, and is positioned as complementing, not replacing, the prior SEM model.
requirements: Requires validated, psychometrically sound multi-item constructs as clustering input, as established in prior SEM validation
constraints: The approach does not model causal relationships; it examines how perceptual constructs naturally combine into user configurations
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting adoption of GenAI chatbots for academic support and learning-related activities
examples: The study applied hierarchical agglomerative clustering with Ward's linkage followed by k-means on 13 composite variables from 192 respondents to construct the personas.

article_title: Between perceived competence and artificial intelligence: academic self-efficacy profiles in university students with motor disabilities
citation: Suriá-Martínez R, García-Castillo F, López-Sánchez C and García del Castillo JA (2026). Between perceived competence and artificial intelligence: academic self-efficacy profiles in university students with motor disabilities. Front. Educ. 11:1956192. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1956192
title: Perception of AI Utility Questionnaire (12 items; educational, informational, and emotional support)
description: A 12-item questionnaire designed for this study measuring students' perceived utility of AI in academic contexts across three dimensions: educational support, informational support, and emotional support, each with four items rated on a 5-point Likert scale. An EFA found "The three factors jointly accounted for 70% of the total variance," with loadings from 0.45 to 0.82, and a CFA on an independent sample of 85 students provided preliminary support for the three-factor structure. Reliabilities were α = 0.85, 0.82, 0.80, and 0.87 overall.
requirements: Administration via an accessible platform compatible with screen readers and assistive technology, or in-person sessions in architecturally adapted spaces
constraints: The CFA sample of 85 was relatively limited, so the factorial structure was interpreted as preliminary evidence rather than definitive psychometric validity
target_learners: higher education students with motor disabilities
target_learning_goals: perceived utility of AI for educational, informational, and emotional academic support
examples: Used as the dependent measure in one-way ANOVAs comparing the three self-efficacy profiles and as the endogenous outcome in the SEM

citation: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation.
title: Persona Problem Builder (PPB) web-based platform
description: The Persona Problem Builder is a web-based platform developed using React for frontend code and Flask API for the backend, with GPT-4o underlying the system and leveraging its math reasoning capabilities. It is hosted on an EC2 instance and designed to integrate with ASSISTments, an online homework system. A teacher provides an ASSISTments problem ID and a topic, and the system generates a personalized version of the problem using a structured prompt that targets topic alignment and preservation of the underlying mathematics.
requirements: A teacher provides an ASSISTments problem ID and a topic; the system integrates with ASSISTments
constraints: GPT-4o underlies the system in this study; the authors note they have since moved to a more capable model
