article_title: Impacts of artificial intelligence on willingness to communicate and its key antecedents in EFL contexts: a systematic review (2015–2026)
citation: Zhang S, Zou B, Liu Y, Chen Z and Yan R (2026) Impacts of artificial intelligence on willingness to communicate and its key antecedents in EFL contexts: a systematic review (2015–2026). Front. Educ. 11:1927432. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1927432
title: Integrate AI tools into EFL instruction in ways that reduce anxiety, build confidence, and sustain motivation while supporting classroom teaching
description: The review recommends that teachers, curriculum designers, and AI developers use AI tools to foster WTC and its antecedent factors across EFL learning settings. AI tools "hold great potential for improving WTC by reducing anxiety, building confidence, and sustaining motivation, while also supporting traditional classroom instruction", and AI "can work as a complement to instruction, providing additional opportunities to practice interactional norms". Integration should be pedagogically guided rather than tool-driven.
requirements: AI use should target the intrapersonal and contextual antecedents of WTC (anxiety, self-confidence, motivation, contextual affordances) and complement, not replace, classroom instruction
constraints: Negative outcomes (technical instability, cognitive overload, over-reliance) may constrain WTC growth, and impacts are contingent on specific educational and cultural contexts
target_learners: EFL learners in classroom and informal settings
target_learning_goals: willingness to communicate in the target language
reduced foreign language anxiety
sustained motivation for oral practice
examples: The review's practical contribution proposes targeted future directions for teachers, curriculum designers, and AI developers based on the synthesized evidence

article_title: \"Is this a trap?\": Student teachers' perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses
citation: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549
title: Personalise or contextualise assessments to reduce students' reliance on GenAI
description: Among the article's implications for practice or policy, it states that "Personalising and/or contextualising assessments helps reduce students' reliance on GenAI." The principle holds that assessment tasks tied to students' own contexts give them less reason or opportunity to offload work to GenAI, addressing the assessment-design reasons students gave for their adoption decisions.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be designed so they can be personalised or contextualised to individual students.
target_learners: teacher education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: independent completion of assessments with reduced GenAI reliance
examples: The study's implications for practice list personalising and/or contextualising assessments as a direct response to students' GenAI adoption behaviour in the three courses.

article_title: Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions
citation: Grion, Valentina; Doria, Beatrice; Agostini, Daniele; Slaviero, Giorgia. (2026). Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions. Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education. https://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2697962
title: Embed AI-generated feedback in a strong pedagogical architecture with assessment literacy and explicit criteria, so its source matters less than its context
description: This principle holds that the effectiveness of formative feedback depends on the surrounding design rather than on whether it comes from a human teacher or a large language model. The article concludes that feedback effectiveness "depends less on its source than on the pedagogical architecture in which it is embedded." When embedded in a course with strong assessment literacy and explicit criteria, AI-generated feedback "can function as a credible component of formative assessment in higher education." The study operationalised this by giving all three feedback conditions the same project-based setting and criteria.
requirements: Strong assessment literacy among participants and staff
Explicit assessment criteria shared across feedback conditions
constraints: Evidence comes from one project-based university course; comparability was established within that embedded architecture, not for AI feedback in general
target_learning_goals: improving project performance through formative feedback
examples: 47 student groups were randomly assigned to GPT-o4-mini, DeepSeek R1, or expert teacher feedback within one project-based course, with equivalence and non-inferiority analyses comparing sources
key_sources: Grion, Valentina; Doria, Beatrice; Agostini, Daniele; Slaviero, Giorgia. (2026). Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions. Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education. https://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2697962

citation: Liu, W.; Li, Y.; Yan, Y.; Wang, J.; Wang, J.; Zhang, H. (2026). Exploring University Faculty’s AI Well-Being: A Structural Equation Model of Social Supports, AI Literacy, and Technological Self-Efficacy. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071168
title: PERMA-based AI well-being scale for faculty in AI-integrated teaching
description: A five-item Likert-scale instrument the authors developed to measure faculty AI well-being, defined as positive psychological functioning in AI-supported teaching and academic work. It is built on Seligman's PERMA model: "It included five items, each corresponding to one dimension of the PERMA framework", covering positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment in relation to AI use. It showed the highest AVE (0.851) and C.R. (0.966) among the study's constructs.
requirements: Deliberately multidimensional framing that captures positive functioning rather than merely the absence of technostress, as the authors state motivated the PERMA choice
constraints: The authors note the very high Cronbach's α (0.966) may indicate item redundancy and that the brief operationalization may not fully capture the multidimensional nature of digital well-being
target_learning_goals: Measuring positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment in AI-supported work
examples: Sample items include "Using AI makes me feel happy and satisfied in my work" and "AI assists my work, giving me a strong sense of achievement"

Utilizing generative AI to promote high school students' personal relevance to math and interest in the math class: An intervention. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Utilizing+generative+AI+to+promote+high+school+students%27+personal+relevance+to+math+and+interest+in+the+math+class%22

Relevance as identification concerns connections of content to students' identity and sense of self, and the article notes the three types are not mutually exclusive. The study targets the least-explored, highest-meaningfulness type using generative AI dialogue.

interest development in math

citation: Song Yafeng, Zhao Kangjian, Li Li, Dong Wei. (2026). Research on the Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage Behavior on the Learning Outcomes of Higher Vocational Students. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071166
title: Higher Vocational Students' Perceived Learning Outcomes Scale
description: A 5-point Likert scale measuring higher vocational students' perceived learning outcomes in three dimensions: knowledge mastery, skill application, and competency development. Items I1 and I3 were deleted for cross-loading in the pilot EFA; the re-run EFA retained three factors, and the article reports an overall Cronbach's α of 0.962 with all sub-dimension α coefficients exceeding 0.9. A comprehensive score is computed via Analytic Hierarchy Process weights of 0.2, 0.4, and 0.4 for the three dimensions respectively, based on pairwise comparisons by 15 vocational education experts.

examples: Used as the dependent variable in the study's descriptive, difference, correlation, and regression analyses of 1110 valid questionnaires

article_title: Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
citation: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713
title: PerFit R package for computing person-fit statistics
description: The study computed the four non-parametric person-fit statistics (G, G*, U3, ZU3) for every examinee using the R package PerFit, which the article cites as "PerFit: An R Package for Person-Fit Analysis in IRT". The statistics were chosen because they "have been shown to be the most effective in identifying cheating" in prior comparisons of 36 PFS measures. The package operationalizes the IRT-based detection approach for researchers wishing to replicate the method on their own assessment data.
requirements: Scored binary response matrices of examinees by items
An IRT or non-parametric PFS computation context
target_learners: any examinee population whose MCQ response data can be analyzed
target_learning_goals: detecting aberrant response patterns indicative of cheating in educational assessment
examples: The Wilcoxon rank-sum and Kruskal-Wallis comparisons in the study were performed on PFS values calculated with PerFit for each chatbot-by-instrument combination.

article_title: When Do Undergraduate Students Prefer AI? Insights into AI Scoring and Feedback
citation: Yildirim-Erbasli, S. N., Ilgun Dibek, M., Thomas, M. L., & Lesoway, N. (2026). When Do Undergraduate Students Prefer AI? Insights into AI Scoring and Feedback. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1196. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071196
title: Perceptions versus preferences as distinct constructs in student evaluation of AI assessment
description: The article distinguishes two constructs in how students respond to AI-based assessment. Perceptions are evaluative beliefs about the systems themselves: "Student perceptions refer to learners' evaluative beliefs and judgments regarding the characteristics of AI technologies, such as their usefulness, credibility, effectiveness, or fairness". Preferences, by contrast, capture "students' choices among alternative assessment arrangements, such as AI-generated scoring, human evaluation, or hybrid models". The framework draws on technology acceptance research and is used throughout the study to explain why positive perceptions of AI usefulness do not translate into preferences for AI authority in grading.
requirements: Both constructs must be measured separately; positive perceptions alone do not indicate preferred assessment arrangements.
constraints: The distinction is drawn for AI-based scoring and feedback in higher education assessment contexts.
target_learning_goals: understanding student acceptance of AI-based assessment and feedback
examples: The survey measured AI scoring perceptions, AI feedback perceptions, AI preferences, and AI-versus-human preferences as separate subscales with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.73 to 0.78.
key_sources: Yildirim-Erbasli, S. N., Ilgun Dibek, M., Thomas, M. L., & Lesoway, N. (2026). When Do Undergraduate Students Prefer AI? Insights into AI Scoring and Feedback. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1196. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071196

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Evaluate physical learning environments from a rigorous pedagogical perspective
description: The review's central recommendation is that evaluation of physical learning environments should be grounded more rigorously in pedagogy rather than relying on building-focused methods alone. As the authors put it, "an argument is put forward for the evaluation of physical learning environments from a more rigorous pedagogical perspective." This principle directs evaluators to judge learning spaces against contemporary teaching and learning approaches, not only against building performance criteria. It follows directly from the gaps the review identifies in existing evaluative approaches.
requirements: Evaluation frameworks must incorporate contemporary approaches to teaching and learning, not only building performance measures
constraints: Existing approaches, including POE-derived methods, are positioned as insufficient on their own for pedagogically rigorous evaluation
target_learners: Students in higher education and school learning environments
target_learning_goals: Aligning physical learning environment evaluation with pedagogical goals and contemporary teaching practices

article_title: The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature
citation: Topping, K.J. (1996). The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00138870
title: A typology of peer tutoring in further and higher education
description: The article provides a clear definition and typology of peer tutoring as an organizing framework for the field. It argues that "The increasing use of peer tutoring in this context necessitates a clear definition and typology, which are outlined", and the review is organized around "the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities". The typology serves to structure the review of effectiveness research across these varied formats.
requirements: A clear definition and typology of peer tutoring is needed to make sense of the increasing use of peer tutoring in further and higher education.

target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes supported through peer tutoring arrangements
examples: The review uses the typology to organize the substantial existing research on the effectiveness of the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities.

article_title: Improving learning achievements, motivations and problem-solving skills through a peer assessment-based game development approach
citation: Hwang, GJ., Hung, CM. & Chen, NS. (2014). Improving learning achievements, motivations and problem-solving skills through a peer assessment-based game development approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9320-7
title: Peer assessment-based game development approach for elementary science
description: An instructional approach in which students develop educational computer games and assess one another's work, proposed "for improving students' learning achievements, motivations and problem-solving skills." It was implemented in a science course at an elementary school, where the experimental group learned with it while a control group learned with the conventional game development approach. The approach pairs game construction activity with peer assessment as its distinguishing component.

constraints: Evaluated with sixth graders in an elementary school science course

learning motivation
problem-solving skills
examples: 82 sixth graders learned with the peer assessment-based game development approach while 85 learned with the conventional game development approach

citation: Elke Peters and Stuart Webb. (2018). INCIDENTAL VOCABULARY ACQUISITION THROUGH VIEWING L2 TELEVISION AND FACTORS THAT AFFECT LEARNING. Studies in Second Language Acquisition. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263117000407

As printed: "The experiment in this article earned an Open Materials badge for transparent practices. The materials are available at https://www.iris-database.org/iris/app/home/detail?id=york:933919." article_title: Peer Assessment Enhances Student Learning: The Results of a Matched Randomized Crossover Experiment in a College Statistics Class
citation: Sun DL, Harris N, Walther G, Baiocchi M (2015) Peer Assessment Enhances Student Learning: The Results of a Matched Randomized Crossover Experiment in a College Statistics Class. PLoS ONE 10(12): e0143177. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0143177
title: Use peer assessment not only where it is the only option, but also in smaller settings where individualized instructor feedback is feasible
description: Because peer assessment saves instructor time while also producing measured learning gains, the authors argue the usual cost-benefit tradeoff of educational interventions does not apply to it. They conclude that "peer assessment should not be limited to MOOCs and large classes where it is the only option, but that it has a place even in smaller settings where it is not strictly needed."
requirements: A workable peer assessment mechanism (e.g., a web-based tool that distributes responses to peer graders) and grading quality comparable to instructor grades.
constraints: The measured gains are small (d = .115 short term, d = .122 long term) and were established in one introductory statistics course.
target_learners: college students in classes of any size, including MOOC learners
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and problem solving
examples: In the study, treatment students graded three peers' homework and received feedback from three peers, with feedback timing and solution key held constant across treatment and control.
key_sources: Sun DL, Harris N, Walther G, Baiocchi M (2015) Peer Assessment Enhances Student Learning: The Results of a Matched Randomized Crossover Experiment in a College Statistics Class. PLoS ONE 10(12): e0143177. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0143177

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Peer assessment develops evaluative judgement most when students engage with criteria, and the provider of feedback may benefit more than the receiver
description: The paper argues peer assessment's formative purpose lies in exercising judgement: by engaging closely with criteria and standards and comparing work to them, students report better understanding of quality work. It notes that "the provider of the assessment may benefit more from the interaction than the receiver, as it is their judgement which is being exercised", and that judging others' work may reduce self-directed cognitive biases in self-assessment.
requirements: Orientation and discussion of criteria and the varieties of ways they may be applied, rather than peer review substituting for teacher marking
constraints: Peer assessment focused mainly on mark accuracy and grade contribution is identified as unlikely to develop evaluative judgement
target_learning_goals: judging quality of peers' work and transferring standards to one's own work
examples: The paper cites Nicol et al. (2014) case studies illustrating the power of peer review in developing evaluative capacity
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later
citation: W. Lewis Johnson & James C. Lester. (2015). Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0065-9
title: Pedagogical agents as autonomous characters cohabiting learning environments
description: The pedagogical agent concept, as formulated in the authors' 2000 article, conceptualizes agents as autonomous characters that cohabit learning environments with students to create rich, face-to-face learning interactions. The framework emphasizes the multimodal, visually embodied nature of agents and enumerates capabilities including interactive demonstrations, navigational guidance, gaze and gesture as attentional guides, nonverbal feedback, conversational signals, conveying and eliciting emotion, virtual teammates, and adaptive pedagogical interaction. The article traces how the concept evolved, with researchers dropping animated and extending the concept to static images, and how roles diversified into teachable agents, learning companions, and virtual role-players.
requirements: The choice of agent realization (animated, static image, or disembodied voice) depends on the educational context and the agent's role in that context
constraints: Relatively little work since 2000 on interactive demonstrations and navigational guidance, because most agents do not cohabit virtual worlds with learners
target_learners: training audiences in business, defense, intelligence, and healthcare
target_learning_goals: domain learning supported by interactive learning environments
cultural and language training
team training
examples: STEVE demonstrating interactive demonstrations and navigational guidance in virtual environments; Herman the Bug giving nonverbal feedback including cartwheels across the screen
key_sources: W. Lewis Johnson & James C. Lester. (2015). Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0065-9

article_title: Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms
citation: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479
title: PERTS 15-item academic mindset survey with four subscales
description: The Project for Educational Research That Scales (PERTS) instrument is a Likert-style self-report scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 6 = Strongly Agree) with 15 items in four subscales: individual mindset (3 items, reverse scored), sense of belonging in the classroom (4 items), task relevance (4 items), and self-efficacy on classroom tasks (4 items). Reliabilities printed in the article were .820 (belonging), .830 (self-efficacy), .820 (task relevance), and .772 (individual mindset). The scale is widely used in testing academic mindset interventions at the classroom level and has strong face validity in large-scale studies.
requirements: Internal reliability above Chronbach's alpha > .80 is the article's cited acceptable level (Nunnally, 1978); individual mindset at .772 falls below it
constraints: Individual mindset subscale reliability (.772) is below the .80 criterion the article cites
target_learning_goals: measuring classroom academic mindset psycho-social constructs
examples: Used with 2,908 students in a rural district for LCAP data collection

article_title: Neural evidence for enhanced attention to mistakes among school-aged children with a growth mindset
citation: Schroder Hans S., Fisher Megan E., Lin Yanli, Lo Sharon L., Danovitch Judith H., Moser Jason S. (2017). Neural evidence for enhanced attention to mistakes among school-aged children with a growth mindset. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2017.01.004
title: Pe as an index of attention allocation to errors within the mindset nomological network
description: The article treats the error positivity (Pe), an ERP peaking 200–500 ms after errors, as indexing "conscious error awareness and attention allocation to errors". It interprets enlarged Pe among growth-minded children as neural evidence for two mindset-theory predictions: that growth-minded children view errors as more motivationally relevant events and expend more cognitive resources processing and adjusting after mistakes. The Pe is distinguished from the earlier, automatic ERN and likened to the P3b, an ERP component reflecting mobilization of attentional resources to motivationally relevant task events.
requirements: ERP measurement during an error-monitoring task with sufficient error trials for reliable Pe estimation
constraints: The authors note the alternative emotional-responsivity interpretation of the Pe has not been well supported, and the attention-allocation reading in children is their interpretation, with engagement vs. disengagement across development left as an open question
target_learning_goals: resilient response to mistakes and errors during learning
examples: The study recorded ERPs while 123 children completed a zoo-animal go/no-go task, finding larger Pe difference waves among growth-minded children
key_sources: Schroder Hans S., Fisher Megan E., Lin Yanli, Lo Sharon L., Danovitch Judith H., Moser Jason S. (2017). Neural evidence for enhanced attention to mistakes among school-aged children with a growth mindset. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2017.01.004

article_title: Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? A Review of Studies into the Relationship Between Oral Communicative Competence and Sociometric Status in Childhood
citation: Femke van der Wilt, Chiel van der Veen, Claudia van Kruistum, Bert van Oers (2019). Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? A Review of Studies into the Relationship Between Oral Communicative Competence and Sociometric Status in Childhood. Educational Psychology Review (2019) 31:699–724. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09479-z
title: Peer nomination procedure for assessing children's sociometric status
description: The peer nomination procedure, developed by Moreno and adapted by Coie et al. (1982), asks children to nominate up to three peers they like and three they dislike. Nominations are used to compute acceptance, rejection, social impact, and social preference, which in turn create the sociometric groups (popular, rejected, neglected, controversial, average). The review reports it is "a reliable and valid method for measuring children 's social position", used in 16 of the 25 reviewed studies, and recommends it remain part of future studies.
requirements: Peer nominations are easy to administer and not time-consuming; they rely on the judgements of peers, who provide unique information on children's behavior
constraints: Reporting on friendships requires verbal skills that younger preschool children often lack, which motivated Nærland's observation-based alternative
target_learners: children aged 1 to 12 years, including young children aged 2 to 5
target_learning_goals: measurement of children's sociometric status within the peer group
examples: Burleson et al. (1992) asked first- and third graders to nominate classmates for four roles and computed standardized social preference and social impact indices

article_title: The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention
citation: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037
title: Perception–action affordance account of situated creativity
description: The article proposes that creativity is situated: creative behaviour emerges from detecting alternative action affordances within the common affordance structures of everyday objects, building on Gibson's ecological approach. An "affordance is defined as the match between what a person currently is able to and interested in, on the one hand, and the relevant properties of the physical environment that trigger and enable particular actions of the person, on the other hand". Detecting uncommon uses requires isolating, foregrounding, and recombining nested subordinate affordances, a process in which selective attention plays a central role.
requirements: Individuals must be able to perceptually or imaginatively isolate nested subordinate affordances and object properties from the fixed structure of common affordances
constraints: The study's own findings ran counter to the hypothesis that a high stimulus environment supports creativity, and the authors state the results "do not support the perception–action view on creativity we proposed" in its strong form
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creative idea generation
examples: The study operationalised the account with a real-object Alternative Uses Task in low and high stimulus conditions, with selective attention measured by the TEA-Ch Sky Search task
key_sources: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Perennial versus contextual skills distinction for 21st century capabilities
description: The chapter distinguishes "perennial" skills, valuable throughout history such as collaboration, from "contextual" skills unique to the new millennium, such as rapidly filtering huge amounts of incoming data. Perennial skills rise in importance and sophistication in the 21st century, while contextual skills are "novel in history as a valuable capability" and thus new in type. Contextual skills are typically absent from the legacy 20th century curriculum, making the distinction important for deciding what schooling must newly add.
requirements: Requires articulating what to deemphasize in an already crowded curriculum to make room for core 21st century understandings
constraints: Contextual skills are typically not part of the legacy curriculum inherited from 20th century educational systems
target_learning_goals: 21st century work and citizenship capabilities
examples: Collaboration is presented as perennial but growing in importance; filtering signal from noise in data floods is presented as contextual and new in type
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment
citation: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844
title: Three-category taxonomy of peer assessment tools: generic, domain-specific, and context-specific systems
description: The review classifies online peer assessment tools into three categories based on their design scope. Generic systems are "designed to be highly configurable and support peer review activities in a wide range of disciplines and contexts." Domain-specific systems target a particular artefact type such as essays or programming code. Context-specific systems were "written for use in a specific course and must be rewritten if they are to accommodate other contexts." This taxonomy organises the review's analysis of features across tools.
requirements: Tools must have been designed specifically for supporting peer assessment activities and used in at least one course
constraints: Excludes tools for reviewing individual contributions to teams, standard communication software repurposed for peer review, unimplemented proposals, and conference management tools
target_learning_goals: peer assessment skills
formative feedback literacy
critical evaluation of peers' work
examples: PeerGrader, Web-SPA, OPAS, CeLS, PRAISE and Aropa are classified as generic; CPR, C.A.P., SWoRD and PeerWise as domain-specific; Peers, NetPeas, OASYS, Wolfe and PEARS as context-specific
key_sources: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Theoretical mechanisms of peer assessment: reflexive cognition, feedback quality, and social constructivist accounts
description: The review proposes that peer assessment is reflexive — "learning by assessing" — engaging assessors in reviewing, summarizing, clarifying, diagnosing misconceived knowledge and identifying missing knowledge, which are cognitively demanding and could consolidate understanding. For assessees, negotiated criteria clarify what constitutes high-quality work, and peer feedback offers greater immediacy, frequency and volume that compensate for lower quality. Theoretically it draws on social constructivism, Vygotskian scaffolded learning and purposeful communication, and Piagetian cognitive conflict for reciprocal same-ability assessment. The review cautions that direct tests of these hypothesized mechanisms are still scarce.
requirements: Assessors should be trained to question, prompt, and scaffold rather than merely supply a notionally right answer
constraints: Establishing a single overarching theory is difficult given the multiplicity of subject specialties; direct tests of mechanism hypotheses are scarce; feedback is useful only when recipients act upon it
target_learners: higher education students acting as assessors and assessees
target_learning_goals: cognitive and metacognitive gains, affective benefits, social and transferable skills
examples: The review reports that simple summative, correctional, or didactic feedback is associated with much lower effect sizes than open-ended, suggestive, and formative feedback
key_sources: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249

article_title: Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age
citation: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age. International journal of speech-language pathology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3094718/
title: Parents’ Evaluation of Aural/oral performance of Children (PEACH) questionnaire
description: The PEACH is an interview-administered parent questionnaire for assessing children’s functional performance in everyday life based on parents’ observations. The article describes it as "applicable for assessing children with hearing loss ranging from mild to profound degrees whose age ranges from 4 weeks to 18 years" and reports it was reliable for evaluating amplification effectiveness in real life. In this study, children’s performance was expressed as deviation from age-appropriate means, and PEACH scores correlated significantly with standardized language measures.
requirements: Administered as an interview with parents; uses normative data and critical differences (Ching & Hill, 2007) to relate performance to normal-hearing peers.
constraints: Performance expressed relative to normative data; applicable across mild to profound hearing loss.
target_learners: children with hearing loss aged 4 weeks to 18 years
target_learning_goals: evaluating aural/oral communicative functioning in everyday life
examples: Used with 61 parents of 3-year-old children in the LOCHI study; mean age-corrected score was −23.5.

article_title: Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School
citation: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015
title: Two-type classification of dysgraphia: perceptual and motor dysgraphia
description: The article presents dysgraphia, described per the American Psychiatric Association (2013) as a neurodevelopmental specific learning disorder of written expression, as classifiable into two types. It states "The dysgraphia can be further classified into two types: the perceptual and motor dysgraphia". Perceptual dysgraphia is a difficulty where the student "cannot make the relationship between the symbolic system and spellings that represent sounds, words and phrases", while in motor dysgraphia students "can speak and read, but find difficulties in fine motor skills to write letters, words and numbers". The study uses this framing to interpret grade-level handwriting deficits.
requirements: Classification presupposes assessment separating perceptual (symbol-sound mapping) from motor (fine-motor letter production) components of written expression.
constraints: The article attributes the DSM-5 framing to the American Psychiatric Association (2013) and the two-type distinction to Martins et al. (2013); it reports no test of the taxonomy itself.
target_learners: elementary school students in literacy instruction
target_learning_goals: handwriting and written expression skills
examples: The study interprets 1st-grade dysgraphia as reflecting deficits in visual-motor integration skills as students begin exposure to print and writing demands.
key_sources: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015

article_title: Ecocultural patterns of family engagement among low-income Latino families of preschool children.
citation: McWayne, C. M., Melzi, G., Limlingan, M. C., & Schick, A. (2016). Ecocultural Patterns of Family Engagement among Low-income Latino Families of Preschool Children. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0040343
title: PEFL parent-report measure of Latino family engagement with four dimensions
description: The Parental Engagement of Families from Latino Backgrounds / Participación Educativa de Familias Latinas is a 65-item parent-report measure developed from qualitative focus-group data with low-income Latino Head Start families. "The first three factors described below represent home-based engagement and are believed to reflect cultural values and socio-economic realities of low-income, Latino families living in the United States": Foundational Education (20 items, α = 0.73), Supplemental Education (12 items, α = 0.77), and Future-oriented Teaching (3 items, α = 0.63), plus School Participation (8 items, α = 0.77). Items are rated on a four-point Likert-type scale from Never to Frequently.
requirements: Parent-report administration in the caregiver's preferred language (Spanish or English versions)
constraints: The Future-Oriented Teaching factor's alpha reliability was lower than the others due to the small number of items, and the article urges caution interpreting that dimension
target_learners: Low-income Latino primary caregivers of Head Start preschool children
target_learning_goals: Measuring culturally-contextualized family engagement across home- and school-based dimensions
examples: Used to derive latent engagement profiles in this study's 650-caregiver Head Start sample

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Agent-characteristic moderator taxonomy: appearance, gender, nonverbal communication, motion, and voice
description: The article organizes its meta-analytic tests around a set of agent characteristics that "may moderate their instructional effectiveness, including appearance, gender, nonverbal communication, motion, and voice." This five-branch taxonomy structures which agent design features were hypothesized (by cognitive load theory, cognitive theory of multimedia learning, computers are social actors, social agency theory, uncanny valley, and the action observation network) to change instructional effectiveness, and it frames the moderator analyses reported for the pooled effect sizes.
requirements: Used when designing or evaluating on-screen pedagogical agents in multimedia environments, where each characteristic can be varied independently.
constraints: The meta-analysis found most of these characteristics, except dimensionality (2D vs. 3D), appeared not to moderate effectiveness.
target_learning_goals: Selection of pedagogical agent design features for multimedia instruction
examples: The meta-analysis of 32 effect sizes tested predictions of six theories against these five agent characteristics.

article_title: The Social and Technological Dimensions of Scaffolding and Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity
citation: Roy D. Pea. (2004). The Social and Technological Dimensions of Scaffolding and Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(3), pp.423-451. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190619
title: Scaffolding is theorized as having both social and technological dimensions relevant to learning, education, and human activity
description: The article's title frames scaffolding as a theoretical concept with two named dimensions — the social and the technological — and situates it among 'Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity'. The article thus treats scaffolding not as a purely interpersonal instructional move but as a construct whose analysis spans both human social interaction and technological tools, within the learning sciences. The supplied text is a repository metadata record, so this characterization rests on the article's own printed title and keyword metadata.
requirements: The framework addresses scaffolding together with related theoretical concepts, rather than scaffolding in isolation, as stated in the article's title.
constraints: Scope is stated as learning, education, and human activity generally, per the article's title.
target_learners: Learners across educational settings, per the article's stated scope of learning, education, and human activity
target_learning_goals: Understanding of scaffolding as a theoretical construct in the learning sciences
examples: The article appeared in The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 2004, 13(3), pp.423-451, and is archived in the TELEARN collection of the HAL open archive.
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (2004). The Social and Technological Dimensions of Scaffolding and Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(3), pp.423-451. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190619

article_title: Sharing Solutions: Persistence and Grounding in Multimodal Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, David Traum. (2006). Sharing solutions: persistence and grounding in multi-modal collaborative problem solving. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 15 (1), pp.121-151. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327809jls1501_9
title: Persistence as an interpretive framework for media use in multimodal collaborative problem solving
description: The article interprets its multimodal collaboration findings through the concept of persistence: information of differing persistence is routed to media of matching persistence. In the studied setting, a shared whiteboard and a MOO text chat were examined, and "More persistent information is exchanged through the more persistent medium." The framework explains why "The whiteboard was used as a shared memory rather than a grounding tool," linking media properties to grounding behavior in collaborative problem solving.
requirements: At least two media differing in persistence available to collaborating partners
constraints: Interprets results of one exploratory study of whiteboard-plus-MOO collaboration; the article frames it as exploratory
target_learners: Collaborative problem solvers in computer-mediated learning environments
target_learning_goals: Grounding of shared information during collaborative problem solving
examples: The exploratory study examined a shared whiteboard and a MOO environment with a text chat facility and found chat used for grounding whiteboard content

article_title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, Fabrice Hong. (2008). The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://hal.science/hal-00692019
title: Perturbation model of CSCL macro script design
description: The article proposes a pedagogical model for designing collaboration scripts in which the script's core action is perturbation: "a script disturbs the natural convergence of a team and in doing so increases the intensity of interaction required between team members". The nature of the perturbation determines which interaction types (argumentation, explanation, regulation) become necessary, giving designers a lever for targeting interaction quality.
requirements: A collaborative task completed by a team whose members would otherwise converge naturally without the script
target_learners: students working in collaborative learning teams
target_learning_goals: knowledge-productive interactions such as argumentation, explanations and mutual regulation
examples: The model is illustrated using three scripts described in the article

article_title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
citation: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750
title: A pedagogical framework built from what it takes to learn, used to challenge digital technologies
description: The article proposes using knowledge of learning to construct a pedagogical framework against which digital technologies can be evaluated and challenged. The abstract states: "The argument put forward in this paper is to use what we know about what it takes to learn, and build this into a pedagogical framework with which to challenge digital technologies to deliver a genuinely enhanced learning experience." The framework functions as an evaluative lens derived from learning theory; the article's keywords include "conversational framework", "learning theory" and "pedagogy", indicating the framework's grounding in the author's conversational framework tradition.
requirements: The framework must be built from established knowledge about what it takes to learn.
constraints: The framework is intended to challenge technologies to enhance learning, not to describe the technologies themselves; technologies are rarely designed with teaching and learning in mind.
target_learning_goals: enhanced learning experience through pedagogically challenged technology design
examples: The paper applies the framework to collaborative technologies that enable learners to share and exchange ideas and digital products.

article_title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic computer-supported collaborative learning environments in schools
citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Pentad-based coding scheme (P, S, T, CS, CL) for classifying authentic CSCL designs
description: The article operationalizes sociocultural design variation with a coding scheme crossing the pentad facets: Participants (P0 teacher, P1 non-authentic practitioners, P2 authentic practitioners), Setting (S0 classroom, S1 non-authentic settings, S2 authentic settings), Time (T0 educational timeframe, T1 authentic timeframe limited by educational timeframe), Computer support (CS0/CS1), and Collaborative learning (CL0-CL2). The scheme "help differentiate between the facets of the pentad in traditional schooling (non-authentic designs), designs for authenticity, and participation in current cultures," giving researchers one shared language across design types.
requirements: Codes for participants and setting are additions to the teacher role; a teacher counts as P2 only if being a practitioner is an intentional part of the design
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers of authentic learning environments
target_learning_goals: analyzing and classifying designs for authenticity
examples: Case descriptions in Table 5 use codes such as P0S0T0CL1 with CS1 for Knowledge Forum-based knowledge building

article_title: Toward a Taxonomy: Insights from the 2025 CSCL paradigm building workshop
citation: Simon, S., Şener, B., Greisel, M., Pifarré Turmo, M., Borchers, C., Chernikova, O., Shahrokhian, B., Tajik, E., Sitjà Martín, M., Čarapina, M., Hu, X., & Ataş, A. H. (2026). Toward a Taxonomy: Insights from the 2025 CSCL paradigm building workshop. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09477-8
title: A dimensional map of CSCL theory diversity: perspective diversity and loci of collaborative learning observation
description: The workshop group described two axes of theoretical diversity in CSCL. Perspective diversity means different theories examine different aspects of the same collaborative learning situation, illustrated with Actor-Network Theory, Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, and cognitive load theory. Dimensional diversity concerns where collaborative learning can be observed: "inside the learner, focusing on individual cognition and learning processes", outside the learner in designed contexts and tools, or both stances together, with a further dimension of level of analysis ranging from the individual to communities and platforms.
requirements: The group noted the ongoing challenge of assuring that these theories complement each other rather than compete
constraints: The frameworks are presented "without claiming exhaustiveness", illustrating rather than enumerating all theoretical perspectives
target_learning_goals: Categorizing and connecting CSCL theories
Developing a holistic vision of collaborative learning across levels of analysis
examples: Links between internal cognition and interactional meaning-making, and bridges between micro-level group dynamics and macro-level sociocultural transformations, were cited as exemplars of connecting theories

article_title: Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning
citation: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285.
title: In early problem-based curriculum years, peer tutors can substitute for staff tutors without achievement loss
description: Because peer tutors were rated higher on supportive behaviors in the first year and no achievement difference was found there, problem-based curricula can deploy student tutors in early years where staff are reluctant to tutor. Staff reluctance arises because lecturing "is not in high demand in tutorial groups". The advantage erodes as the curriculum advances and subject-matter expertise matters more.
requirements: Student tutors should themselves have experienced problem-based learning, so they are sensitive to tutorial groups' needs in support, information and guidance
constraints: Applicable to the first curriculum year only; staff-tutored groups achieved significantly better overall, and staff were rated higher in years 2-4
target_learners: First-year higher education students in problem-based health sciences curricula
target_learning_goals: Small-group problem explanation, self-directed learning goal setting
examples: In the field experiment, 400 tutorial groups guided by student tutors were compared with 334 guided by staff tutors across 98 courses

article_title: How to design and evaluate personalized scaffolds for self-regulated learning
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Mladen Raković, Yizhou Fan, Lyn Lim, Shaveen Singh, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Inge Molenaar. (2023). How to design and evaluate personalized scaffolds for self-regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09361-y
title: Personalize scaffolds based on learners' actual SRL processes detected in real time, removing options the learner has already executed.
description: The article recommends personalizing scaffold content to the self-regulated learning processes a student has actually executed, detected in real time from log data. Personalization works by removing any suggested option already performed, so scaffolds become more directive and less cognitively demanding. The authors state: "We, therefore, recommend personalizing scaffolds based on learners' SRL processes." In their study this changed learning behavior: students in the personalized condition generally showed the most monitoring and high cognition while receiving fewer suggestions than the generalized condition.
requirements: Real-time detection of SRL processes from unobtrusive log data, with rules for each scaffold option determining whether the associated process was already executed
constraints: Personalization was built on prior work in the same task and context; the article recommends first getting a thorough understanding of actual SRL in a specific context before developing a support system
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during reading and essay writing
examples: In the personalized condition, the option of checking the learning goal and instruction was not displayed when students spent at least five seconds on the instruction page

article_title: Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4
title: Teaching should be personalized to respond to children's individual learning needs rather than one-size-fits-all
description: The article argues that acknowledging genetic influences on learning differences supports teaching that recognizes children's inherent heterogeneity in abilities, skills, and interests. It states that effective teaching must be "personalized" to respond to and remediate children's vastly different, individual learning needs, rather than applying "one-size-fits-all" pedagogical approaches. Existing differentiated practices such as individual education plans for students with SEND are cited as partial implementations.
requirements: Teaching must respond to and remediate children's vastly different, individual learning needs, recognizing inherent heterogeneity in abilities, skills, and interests
constraints: While teachers strongly and unanimously endorse the principles of personalized learning, the practical implementation of corresponding pedagogies within current schools and education settings remains difficult
target_learners: school pupils, including students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND)
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes through instruction tailored to individual learning needs
examples: The article cites individual education plans supporting students with SEND to monitor their learning progress, and notes that in 2022, 17% of UK pupils received support for SEND, including 4% taught according to personalized education, health, and care plans.
key_sources: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4

article_title: Interventions to Teacher Well-Being and Burnout A Scoping Review
citation: Pauliina Avola, Tiina Soini-Ikonen, Anne Jyrkiäinen, Viivi Pentikäinen. (2025). Interventions to Teacher Well-Being and Burnout A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09986-2
title: PERMA-H model of positive psychology as a unifying framework for teacher well-being intervention research
description: The PERMA-H model is Seligman's multidimensional well-being theory, "later expanded to include physical health (H) by Norrish et al. (2013)", comprising positive emotions (P), engagement (E), relationships (R), meaning (M), accomplishment (A) and health (H). The review applies it to unify the heterogeneous field of teacher well-being intervention research, mapping 43 of 46 interventions' contents onto its elements. Alignment was broadest for engagement, positive emotions, relationships and health, with no intervention content identified for meaning or accomplishment.
requirements: Interventions must have describable content activities that can be interpreted as similar to one or more PERMA-H elements; the review created an O (other) category for interventions without clear connections to the model
constraints: The review found no intervention contents related to meaning (M) or accomplishment (A), and three studies showed no PERMA-H alignment at all
Alignment was the reviewers' interpretation of similarity, not the original studies' deliberate use of the framework
target_learners: Teachers across educational domains from early childhood education to higher academia
target_learning_goals: Teacher well-being and flourishing
Prevention of teacher burnout and ill-being
examples: The review classified interventions aligned with P as focused on emotional skills, E on mindfulness, R on interaction or classroom management, A on goal setting or self-leadership, and H on physical well-being
key_sources: Pauliina Avola, Tiina Soini-Ikonen, Anne Jyrkiäinen, Viivi Pentikäinen. (2025). Interventions to Teacher Well-Being and Burnout A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09986-2

article_title: Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review
citation: Melanie Turner, Flaviu A. Hodis. (2025). Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10016-4
title: Three-level personality hierarchy with bottom-up (and optionally top-down) change frameworks guiding conscientiousness interventions
description: The review organizes personality change around a hierarchy of trait, habit/habit-building, and state levels, noting that "Change can manifest at any of the three levels of personality hierarchy: trait, habit/habit-building, and states". Bottom-up frameworks (TESSERA; Sociogenomic theory) hold that accumulated changes in state expressions become habitual and integrated into self-concept, producing trait change; the General (Common) Change Factors model adds top-down processes via four mechanisms: discrepancy awareness, strengths orientation, insight, and practice. All 11 reviewed interventions used a bottom-up approach, and 55% also theorized top-down processes.
requirements: Interventions require theoretical grounding to identify specific targets (e.g., trait-relevant behaviors, habits, or state expressions) and to explain how state-level change leads to trait change
constraints: The review states that not all short-term changes in personality states lead to changes in the corresponding trait; only habitualized, integrated changes do
target_learning_goals: strengthening conscientiousness (industriousness, orderliness, impulse control) to support learning, achievement, and well-being
examples: The reviewed digital coaching interventions were guided by the General (Common) Change Factors framework; behavior activation interventions by Behavior Activation theory; in-person coaching by the Stepwise process, GROW model, and Intentional Change theory
key_sources: Melanie Turner, Flaviu A. Hodis. (2025). Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10016-4

article_title: Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations
citation: Krijnen, M. A., Wansink, B. G. J., van den Berg, Y. H. M., van Tartwijk, J., & Mainhard, T. (2024). Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09870-5
title: Peer nomination (sociometric) methodology for assessing classroom citizenship behaviors and relationships
description: Peer nomination methods ask children to nominate classmates on behavioral and affective items, so that "children act as multiple observers of classmates' typical behaviors and of their relationships with others." Behavioral items describe interpersonal behavior (e.g., who helps others) and affective items capture relationships (e.g., whom classmates like most). The review proposes this approach as a systematic, quantitative complement to self-report measures in citizenship research, mapping classroom social dynamics into a social network.
requirements: Peer group of classmates who observe each other regularly; nomination items for behaviors and affective relationships
constraints: The review notes equating low aggression with peace is arguably too simplistic, and nominations may reflect perceivers' biases
target_learning_goals: Assessing enacted solidarity, peace, and social cohesion in the classroom
examples: The review's Fig. 1 example: child A nominated by 11 classmates for helping, child B by 1, with a classroom density of 0.32

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Perturbation-based framework: structured interventions as diagnostic probes of cognitive architecture
description: The article advances a framework in which interventions that alter physiological or motivational states in predictable ways serve as diagnostic tools for probing the organization of cognitive systems, analogous to lesion studies and pharmacological or stimulation manipulations. Its core inferential logic is that "What unites these approaches is not the severity of the manipulation, but its structured nature." When constructs change in parallel, shared mechanisms are implicated; when they decouple, claims of functional unity are weakened. Null effects and selective effects are both treated as theoretically informative outputs of this framework.
requirements: Perturbations must alter broad physiological or motivational states in predictable ways so researchers can observe which cognitive functions covary and which remain stable
constraints: Frequentist null effects do not constitute affirmative evidence for invariance; the framework's inferences require methodologically sound conditions where change would otherwise be plausible
target_learning_goals: understanding how executive processes are recruited and expressed during instruction
examples: The commentary interprets Zhang et al. (2026)'s dissociation between a mathematics-specific negative priming task and the Flanker task through this framework, with the logic summarized schematically in Fig. 1.
key_sources: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Two goal-relative criteria — specification and assessment demand — locate operations on a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum
description: The framework supplies criteria applicable before instruction for classifying cognitive operations relative to a learning goal. The specification criterion asks whether the operation or its reasoning is named in the learning goal or its underlying standard; the assessment-demand criterion asks whether the criterion assessment, an unaided task at a delay, would require the learner to perform the operation or its equivalent. These yield a graded quantity, constitutive weight, with erosion risk rising monotonically in that weight. The learner's developmental status is kept separate, modulating how much practice a given learner still needs without changing the classification.
requirements: Explicit specification of the learning goal, which the article treats as an instructional design act
Measurement of learners' prior competence on constitutive operations before instruction to set the level of protection each operation warrants
constraints: Classification is goal-relative: the same content can be peripheral in one context and constitutive in another
target_learning_goals: Constructing and justifying models, solutions, and proofs within specified learning goals
examples: In a bacterial-growth modeling task, selecting and justifying a model family and interpreting fitted parameters are constitutive by both criteria, while entering data and writing up are peripheral
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Peripheral–constitutive mapping across STEM disciplines: routine operations tend to augment, generating the disciplinary product itself unprocessed tends to erode
description: Table 1 maps the peripheral–constitutive distinction across mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, and engineering at the level of typical focal learning targets. For each discipline it lists the constitutive process (e.g., constructing and justifying a solution method in mathematics; designing an algorithm in computer science), peripheral offloads that tend to augment (routine arithmetic, unit conversion, boilerplate syntax), and constitutive offloads that tend to erode when unprocessed (generating the solution method, mechanism, or design rationale itself). The distinction is graded and goal-relative, not content-intrinsic.
requirements: Application of the specification and assessment-demand criteria within each discipline cell
A specified focal learning target for the activity
constraints: Whether an offload is peripheral or constitutive is defined relative to the focal learning target, not by the content as such; a mastered process may be peripheral for acquisition but sustained non-exercise can still erode maintenance
target_learners: STEM learners across mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, and engineering
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary practices such as modeling, mechanism proposal, algorithm design, and design reasoning under constraint
examples: In mathematics, offloading routine arithmetic tends to augment while generating the solution method or proof itself unprocessed tends to erode

article_title: How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning
citation: Glaser, M., Lengyel, D., Toulouse, C., & Schwan, S. (2022). How Do We Deal with Uncertain Information? Effects of Verbal and Visual Expressions of Uncertainty on Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1097–1131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09659-4
title: Pergamon multimedia learning environment with temple reconstructions and uncertainty expressions
description: A computer-based, linear learning environment about the ancient city Pergamon used as the study material. Participants worked through "a computer-based, linear learning environment about the ancient city Pergamon and two of its most important buildings—the temple of Athena and the temple of Demeter", including pictures of reconstructions with audio explanations in which lexical hedges expressed uncertainty values of twelve architectural elements per temple, each with a scientific justification. Four picture conditions varied the uncertainty visualization: none, stop light colors, geometric contrast, or both combined.
requirements: Audio explanations with the reconstructions had to be played in full length and could not be paused; navigation backwards was not possible
constraints: Uncertainty values and their verbal scientific justifications were fictional, created for experimental reasons
target_learners: Adult participants from a broad variety of disciplines without archeology, history, or architecture background
target_learning_goals: Memory for architectural elements, uncertainty values, and their scientific justifications
examples: Lexical hedges ranged from "maybe" (uncertain) through "highly probable" (medium) to "definitely" (certain)

description: Personal investment theory is the framework with which McInerney and colleagues studied student motivation across cultures; a chapter he co-authored is titled "Personal investment theory: A cross-cultural framework for the study of student motivation". The tribute lists it among his scholarly contributions and lists "Personal investment theory" as a keyword of the article, positioning it as the vehicle for capturing cross-cultural universality and variability in motivation.

article_title: Peer Mindset Culture as a Developmental Context for Belonging
citation: Eunjin Seo, Margarett Clapper, Cameron A. Hecht, Robert Crosnoe, David S. Yeager. (2025). Peer Mindset Culture as a Developmental Context for Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10082-8
title: Peer mindset culture framework: two pathways linking fixed-mindset peer norms to belonging
description: The article proposes that peer mindset culture—"peers' shared beliefs about whether ability is fixed or can grow"—functions as a developmental context shaping adolescent belonging. Drawing on the Many Questions of Belonging and Integrative Framework of Belonging perspectives, it maps two broad pathways: identity threat and reduced opportunities for connection. Within these, five empirically testable mechanisms are proposed: stereotype threat, mindset-culture mismatch, social contagion, peer selection, and low social support, each with stated applicability to particular student populations.
requirements: The five mechanisms are proposed as illustrative and testable, not exhaustive or mutually exclusive
constraints: The mechanisms are currently theoretical and require rigorous testing to establish their validity and impact
The pathways are not necessarily equally potent, nor are they exhaustive
target_learners: adolescents and early adulthood students in academic settings
target_learning_goals: sense of belonging in learning environments
examples: Figure 1 presents the proposed mediation model of peer mindset culture and belonging; Table 1 defines the five mechanisms and their applicability

article_title: Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers’ Wellbeing: A Systematic Review
citation: Rhoda Lai, Jennifer Southam, Luella Mageean, Sue Roffey, Kelly-Ann Allen. (2026). Associations Between Teacher-Student Relationship Quality and Middle and Secondary School Teachers' Wellbeing: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10107-2
title: PERMA model as a framework for teacher wellbeing in the review
description: The PERMA model posits that wellbeing is built on five main elements: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment (Seligman, 2011). The review used it to structure its synthesis because it captures both hedonic and eudaimonic elements and, per Hone et al. (2014), "demonstrated the highest level of correlation to each of the other theories" among positive psychology wellbeing theories. The review widened wellbeing definition to include each PERMA facet beyond stress and burnout.
requirements: Studies must report at least one PERMA element or its opposite (e.g., negative emotions) as a wellbeing outcome.
constraints: The review does not explore links between clinically relevant symptoms or diagnoses of ill mental health and teacher-student relationships; elements of other theories such as self-esteem and social contribution are not treated as wellbeing components.
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
teacher-student relationship quality
examples: The review classified each included study's wellbeing measures by PERMA element (e.g., MBI for emotions, work enthusiasm scales for engagement, efficacy scales for accomplishment).

article_title: Testing the Relative Universalism of Psychological Theories: A Person-Centered Analysis of Control-Value Theory
citation: Dirk Tempelaar · Alexandra Niculescu. (2026). Testing the Relative Universalism of Psychological Theories: A Person-Centered Analysis of Control-Value Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10155-2
title: Person-centered analysis (latent profile analysis) as a framework for testing the relative universalism of psychological theories
description: The article proposes testing a theory's relative universalism—functional forms invariant while parameter magnitudes vary—by combining latent profile analysis with within-profile structural equation modeling. Person-centered methods, following Howard and Hoffman (2018), "balance both" parsimony and specificity by "grouping individuals into relatively homogeneous subpopulations while maintaining analytical tractability," addressing the homogeneity condition of ergodicity for static cross-sectional models. Four pre-specified criteria operationalize the test: functional-form invariance, sign stability, bounded magnitude flexibility, and contextual robustness after covariates. The framework is offered as replicable for other educational-psychology theories.
requirements: Large samples, since mixture modeling methods are described as data-intensive and require large samples
Integration of person-centered subgroup identification with variable-centered model testing, since identifying profiles alone does not test theory-driven relations
constraints: Person-centered methods do not address the stationarity condition of ergodicity, which the authors deem non-critical for static theories like CVT
Cross-sectional data mean all reported associations are predictive rather than causal
Within-profile variance restriction can mechanically attenuate standardized coefficients and R2
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions in learning processes
motivation and engagement
examples: Applied to 14,534 first-year business and economics students, the framework identified five emotion profiles and showed CVT relations hold across demographic groupings but partially diverge across profiles
