article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Two-step person-centered approach: latent profile analysis of learner characteristics followed by BCH-based modeling of profile-by-intervention interactions
description: The article proposes moving "the focus of analysis from the interactions of single variables to entire persons and their characteristic constellation of learning prerequisites". In step one, learners are grouped by latent profile analysis, chosen because it is "a model-based clustering approach" allowing measurement-error-corrected estimates. In step two, profiles are related to instructional parameters via the manual BCH approach, which "enables relating latent profiles to any parameters that can be modeled in the framework of structural equation modeling". Grouping many learners into few categories helps achieve high statistical power while capturing multivariate, potentially non-linear information.
requirements: Learner characteristics that presumably interact with instructional effects must be measurable on multiple indicator variables and grouped via latent profile analysis or similar model-based clustering
Instructional parameters must be assessed so profiles can be related to treatment effects in a structural equation modeling framework
constraints: The study is exploratory and not pre-registered; inference relies on 90% confidence intervals rather than significance testing
Very small profiles (poor readers, about 16 students in the subsample) cannot support reliable differential-effectiveness estimates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
differential effectiveness of instruction across learner profiles
examples: Applied to German third-grade reading instruction: profiles of decoding, syntactic comprehension, vocabulary, and pretest reading comprehension were related to teachers' instructional foci over one school year
key_sources: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: Person × Task × Circumstances perspective extends MASRL and information processing SRL models to the learner's broader ecological system
description: The article extends Efklides' MASRL model and Winne and Hadwin's personal and task affordances and constraints "to a Person × Task × Circumstances perspective." It applies Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, mapping the intraindividual system, microsystem, exosystem, and macrosystem around a focal learning task, building on the authors' earlier integrated SRL (iSRL) model. This captures idiosyncratic affordances and constraints learners appraise when engaging a task within their larger learning ecosystem.
requirements: Modeling requires mapping internal and external conditions at layers of the ecological system relative to the focal task
constraints: The article notes contemporary SRL models' constrained focus enabled online behavioral measures; the broadened view is a theoretical proposal, not an empirically validated model
target_learners: Learners across ecological contexts, including those facing poverty, crisis, or disrupted environments
target_learning_goals: Representing task context comprehensively in models of self-regulated learning
examples: Figure 2 depicts the ecological system of the learner, with distal systems exerting depleting or replenishing effects on students' limited resources to self-regulate in a learning task
key_sources: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5

article_title: Learning scientific concepts through material and social activities: Conversational analysis meets conceptual change
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572
title: A sociocultural framework informed by conversation analysis explains conceptual change through meaning negotiation and appropriation
description: The article describes a sociocultural framework for learning scientific concepts that is informed by studies of conversation analysis. Within this framework, "meaning negotiation and appropriation are identified as mechanisms for achieving such conceptual change" — that is, learners' conceptual change in scientific thinking is explained by social and material processes of negotiating meanings in activity and appropriating them. The framework is offered as a bridge between macrosocial theories of cultural learning and microanalytic details of situated human learning activities.
requirements: The framework is applied to learning situated in a material and social world, connecting macrosocial cultural-learning theory with microanalysis of situated activity.
constraints: The framework is presented for conceptual change in scientific thinking as the central case domain.
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in scientific thinking
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572

article_title: Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors
citation: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656
title: Perceived Social-Emotional Competence Scale (five dimensions)
description: A student self-report scale (Collie, 2021b) assessing five dimensions of perceived-SEC on a 1-7 agreement scale. As printed: "Five dimensions of perceived-SEC were assessed: perceived competence for assertiveness (4 items; e.g., “I feel capable to make sure my ideas are heard in group work at school”), tolerance (3 items; e.g., “I feel capable to be respectful of different cultures”)" plus social regulation, emotion regulation, and emotional awareness. In this study it was analyzed via bifactor ESEM with adequate omegas (global ω = .95).
requirements: Student self-report administration; omega estimates of ≥ .50 considered adequate for specific-factors in bifactor ESEM
constraints: The five dimensions are not all-encompassing; different dimensions may be required in different cultures and contexts
target_learning_goals: assessing perceived competence for social-emotional skills
examples: Used with 414 Australian secondary students in 2021 via an online questionnaire
key_sources: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656

article_title: Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas?
citation: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286
title: Perspective-affordance theory (PAT) of creativity as the framework linking perspective taking to creative idea generation
description: The article adopts Glăveanu's (2020) perspective-affordance theory as its explanatory framework for how creativity emerges in social interaction. It defines perspective as a relational construct linking a person and the world, and affordance as the action possibilities of materials relative to people's perspectives. The article states that "perspective diversities increase the creative potential of individuals and groups, and creativity essentially emerges from perspective taking—a relational, dialogical process that consists of an exchange of perspectives". The study operationalizes this framework in its two-part coding scheme distinguishing cognitive and social-emotional perspective taking.
requirements: Perspective taking requires an exchange of positions between social partners, which the article states can be challenging when differences are substantial and surface positions are incompatible.
constraints: The article notes social-emotional unease while changing positions, rooted in the difficulty of being truly open to others' perspectives and in perceived judgement, can make partners defensive of their own ideas.
target_learners: children aged 4-6 years in dyadic creative activities with adults
target_learning_goals: generation of creative (original and appropriate) ideas through social interaction
examples: The study built its coding scheme on the PAT theory and applied it to child-adult dyads generating unusual uses for everyday objects in the AUT.
key_sources: Bai, H.; Chan, L.; Luo, A.; Kroesbergen, E.H.; Christie, S. (2026). Creativity in dialogues: How do children interact with parents vs. strangers for generating creative ideas? Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102286

article_title: Preparation of the high school teacher.
citation: J. Carleton Bell. (1914). Preparation of the High School Teacher. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Warwick & York, Inc., Baltimore, MD.
title: Teacher scholarship should be selected for its bearing on the situations the high school teacher will meet, centered on adolescents' interests and development.
description: The editorial proposes a standard of teacher scholarship judged by relevance to teaching situations rather than amount or technical elevation. It states the needed scholarship "should be a scholarship that has some bearing upon the situations that the high school teacher will meet," with its center in the interests and activities of adolescent boys and girls. It argues this standard calls for a complete reorganization of the college courses currently recommended for prospective high school teachers.
requirements: College courses recommended for the preparation of high school teachers must be reorganized so that their content bears on the situations the teacher will meet in high school teaching.
constraints: The editorial presents this as an argued standard, not a tested result; it offers no empirical evidence for the claim.
target_learning_goals: effective teaching of high school subjects such as English, history, and mathematics
examples: The editorial asks what advantage courses in analytical geometry, calculus, the Punic wars, or early English would give a teacher of high school algebra, history, or English, and notes teachers' ignorance of subjects like economics, sociology, and ethics that help interpret culture to adolescents.
key_sources: J. Carleton Bell. (1914). Preparation of the High School Teacher. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Warwick & York, Inc., Baltimore, MD. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0067530

article_title: A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task.
citation: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001000
title: Use person-centered approaches to identify distinct motivational patterns that variable-centered analyses miss
description: The article argues that a person-centered approach to motivational factors reveals heterogeneity between and within individuals, enabling identification of key patterns of values across variables. It states this makes it possible "to more accurately detect hindering nonlinear and interactive effects compared to the variable-centered approach." Applied to students with SEN, this approach uncovered four distinct belief profiles and showed that SEN status relates probabilistically, not deterministically, to maladaptive motivation. The authors highlight its importance for identifying different reasons and consequences for performance.
requirements: Motivational belief measures suitable for latent profile analysis and a sufficiently large sample for profile enumeration
constraints: Fit indices for class enumeration are sample-size dependent, especially information criteria in large samples, requiring supplementary elbow-plot and theoretical judgment
target_learners: students with diverse motivational profiles, including students with special educational needs
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting motivation and effort related to academic performance
examples: Latent profile analysis of 6,942 Finnish ninth graders identified agentic, moderate, avoidant, and mixed profiles, with SEN students distributed across all four
key_sources: Nyman, L., Koivuhovi, S., Greiff, S., Hotulainen, R., Little, T. D., & Vainikainen, M.-P. (2025). A person-centered approach to action-control beliefs of students with special educational needs and their relation to student performance and time on task. Journal of Educational Psychology. article_title: To confirm or to conform? Performance goals as a regulator of conflict with more-competent others.
citation: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240
title: Performance goals as social tools regulating interpersonal behavior with more-competent others
description: The article conceives performance goals not merely as intrapersonal motivators but as "a social tool for regulating interpersonal behaviors with more-competent others." Drawing on the interpersonal circumplex model's agentic dimension, it proposes that performance-approach goals trigger an appetitive self–other regulation system producing dominant behavior, while performance-avoidance goals trigger an aversive system producing submissive behavior. This account explains why responses to socio-cognitive conflict with more-competent others vary between self-confirmation and compliance.
requirements: A competence-relevant social setting in which the learner confronts a disagreeing other whose relative competence is salient (higher, equal, or unspecified).
constraints: The account targets relational (not epistemic) conflict regulation in confrontations with more-competent others; the approach/avoidance distinction within mastery goals is explicitly not brought into play.
target_learning_goals: Regulation of interpersonal behavior during socio-cognitive conflict and disagreement in collaborative learning
examples: In Study 2, performance-approach versus performance-avoidance goal instructions were given before participants rated a confirmation versus compliance model after disagreeing with a partner presented as same-grade or higher-grade.
key_sources: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240

article_title: Supplemental Material for Toward an Evidence-Based Framework for Training Students’ Collaborative Problem-Solving Skills: Introducing and Testing the PEER Model
citation: Krstić, K., Nikitović, T., Altaras Dimitrijević, A., Jolić Marjanović, Z., Jošić, S., Mojović, K., Baucal, A. (2025). An Evidence-Based Framework for Training Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Skills: Introducing and Testing the PEER Model. https://osf.io/rstwe/
title: The PEER Model is a framework for training students' collaborative problem-solving skills
description: The article introduces the PEER Model, described in its own title as an evidence-based framework aimed at training students' collaborative problem-solving skills. The title states the framework is both introduced and empirically tested in the article. The supplied text consists of the article's Open Practices Disclosure form, so the framework's internal structure and components cannot be described beyond what the title and disclosure print.
requirements: The framework is presented as evidence-based, implying empirical testing of the model as described in the article title
constraints: The supplied text is limited to the Open Practices Disclosure; the framework's components are not described in the available text
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving skills

article_title: The measurement of ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence tests.
citation: Henmon, V. A. C. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part II. Sentence Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Henmon+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin+Sentence+Tests
title: P.E.-based scaling of sentence difficulty assuming normal distribution and equal year variability
description: The article scales each sentence's difficulty by the same method used for vocabulary words: given the per cent of pupils translating it correctly, its position is located on the base line of the normal frequency surface in P.E. deviations. Two assumptions are made: "that ability to translate Latin is distributed normally, and that the real variability for each year is approximately the same." A reference zero point of -3.8 P.E. obviates plus and minus values, and general scale values combine year values using the intervals between year medians.
requirements: Per cent correct for each sentence in each year must be known from large administrations
The two stated assumptions of normality and approximately equal year variability must hold
constraints: The design of uniformly stepping, year-equal lists "has not as yet been fully realized"; a much larger number of sentences must be constructed and tried out
target_learners: first- to fourth-year secondary school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: ability to translate Latin sentences
knowledge of Latin grammar
examples: Intervals between year medians were averaged from six direct and derived P.E. values: Test A M I-II 1.151 P.E., M I-III 2.490 P.E., M I-IV 3.011 P.E.

article_title: Achievement goals, reasons for goal pursuit, and achievement goal complexes as predictors of beneficial outcomes: Is the influence of goals reducible to reasons?
citation: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240
title: Performance goals as social tools regulating conflict with more-competent others: competitive vs. protective relational regulation
description: The article proposes that performance goals function as regulators of interpersonal behavior during socio-cognitive conflict with a more-competent disagreeing other. Drawing on the interpersonal circumplex's agency dimension, it predicts that "performance-approach goals (focus on approaching normative competence) should be associated with more-dominant behavior (i.e., competitive conflict regulation), whereas performance-avoidance goals (focus on avoiding normative incompetence) should be associated with more-submissive behavior (i.e., protective conflict regulation)". Competitive regulation means confirming one's own viewpoint and invalidating the other's; protective regulation means complying with the other's viewpoint and subordinating one's own. The framework treats the superior competence of a partner as a self-evaluation threat that activates these opposing self–other regulation systems.
requirements: A competence-relevant disagreement situation in which the partner's relative competence is perceived as equal, superior, or unspecified
Learners' endorsement (or induced adoption) of performance-approach or performance-avoidance goals
constraints: The framework concerns relational conflict regulation with more-competent others, not epistemic regulation in which the other is treated as an informational support
The approach/avoidance distinction applies to performance goals; mastery goals are not brought into the account
target_learners: learners in dyadic or group interactions with more-competent peers
target_learning_goals: regulation of disagreement during collaborative learning
socio-cognitive conflict resolution
examples: In Studies 1 and 3 participants reacted to a fictitious disagreeing partner on the Internet; in Study 2 goals were induced via instructions; in Study 4 participants took part in face-to-face videotaped interaction
key_sources: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240

article_title: The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence.
citation: Ansari, A. (2018). The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000255
title: Three developmental models of long-term preschool effects: persistence, convergence, and sleeper effects
description: The article organizes its inquiry around three conceptual models proposed to explain whether and why preschool programs may have long-term academic and psychosocial benefits: "models of persistence, convergence, and sleeper effects." Persistence holds that early skills lay foundations for later success; convergence holds that initial advantages dissipate as non-attendees catch up or attendees fade; sleeper effects hold that benefits emerge later without initial gains. The study tests these models against matched ECLS-K data.
requirements: The models are evaluated using longitudinal data following children from kindergarten through the end of middle school, with propensity-score-matched preschool and informal care samples
constraints: The article notes there was limited empirical evidence about when and why convergence occurs prior to this study, and that proximal indicators of preschool quality were not available in the ECLS-K: 1998 Cohort
target_learners: middle-class children attending preschool at age 4 in the United States
target_learning_goals: long-term academic achievement and psychosocial development following early childhood education
examples: The study operationalizes persistence as significant preschool paths through eighth grade, convergence as shrinking effect sizes between waves, and sleeper effects via three stated conditions on paths B1 and B2-B6
key_sources: Ansari, A. (2018). The persistence of preschool effects from early childhood through adolescence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(7). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000255

article_title: A standardization of certain opposites tests.
citation: Harry A. Greene. (1918). A Standardization of Certain Opposites Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070589
title: Probability-curve percentile weighting of item difficulty for scoring opposites tests
description: A scoring account in which each stimulus word's difficulty is estimated from the percentage of subjects failing it, then converted to a percentile value by reading from a table based on the area of the probability curve, assuming the tested ability fits that curve. The article states that "the percentage scores were changed directly into percentile values by reading directly from table based upon the area of the probability curve" with 0 set at -3σ, 50 at the mean, and 100 at +3σ. This replaces earlier scoring that treated every error identically. As an illustration, the word suave, "missed by 96% of the subjects", is valued at 79 on the percentile scale.
requirements: Group-administration response data large enough to estimate the percentage failing each stimulus word
A conversion table based on the area of the normal probability curve
constraints: The scaling assumes the particular abilities involved in the test fit the probability curve
Scores are calculated for group use; the time-to-correct-response method is presented as better suited to individual testing
target_learners: school children assessed with opposites tests
target_learning_goals: accurate, difficulty-weighted scoring of opposites tests in educational measurement
examples: Word values were derived from responses of University of Iowa freshmen in 1916 and 1917
Percentile values were totaled and divided by the total to yield relative point values from .5 to 2.0
key_sources: Harry A. Greene. (1918). A Standardization of Certain Opposites Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070589

article_title: Learning environments are associated with age-related differences in thalamocortical attention circuits in childhood
citation: Mino-Matot, T., Kebiri, H., Jorge, J., Ledoux, J.-B., Fornari, E., Bach Cuadra, M. & Denervaud, S. (2026). Learning environments are associated with age-related differences in thalamocortical attention circuits in childhood. npj Science of Learning, Article in Press. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00452-4
title: The pediatric thalamus as a set of specialized modulatory units with dissociable large-scale connectivity profiles
description: The article proposes viewing the child thalamus not as a unitary relay but as functionally differentiated territories with distinct large-scale "connectivity proﬁles". Cluster 1 couples with the visual network and anticorrelates with limbic regions; Clusters 2 and 5 jointly engage subcortical structures and the ventral attention network, a profile associated with salience detection and reorienting; Cluster 4 preferentially couples with somatomotor and dorsal attention networks. The framework grounds the study's hypothesis that pedagogy co-varies with specific attention-related thalamic channels during development.
requirements: Data-driven, pediatric-adapted functional parcellation of thalamic voxels from resting-state fMRI, with cluster quality guided by spatial coherence, hemispheric symmetry, and functional specificity criteria
constraints: The K = 8 solution is cohort-specific until externally replicated in larger developmental samples
Resting-state measures may underestimate condition-dependent dynamics
target_learners: children aged 4–15 years in school settings
target_learning_goals: attention and salience detection supporting learning
sensorimotor–attentional integration
examples: The article's K = 8 parcellation yielded dissociable, interpretable connectivity profiles across large-scale networks (Fig. 1C), supporting a view of the pediatric thalamus as "a set of specialized modulatory units rather than a unitary hub".
key_sources: Mino-Matot, T., Kebiri, H., Jorge, J., Ledoux, J.-B., Fornari, E., Bach Cuadra, M. & Denervaud, S. (2026). Learning environments are associated with age-related differences in thalamocortical attention circuits in childhood. npj Science of Learning, Article in Press. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00452-4

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: Highlight the pedagogic potential of informal transitional spaces adjacent to lecture theatres to support active learning before costly redesign
description: Rather than redesigning lecture theatres wholesale — which the article notes is time- and cost-intensive — institutions can use a mixed-method ecological approach to recognise the pedagogic potential of the informal spaces and periods between formal ones. The authors write that "ecotone thinking can empower teachers to reconsider their use of existing spaces", for example by inviting students to move between spaces to aid group formation and transitions between lecture segments and group-based interactions. This understanding informed student-staff partnership projects that redesigned 'transitional spaces' outside lecture theatres.
requirements: Requires recognising formal and informal spaces as interconnected ecological zones rather than isolated entities
Requires occupancy and qualitative data to identify where transitional pedagogic potential exists
constraints: Full architectural redesign aligned with active learning classrooms is time- and cost-intensive, and disproportionate capital investment in UK university education space renders broad redesign difficult
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in lecture-based courses
target_learning_goals: facilitating group formation
connecting timetabled learning to other contexts
enabling transitions between transmission and active learning
examples: Findings informed student-staff partnership projects redesigning 'transitional spaces' just outside lecture theatres, and a 'regenerative design' approach in which spaces were redesigned more cost-effectively
key_sources: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1

article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Assess an individual's likelihood of benefiting from stimulation before administering atDCS, to target those with less efficient learning mechanisms
description: The article proposes personalized clinical deployment of atDCS: "healthcare providers could assess the likelihood of an individual beneﬁting from stimulation based on a set of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated". Because stimulation benefits individuals with less efficient learning mechanisms and can harm those with optimal ones, screening baseline task performance narrows the administration scope and may increase efficacy in clinical applications. This requires identifying relevant parameters for each treated mechanism in advance.
requirements: Prior identification of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated (e.g., rehabilitation, memory)
constraints: The identified parameter set applies to a well-delimited context constituted by the finger-tapping task; additional investigations are needed for other behaviors and cognitive functions
target_learners: older and middle-aged adults undergoing motor rehabilitation or enhancement
target_learning_goals: improved acquisition of sequential motor skills through personalized neuromodulation
examples: In the article, the likelihood was assessed from a baseline block and first training block of the finger-tapping task before classifying participants into four learner tiers
key_sources: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y

article_title: Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology
citation: Anil Kamat, Basiel Makled, Jack Norfleet, Steven D. Schwaitzberg, Xavier Intes, Suvranu De, Anirban Dutta. (2022). Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology. npj Science of Learning 7:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00138-7
title: Perception-action cycle account of surgical skill acquisition via internal models, efference copy and corollary discharge
description: The article organizes its findings within a perception-action cycle framework in which motor learning "involves making sensory predictions from efferent copies of motor commands" and validating them with reafferent sensory input. Internal models (inverse and forward) support "perceptual decision-making to reduce behavioral variability", with the cerebellum providing "a substrate for error-based learning through updating a forward model, whereas the striatum underpins habit formation". Directed information flow (efference copy, corollary discharge) within the dorsal stream from PFC to SMA to PMC is used to interpret expert-novice and simulator-technology differences in fNIRS connectivity.
requirements: Learners must interact with the simulation environment so reafferent sensory feedback generated by their own actions can be compared against sensory predictions
constraints: The fNIRS montage captured only five regions (LPFC, RPFC, LPMC, RPMC, SMA); ventral-stream regions such as the VLPFC were not investigated
fNIRS has limited spatial resolution and depth sensitivity, which the authors state needs to be considered for brain-behavior analysis
target_learners: medical students (novices) and experienced surgeons (experts) training in laparoscopic surgery
target_learning_goals: acquisition of bimanual laparoscopic psychomotor skills such as FLS pattern cutting
examples: The authors propose that experts in the novel VR simulator could have used directed exploration whereas novices depended on random exploration in the initial stages of the FLS task
key_sources: Anil Kamat, Basiel Makled, Jack Norfleet, Steven D. Schwaitzberg, Xavier Intes, Suvranu De, Anirban Dutta. (2022). Directed information flow during laparoscopic surgical skill acquisition dissociated skill level and medical simulation technology. npj Science of Learning 7:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00138-7

article_title: An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children
citation: Denervaud, S., Fornari, E., Yang, X.-F., Hagmann, P., Immordino-Yang, M. H., & Sander, D. (2020). An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0069-6
title: Pedagogical experience shapes the development of error monitoring and its neural correlates
description: The article proposes that daily pedagogical experience modulates how children detect and respond to their own errors. Traditional pedagogy provides direct correctness feedback, while Montessori pedagogy avoids direct correctness information and encourages children "to notice their own incorrect thinking" and to help peers identify incorrect thinking pro-socially. The framework predicts different neural and behavioral error-monitoring patterns by pedagogy, which the fMRI study tests via activation and PPI connectivity in a math proofreading task.
requirements: Children must be enrolled long-term in a consistent pedagogical system (from Kindergarten on, or at least 3 years for the youngest children in this study)
constraints: Groups were not randomly assigned, so family-related or motivation-related factors could drive effects; modest sample size and cross-sectional design; conclusions drawn from a single math task
target_learners: children aged 8–12 in Montessori or traditional schools
target_learning_goals: error monitoring and self-regulated learning from incorrect responses
examples: Comparing 32 Swiss Montessori and traditionally-schooled children on a math proofreading fMRI task with feedback
key_sources: Denervaud, S., Fornari, E., Yang, X.-F., Hagmann, P., Immordino-Yang, M. H., & Sander, D. (2020). An fMRI study of error monitoring in Montessori and traditionally-schooled children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0069-6

article_title: Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics
citation: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3
title: Personalized TMR protocol: response-contingent cue repetition schedule (1/2/4 PRES by difficulty and accuracy)
description: A sleep-based intervention in which auditory cues for 104 semantically related word pairs are replayed during stable NREM 2/NREM 3 sleep, with the number of presentations (PRES) adjusted by learners' prospective difficulty ratings and pre-sleep recall accuracy: "1 PRES for correct responses at L2, 2 PRES for incorrect responses at L2, and 4 PRES for any response at L3"; no cues were delivered for L1 items. Unlike fixed TMR, cue frequency tracks individual memory trace strength and task difficulty. Prospective three-level difficulty self-ratings (L1–L3) taken after each retrieval trial drive the schedule.
requirements: A sleep expert monitoring EEG in real-time to deliver cues during stable NREM 2 or NREM 3 for at least 10 consecutive 30-s epochs
Prospective difficulty self-ratings and pre-sleep retrieval accuracy for each word pair
Cue-to-cue spacing of approximately 5 s exceeding the spindle refractory period
constraints: Manual administration of auditory stimuli by sleep experts poses challenges for real-world applications
The small sample per group may limit generalizability of the findings
target_learners: Healthy young adults learning semantically related word pairs (mean age 26.57)
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and error correction of paired-associate verbal memories over a 12-hour sleep interval
examples: 12 participants received cues tailored to difficulty: 6.8 ± 4.1 cues in the 1-PRES condition, 39.7 ± 66.4 in 2-PRES, and 877.0 ± 299.5 in 4-PRES, totaling 923.4 ± 318.2 cues over 67.1 ± 23.3 min
key_sources: Check, G.-H., Kweon, Y.-S., Oh, S., & Lee, S.-W. (2025). Personalized targeted memory reactivation enhances consolidation of challenging memories via slow wave and spindle dynamics. npj Science of Learning 10:47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00340-3

article_title: Research-Based Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles: a Review, Progress, and Recommendations
citation: Kim, Y., & Baylor, A. L. (2015). Research-Based Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles: a Review, Progress, and Recommendations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0055-y
title: Three systematically operationalized pedagogical agent roles: Expert, Motivator, and Mentor
description: Baylor and Kim (2005) designed three instructional agent roles grounded in social-cognitive perspectives of learning. The Expert provided accurate information with authoritative speech and deictic gestures; the Motivator modeled coping strategies as a peer with emotional expressions; the Mentor combined both functions. Table 1 operationalized each role by "Appearance (image), Animation, Voice, Affect and messaging (script)." The roles were instantiated through pre-scripted agents with controlled gender, lip synchronization, and script length.
requirements: Learners must perceive the agent as intended; role instantiations require coordinated appearance, animation, voice, affect, and script
constraints: Agent-learner interactions were pre-scripted so each learner received all guidance, which limited the intelligence of the agents
target_learning_goals: computer literacy skills
instructional design skills
examples: Experiment 1 with 78 undergraduates learning computer literacy; Experiment 2 with 71 pre-service teachers learning instructional design skills
key_sources: Kim, Y., & Baylor, A. L. (2015). Research-Based Design of Pedagogical Agent Roles: a Review, Progress, and Recommendations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0055-y

article_title: Intelligent Textbooks
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9
title: Design intelligent textbook technology around an effective instructional approach, not technology-driven innovation alone
description: The article argues that pedagogical research on intelligent textbooks is underrepresented yet essential: technology must enable an effective instructional approach to yield a useful educational tool. It notes that although the technology side progresses rapidly, "empirically proven recipes for effective use of these technologies are still in short supply," and warns that "excessive focus on technology-driven innovation without considering whether or not a developed technology can enable an effective instructional approach is unlikely to produce a useful educational tool." Designers should therefore ground textbook features in established didactic approaches.
requirements: Evaluation of whether the developed technology enables an effective instructional approach
constraints: Pedagogy-focused work has not been among the most popular directions of reported research
target_learners: students using intelligent textbooks in any subject domain
target_learning_goals: effective use of intelligent textbook technologies for learning
examples: Workshop papers explored organizing interaction with digital textbooks according to programmed instruction, orchestrating lessons around textbooks, and interacting with causal concept maps to understand textbook material
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky, Peter Brusilovsky, Andrew Lan. (2025). Intelligent Textbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00451-9

article_title: Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality
citation: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7
title: Validated personality trait stories for conveying learner personality at a polarised level
description: Short stories about fictional learners, adapted from IPIP-NEO self-report questionnaire items (Goldberg et al. 2006), describe one Big Five trait at a high or low polarised level. They were used instead of simplistic labels "such as 'John is an extrovert'" so participants could identify and empathise with the learner. A validation experiment had participants rate each story with the Mini-Markers scale (Saucier 1994), and stories were adjusted and re-validated as needed.
requirements: Stories must express the intended trait and not inadvertently express another trait at the same time, verified via validation with the Mini-Markers scale
target_learners: adult online participants taking the role of a teacher giving feedback
target_learning_goals: tailoring progress feedback and emotional support to learner personality
examples: Stories were created for each of the five traits (e.g. high and low conscientiousness 'Josh'), validated, and used in five between-subjects experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk
key_sources: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7

article_title: Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality
citation: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7
title: Algorithm for adapting emotional support and slant to learner personality and performance
description: Based on the five experiments, the authors created algorithms describing how feedback should be adapted to learner personality and performance. "Two algorithms were created using different methods to describe the adaptations and evaluated on how well they described the experimental data using DICE scores", and a refined algorithm was created from the results. It recommends slant (positive, neutral, negative) and emotional support types and quantities for given trait levels and scores. A qualitative study with teachers and trainee teachers was run to evaluate and further refine the algorithm.
requirements: Experimental data on which emotional support types and slant participants use for each trait level and score, with recommendations derived from homogeneous subset means (e.g. subset mean ≥ 0.5 for recommending an emotional support type)
target_learners: learners of conversational agents and intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: motivating learners through tailored progress feedback and emotional support
examples: For slant, a subset mean ≤ −0.5 led to a recommended negative slant and ≥ 0.5 to a positive slant; otherwise a neutral slant was recommended
key_sources: Matt Dennis, Judith Masthoff, Chris Mellish. (2016). Adapting Progress Feedback and Emotional Support to Learner Personality. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0059-7

article_title: Solving instructional design dilemmas to develop a Video Enhanced Rubric with modeling examples to support mental model development of complex skills: the Viewbrics-project use case
citation: Kevin Ackermans, Ellen Rusman, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Marcus Specht. (2019). Solving instructional design dilemmas to develop a Video Enhanced Rubric with modeling examples to support mental model development of complex skills: the Viewbrics-project use case. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09668-1
title: Select video models slightly older than learners who can perform the complex skill with a perception of mastery
description: When casting video-modeling examples, the article recommends actors slightly older than the learners who can perform the complex skill with a 'perception of mastery', while maintaining acceptable model-observer similarity for motivation. The authors report that 13-year-old peer-aged models seemed unable to perform a complex skill such as collaboration with acceptable perceived mastery, so, in collaboration with a focus group of teachers and students, "we selected four 15-year-old professional actors to be both identifiable as peers and capable of performing complex skills with a perception of mastery".
requirements: Actors must be selected on fluent, enthusiastic and accent-free speech per Mayer's personalization principle, and casting should vary gender, ethnicity, personal traits and educational level to foster identification
constraints: Peer-aged models may be unable to display complex skills with perceived mastery when the skill requires experience to build a schema
target_learning_goals: Observational learning of complex skills such as collaboration, presentation and information literacy
examples: The Viewbrics casting process used a focus group of teachers and students and resulted in four 15-year-old professional actors playing identifiable peers
key_sources: Kevin Ackermans, Ellen Rusman, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Marcus Specht. (2019). Solving instructional design dilemmas to develop a Video Enhanced Rubric with modeling examples to support mental model development of complex skills: the Viewbrics-project use case. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09668-1

article_title: Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews
citation: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1
title: Pedagogical model for IVR safety training with four phases plus trainer pre- and post-training activities
description: A multidisciplinary pedagogical model combining a simulation learning framework, IVR scenarios, and elements of the Cognitive Affective Model for Immersive Learning, framed socioculturally. It proposes "four essential training phases: introduction, IVR briefing, IVR scenario, and debriefing", with facilitated discussions before and after the individually performed IVR scenario enacting social learning. Based on the trainer interviews, the authors "include the trainers' pre- and post-activities in the pedagogical model to encourage the practitioners to strive for a good fit between the training goals, the learners' work tasks, and the organizational safety culture." The model considers learners' sense of agency, presence, body ownership, embodiment, and cognitive load.
requirements: Trainers must be provided with sufficient training and facilitation materials beforehand; some may need coaching and support to create positive learner–facilitator interaction
constraints: The IVR environment used in the interventions only accommodates individual learning; the model has not yet been empirically tested in this study
target_learners: vocational and higher education learners in practice-based learning
target_learning_goals: safety knowledge
safety attitudes and motivation
self-efficacy
procedural and psychomotor skills
examples: Pre-training activities include organizing training programs, choosing pedagogies, and adapting the training to the learners' work context; post-training activities encompass feedback collection and outcome evaluation
key_sources: Lehikko, A., Nykänen, M., & Ruokamo, H. (2025). Conceptualizing a pedagogical model for immersive virtual reality safety training: pedagogical practices in trainer interviews. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10490-1

article_title: Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers’ construct restructuring following computer vision professional development
citation: Kurz, T. L., Jayasuriya, S., Swisher, K., Mativo, J., Pidaparti, R., & Robinson, D. T. (2026). Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers' construct restructuring following computer vision professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10594-2
title: Personal Construct Theory with repertory grids and hierarchical cluster analysis as a method for mapping teachers' cognitive restructuring
description: Personal Construct Theory (Kelly, 1955) frames the study's methodology: constructs are elicited directly from participants through pairwise comparisons of elements (here, computer vision and human vision), avoiding researcher-imposed survey instruments. The authors note it "can provide unique insight because it has the potential to show how cognitive structures changes through the analysis of dendrograms using hierarchical cluster analysis." Repertory grids serve as cognitive mapping tools whose cluster membership reveals how participants perceive constructs as similar or dissimilar, enabling pre-post comparison of cognitive structure.
requirements: Constructs must come directly from participants via pairwise comparisons to reduce researcher bias
Sample sizes of no more than 20 are recommended due to the intense nature of data collection
constraints: Construct language generated by one subgroup may not represent all participants; here constructs came only from Arizona participants, skewing results
Personal Construct Theory is more reliant on cognition than emotion
Participants may lack the framework (language and concepts) needed to elicit meaningful constructs
target_learning_goals: Mapping changes in teachers' conceptual understanding of computer vision
examples: The study elicited 18 constructs from pairwise comparisons of computer vision and human vision and analyzed pre/post repertory grids using Ward's Method with squared Euclidean distances.
key_sources: Kurz, T. L., Jayasuriya, S., Swisher, K., Mativo, J., Pidaparti, R., & Robinson, D. T. (2026). Computer vision versus human vision: analyzing middle school teachers' construct restructuring following computer vision professional development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10594-2

article_title: Advancing automatic guidance in virtual science inquiry: from ease of use to personalization
citation: Zhai, X. (2021). Advancing automatic guidance in virtual science inquiry: from ease of use to personalization. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 255–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09917-8
title: Personalize CoSIL guidance to individual students, because guidance is critical to student success in computer-supported inquiry learning
description: The principle holds that guidance in computer-supported inquiry learning (CoSIL) should be personalized to individual students rather than generic. The author states that "As CoSIL guidance is critical to student success in CoSIL" and agrees with the reviewed work "that the personalization of CoSIL guidance is vital." The commentary uses this principle to motivate machine learning as a route to personalization without adding teacher workload.
requirements: Guidance tools must be matched to individual students' needs rather than applied uniformly
constraints: Existing guidance tools, per the reviewed literature, increased ease of use but failed in personalizing CoSIL to individual students
target_learners: K-12 and higher education science students using virtual or remote labs
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills in virtual and remote lab environments
examples: The commentary responds to Zacharia et al.'s (2015) review of forms and efficacy of guidance tools associated with each phase of scientific inquiry, using its personalization gap to argue for machine-learning-supported guidance
key_sources: Zhai, X. (2021). Advancing automatic guidance in virtual science inquiry: from ease of use to personalization. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 255–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09917-8

article_title: Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences
citation: Wardrip, P.S. (2021). Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 213–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09883-1
title: Pedagogical roles educators could consider in remote learning environments, adapted from Nacu et al.'s online learning support roles
description: The article proposes a set of pedagogical roles that educators can enact when facilitating remote learning, extending the online learning support roles framework of Nacu et al. (2018). As the abstract states, "this paper introduces pedagogical roles educators could consider in remote environments and a heuristic evaluation method to focus on how those moves might relate to the technologies they are using." The framework is offered as a practical lens for educators adapting their instructional practice during pandemic-driven school closures.
requirements: Educators need a way to relate their instructional moves to the technologies they are using, per the article's stated focus
constraints: The roles are framed for remote environments during the COVID-19 pandemic shift, and the author notes some remote learning is not mediated by a computational device
target_learners: K-12 and other school students in remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learning_goals: Supporting student learning through educator facilitation roles in remote settings
examples: The article positions itself as "a response to Nacu et al. (2018) from a practice perspective," adapting that framework for pandemic-era remote teaching
key_sources: Wardrip, P.S. (2021). Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 213–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09883-1

article_title: Exploring the influence of learners’ personal traits and perceived course characteristics on online interaction and engagement
citation: Purarjomandlangrudi, A; Chen, D. (2020). Exploring the influence of learners' personal traits and perceived course characteristics on online interaction and engagement. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09792-3
title: Research model linking learners' personal attributes and perceived course characteristics to online interaction and engagement
description: The article proposes a research model in which two classes of predictors — the student's personal attributes and their perceived course characteristics — are assessed for their possible impact on online interaction and engagement. The model is stated as a hypothesis-testing framework: "This study proposes a research model to assess the possible impact of the student's personal attributes and perceived course characteristics on their online interaction and engagement." It was operationalised as survey-based constructs and tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling.
requirements: Survey measurement of learners' personal attributes and perceived course characteristics
Structural equation modelling (partial least squares) to test the hypothesised relationships
constraints: Tested with students in online courses at one Australian university
target_learning_goals: online interaction and engagement in e-learning
examples: The model was tested using survey data from 246 online course students, with partial least squares used to test the research model and hypotheses.
key_sources: Purarjomandlangrudi, A; Chen, D. (2020). Exploring the influence of learners' personal traits and perceived course characteristics on online interaction and engagement. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09792-3

article_title: Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art
citation: Habeeb Yusuf, Arthur Money, Damon Daylamani-Zad. (2025). Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10447-4
title: Conceptual framework of pedagogical AI conversational agents organised by pedagogical applications and technological functions
description: The article develops a conceptual framework from thematic analysis of 92 studies, organising pedagogical AI conversational agents into two overarching themes. As the article states, "pedagogical AI conversational agents can primarily be considered in terms of their pedagogical applications and their pedagogical purposes, which include pastoral, instructional and cognitive", further considered in terms of mode of study and intent, and technological functions in terms of embodiment, functional type and features. The two themes complement each other: increased technological functions enable wider pedagogical applications, and specified applications require specialised functions.
requirements: Serves as an interpretative visual representation of how themes from the literature analysis may be organised conceptually
constraints: Derived from literature published between 2014 and 2022 within a pre-defined set of search criteria in higher education settings
target_learning_goals: teaching and learning support across instructional, pastoral and cognitive purposes
examples: Figure 2 presents the resulting conceptual framework; Tables 4–7 map each category to the surveyed literature
key_sources: Habeeb Yusuf, Arthur Money, Damon Daylamani-Zad. (2025). Pedagogical AI conversational agents in higher education: a conceptual framework and survey of the state of the art. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10447-4

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Pedagogies of care and self-care as meso- and micro-level postdigital pedagogies
description: The article discusses pedagogies of care, founded on Noddings' reciprocal relations of listening, receptiveness and presence, and pedagogies of self-care, arguing that caring for the self is only possible through caring for others and that collective caring requires sufficient resources. Distributed care involves "attending to the relations between all elements in a learning ecology", requiring collective action at micro, meso and macro levels. The article notes these pedagogies can be in tension with neoliberal institutional priorities focused on job-market-ready graduates.
requirements: A system that allows space, time and energy to care, and individuals knowing their own limits and values
constraints: Care in higher education is particularly challenging in relation to AI and automatic technology, such as learning analytics that constrain legitimate behaviour or knowledge
target_learning_goals: enacting ethics, empathy and social justice in teaching
teacher wellbeing
examples: During Covid-19, enacting an ethic of care included considering differences in students' technological access and home infrastructures, and what happens with students' data
key_sources: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z

article_title: Medical students with specific learning disabilities: mixed-methods systematic review of the prevalence, academic performance, challenges, and perceived impact of support interventions.
citation: Pavletič Bernarda, Babuder Milena Košak, Homar Vesna. (2026). Medical students with specific learning disabilities: mixed-methods systematic review of the prevalence, academic performance, challenges, and perceived impact of support interventions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09574-0
title: Performance outcomes versus learning processes: comparable scores do not indicate equitable learning conditions
description: The review's central integrative framework distinguishes "performance outcomes" (measurable indicators such as examination scores, progression, graduation) from "learning processes and experiences" (effort, strategies, cognitive load, emotional burden, institutional barriers). It uses this distinction to interpret the meta-analytic parity in accommodated MCQ assessments alongside qualitative reports of substantial compensatory effort, arguing that "comparable assessment outcomes may be achieved alongside substantial compensatory effort and should not be assumed to indicate equitable learning conditions." The framework reframes assessment design and support policy toward equity of learning conditions rather than parity of scores.
requirements: Requires mixed-methods synthesis combining performance data with students' reported experiences to operationalize the distinction
constraints: Developed from evidence geographically concentrated in UK medical education and focused mainly on dyslexia, limiting transferability; the authors note similar scores "may reflect successful compensation under accommodated conditions rather than the absence of educational disadvantage"
target_learners: undergraduate medical students with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: equitable academic performance and progression
wellbeing and inclusion in medical education
examples: The review integrated meta-analytic MCQ parity findings (d = 0.045) with meta-aggregated qualitative accounts of extra preparation time and anxiety to argue equity requires looking beyond scores
key_sources: Pavletič Bernarda, Babuder Milena Košak, Homar Vesna. (2026). Medical students with specific learning disabilities: mixed-methods systematic review of the prevalence, academic performance, challenges, and perceived impact of support interventions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09574-0

article_title: Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
citation: Tian Qi, Liu Yaowen, Wang Ziyu, Qin Gang. (2026). Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1905122
title: Nine-node harmonized taxonomy of physical education teaching models for network meta-analysis
description: The review harmonizes study-level intervention labels into a connected treatment network of nine nodes: "Control, Functional games, Game-based, Hybrid TGfU-SE, Linear, Nonlinear, Sport Education, TGfU, and Traditional." Labels were mapped "according to instructional logic rather than name alone" — e.g., classical, technical, and direct-instruction labels were assigned to Traditional or Linear by degree of explicit technical sequencing, and constraint-led approaches to Nonlinear. Control denotes minimal or regular PE; Traditional denotes structured teacher-centered instruction; Cooperative appears only in the broad sensitivity network. The harmonization was intended to preserve interpretability and network connectivity rather than erase pedagogical nuance.
requirements: Each study must provide an independent between-pedagogy contrast and sufficient quantitative information to derive a standardized mean difference within a connected treatment network
constraints: Studies with mixed cognitive-psychomotor, visual-motor integration, or cognitive-visual processing outcomes, university participants, or club settings were restricted to the broad sensitivity network; Cooperative was retained only in the broad network
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in school physical education
target_learning_goals: Motor skill development and motor-related performance outcomes
examples: Hybrid TGfU-SE and Functional games were kept as distinct nodes because their intervention structures were identifiable and connected
key_sources: Tian Qi, Liu Yaowen, Wang Ziyu, Qin Gang. (2026). Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1905122

article_title: Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education.
citation: Yahya Fahmi, Rusijono Rusijono, Dewi Utari, Metafisika Kartika, Lestiani Winda, Hermansyah Hermansyah, Asbanu Dens E. S. I. (2026). Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education. F1000Research 15:1682. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.191181.1
title: Design pedagogy, not just technology: the benefit of combining laboratory modalities depends on complementary information
description: The review concludes that the advantage of virtual laboratories comes from the quality of the pedagogical design around them rather than from the technology itself. Modalities should be combined so that each contributes information the other cannot: real experiments supply the phenomenological referent while simulations supply representations physical apparatus cannot show, such as force vectors and dynamic graphs. The review states "the benefit depends on whether the combined components contribute complementary information, not simply more of it", so adding media without added information yields no gain.
requirements: The combined components must contribute complementary information rather than redundant content
Guidance must be matched to learners' prior knowledge to avoid adding cognitive load
constraints: One documented exception: virtual experiments plus video showed no advantage over virtual experiments alone
Skill outcomes resting on instrument handling, such as graph reading, are not fully replaceable by simulation
target_learners: Physics learners in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding
Inquiry skills
Motivation and self-efficacy
examples: Ben Ouahi et al. (2024) reported the largest electricity gains for a real-plus-virtual combination within a 5E cycle across 166 students, and Mihret et al. (2023) found a blended modality most effective for understanding the nature of science
key_sources: Yahya Fahmi, Rusijono Rusijono, Dewi Utari, Metafisika Kartika, Lestiani Winda, Hermansyah Hermansyah, Asbanu Dens E. S. I. (2026). Bridging Pedagogy and Technology: A Systematic Literature Review on Inquiry-Collaborative Models Assisted with Virtual Laboratory in Physics Education. F1000Research 15:1682. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.191181.1

article_title: The Competencies and Implementation of Peer Support Interventions for People with Serious Mental Health Challenges: A Systematic Review.
citation: Lara Ernesto Isaac MA, Bond Laura PhD, MA, Ratnakaran Adarsh MSc, Zheng Muxi MS, Song Emily MPH, Fang Kacey MSc, Suneja Priyanka MBPsS, MABP, Ballikar Saniya MSc, Mendes Malvina Carmel MSW, O'Neill Kathryn MPH, Carmio Natali PsyD, MPH, Agrawal Ravindra Narayan MBBS, DPM, MPM, MRCPsych, MBA, Patel Vikram PhD, MBBS. (2026). The Competencies and Implementation of Peer Support Interventions for People with Serious Mental Health Challenges: A Systematic Review. Harvard Review of Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1097/HRP.0000000000000460
title: A 16-competency taxonomy of peer support work, comprising 12 peer support competencies and 4 clinical competencies
description: The review developed a taxonomy of training components comprising the skills and competencies used across peer support interventions for adults with serious mental health challenges. Competencies were categorized as either a peer support competency, as outlined by SAMHSA, or a clinical competency, defined as techniques or skills typically used by clinical providers. The final taxonomy was composed of 12 peer support competencies (e.g., collaboration and care, providing support, recovery planning, sharing lived experience of recovery) and 4 clinical competencies (mental health diagnosis and psychoeducation, basic counseling skills, case management, cognitive behavioral techniques), developed through thematic content analysis, two rounds of pilot coding by eight researchers, and expert panel review.
requirements: Developed based on SAMHSA's peer support core competencies guidelines plus additional thematic content analysis of included trials
constraints: Competency frequencies were estimated from a subset of trials that provided relevant information; a large percentage of studies did not report on implementation components
target_learners: Adults with serious mental health challenges receiving peer support services
Peer supporters in mental health systems
target_learning_goals: Peer supporter competencies for delivering peer support interventions
examples: The taxonomy was pilot-tested in two rounds whereby eight researchers independently coded two or more eligible trials, and an expert panel of mental health providers and peer support experts reviewed the final taxonomies

article_title: Understanding simulation-based learning for health professions students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds: a scoping review.
citation: Zhang Luocheng, Patterson Freyr, Penman Adriana, Forbes Roma. (2025). Understanding simulation-based learning for health professions students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds: a scoping review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10384-6
title: Include peer and faculty support, including minority staff, in SBL for CALD students
description: The review finds faculty and peer support "contribute to the success of SBL for students from CALD backgrounds, providing them with a sense of belonging and psychological safety". Minority staff were perceived as more understanding and approachable, and peer support from similar backgrounds built solidarity and helped overcome language and cultural barriers.

constraints: more research on involving staff or simulated patients from diverse ethnic backgrounds is needed, per the review

sense of belonging
examples: students preferring faculty from minority backgrounds who stayed back to explain things in detail

article_title: Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature.
citation: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530
title: Person, Process, and Context framework as a structured lens for understanding SDL readiness among healthcare professionals
description: The review identifies "three factors—Person, Process, and Context— as a structured lens through which to understand how individual traits, learning methods, and environmental influences interact to facilitate SDL readiness among HCPs." Personal factors include intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and confidence in SDL abilities. Process factors include goal achievement strategies and support from digital tools. Contextual factors include social interactions, learning environment, learning programs, and organizational support with digital tools. The review uses this lens to organize both promoting factors and barriers to SDL in healthcare organizations.
requirements: The framework requires distinguishing individual traits, learning methods, and environmental influences when analyzing SDL readiness.
constraints: The review notes a clear separation between these factors is often lacking, causing terminological overlap, and that a distinct categorization between factors that promote or hinder SDL was first suggested in this publication.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals including nurses, pharmacists, and physicians in clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning readiness and continuous professional development
examples: The review's Table 2 categorizes promoting factors and barriers into Personal, Process, and Contextual factors, listing items such as intrinsic motivation, goal achievement strategies, and supportive organizational policies.

article_title: Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education
citation: Paul, U., Mantravadi, A., Shah, J., Shah, S., Mylavarapu, S. V., Rashid, M. P., & Gehringer, E. (2025). Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11677
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of peer grading systems: evaluation approaches and reviewer weighting strategies
description: The review develops a taxonomy organizing peer-grading systems along two orthogonal dimensions: Evaluation Approaches (summative feedback via rating, ranking, and categorization, plus formative feedback) and Reviewer Weighting Strategies (calibration, back-evaluation, consensus, and reputation). It was built bottom-up: two authors independently analyzed all 122 included studies, identified features (11 and 10, with eight overlapping), and refined them through iterative discussion into the consolidated dimensions. The taxonomy serves as "a descriptive framework and a critical lens to assess the strengths and limitations of various peer-grading approaches across multiple factors such as accuracy, graders learning outcomes, engagement, and scalability."
requirements: Requires analysis of included studies' methodologies, strategy descriptions, and evaluation techniques to identify and consolidate features into orthogonal dimensions
constraints: The review states the taxonomy "may require adaptation for specific contexts" and "does not deeply address other important factors, such as reviewer assignment or incentive structures"
target_learners: students in large and online courses including MOOCs acting as peer graders
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair peer assessment of student work
understanding assessment criteria through grading others' work
examples: Table II reports adoption counts: Rating 95 papers, Ranking 17, Categorization 10, Formative 62; Calibration 21, Back-Evaluation 11, Consensus 27, Reputation 22

article_title: Does a PBL-based medical curriculum predispose training in specific career paths? A systematic review of the literature.
citation: Tsigarides Jordan, Wingfield Laura R., Kulendran Myutan. (2017). Does a PBL-based medical curriculum predispose training in specific career paths? A systematic review of the literature. BMC Research Notes. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5219658/
title: Personality-based selection hypothesis for PBL-career associations
description: The review proposes that any association between PBL curricula and career choice may arise because problem-based learning appeals to students with particular personality characteristics due to its open and group-based nature. The review cites Holen et al. finding that "students that were outgoing, curious, sociable and conscientious appreciated a PBL curriculum" and Bexelius et al. finding that graduates choosing surgical careers scored higher in conscientiousness. It also notes the hypothesis that problem-based curricula may be more likely to produce graduates who select primary care careers.
requirements: The hypothesis requires that personality traits influence both preference for PBL curricula and subsequent career path selection
constraints: The review presents this as argument and cited hypothesis rather than as a tested result of the included studies
target_learning_goals: career choice formation in medical education
examples: The review cites Holen et al. on students who appreciated PBL curricula and Bexelius et al. on conscientiousness among surgical career choosers as supporting background
