article_title: Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment
citation: Zeynep Tatli & Alipasa Ayas. (2012). Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 13(1). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde
title: Permit virtual laboratory use outside class hours to exploit its independence from time and place
description: The article recommends extending access to the virtual laboratory beyond scheduled lessons because virtual learning environments are free from location and time. Given students' success within a limited in-class access period, the authors argue higher success rates would be achieved by permitting virtual environments to be used out of classes. This treats the VCL as a supportive complement to, not a replacement for, real laboratory work.
requirements: Virtual laboratory software accessible to students outside scheduled chemistry lessons
constraints: The article frames this as speculation about higher success rates, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: Independent and self-paced experimentation in chemistry
examples: In the study EG students were permitted to use VCL software only within chemistry lessons and applications lessons

article_title: Gender Differences and Mathematics Achievement of Senior High School Students: A Case of Ghana National College
citation: Ato Kwamina Arhin & Adelaide Koryoe Offoe. (2015). Gender Differences and mathematics Achievement of Senior High School Students: A Case of Ghana National College. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.33. https://www.iiste.org
title: Senior high school mathematics teachers should make performance-based assessment tasks part of their lessons
description: The article recommends embedding performance assessment tasks, defined as "testing students' abilities and competencies in solving open-ended mathematics problems which border on higher order thinking skills", into regular mathematics teaching. It argues assessment stands "in a dynamic interaction" with teaching and learning, and that PA-driven instruction improved achievement for both sexes in its study. The recommendation is grounded in the study's significant post-test gains for treated males and females.
requirements: Open-ended performance-based assessment tests aligned to syllabus objectives, with answers developed with assessment and mathematics experts
constraints: The study's tasks were not the extended types requiring weeks of work; each test lasted two hours
The sample was not large enough to permit meaningful generalisations to other Senior High School students in Ghana
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem-solving and higher order thinking skills
examples: The experimental group received six weeks of treatment focused on group work and sharing of ideas in solving mathematical problems, with 320 minutes of mathematics per week

article_title: Examining Personalisation of Instruction, Attitudes toward and Achievement in Mathematics Word Problems among Nigerian Senior Secondary School Students
citation: Awofala, A. O. A. (2014). Examining Personalisation of Instruction, Attitudes toward and Achievement in Mathematics Word Problems among Nigerian Senior Secondary School Students. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 2(4), 273-288. https://www.ijemst.com
title: Personalisation of instruction as an individualised instructional design grounded in constructivism, situated cognition and social cognitive theory
description: Personalisation of instruction is an instructional design in which problem contexts are made meaningful by incorporating learners' familiar referents and preferences into instructional content. Miller and Kulhavy are cited defining it as "the act of using verbal modifiers and exemplars which have been lifted directly from an individual’s own repertoire of life experience". The article grounds it in constructivism, situated cognition and Bandura's social cognitive theory, viewing personalisation as a form of modelling attending to attention, retention, production and motivation, and lists seven functions including stronger encoding, concreteness, attentiveness, motivation, reduced cognitive load, intrinsic interest and confidence.
requirements: Learners must supply personal preferences and interests (via an interest inventory) that can be incorporated into the problem content
Instructional contexts must be transformable to contain familiar referents
constraints: The article notes the strategy has been criticized for enhancing sex-stereotyped contexts that favour males
Effectiveness may wear off over time as novelty fades (Ross and Anand)
Time constraints in preparing individualised materials could reduce its use
target_learners: senior secondary school year one students
target_learning_goals: solving mathematics word problems
positive attitudes toward mathematics word problems
examples: The study personalised word problems using the most popular referents from a Students' Interest Inventory, e.g., a Tantalizer fast-food mall context replacing an unfamiliar gym context, with identical numbers and computational skills across the two parallel versions
key_sources: Awofala, A. O. A. (2014). Examining Personalisation of Instruction, Attitudes toward and Achievement in Mathematics Word Problems among Nigerian Senior Secondary School Students. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 2(4), 273-288. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1059026

article_title: The Use of Personalized Texts for Teaching Turkish as a Second Language
citation: Kardaş, D. (2016). The use of personalized texts for teaching Turkish as a second language. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2538
title: Personalization of instructional content as cognitivist and structuralist grounding for learning
description: The article frames personalized teaching theoretically: newly learned information is re-organized and a new schema is built on existing cognitive structure (cognitivism), while students become active participants who develop their own strategies and help shape a suitable learning environment (structuralism). Personalization places "students are in the center of the instructional material", with texts and examples created from their background and interests, so content approximates the real world and learning becomes permanent.
requirements: Instructional content must make reference to students' lives, embedding people, events, objects or interests drawn from those lives
constraints: The article notes most existing personalized-learning applications are web-based and concentrated in secondary and higher education, suggesting use at earlier levels as well
target_learners: students in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: grammar comprehension and expression in a second language
permanent (durable) learning of instructional content
examples: The study applied the framework by embedding students' countries, family names, physical appearance and residence into grammar example sentences and test questions

article_title: Holy Psychopathology Batman: The Pedagogical Use of Comic Books in the Teaching of Abnormal Psychology
citation: Rahman, R. O. & Zeglin, R. J. (2014). Holy psychopathology Batman: The pedagogical use of comic books in the teaching of abnormal psychology. Psychology Teaching Review, 20(1). https://www.bps.org.uk/journals/psychology-teaching-review
title: Pedagogical constructivism as a framework for teaching abnormal psychology
description: Pedagogical constructivism is the explanatory framework the article uses to justify active, application-based instruction in abnormal psychology. It "posits that learning takes place as a result of explo ration and questioning of existing knowl edge", that learning occurs during application rather than prior to it, through participation in realistic activities, debate with peers, and highly individualised projects. The authors use it to frame the comic-book diagnostic assignment as a constructivist-inspired activity.
requirements: Assignments must present problems to solve or themes to explore freely, encourage critical reflection on existing and alternative perspectives, and facilitate students making personal meaning of the material
target_learning_goals: understanding of psychological disorders and diagnostic processes
examples: The experimental section diagnosed a character from a self-selected graphic novel and wrote a psychological report, which the authors describe as adhering to constructivist tenets

article_title: Performance-Based Scholarships: Replication at Six Sites Using Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Alexander Mayer, MDRC. (2014). Performance-Based Scholarships: Replication at Six Sites Using Randomized Controlled Trials. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Performance-based scholarship program model for low-income college students
description: A financial aid intervention in which students are paid at multiple points during a semester if they earn a specified number of credits with a "C" or better grade, conditioning additional aid on meeting performance benchmarks. Students received between $500 and $1,300 per term (site-dependent) for two to four semesters, paid directly to students with complete discretion over use, in addition to Pell Grants and other aid. Eligibility is based on current-term performance, not prior performance like high school GPA. The model was evaluated in randomized controlled trials at eight institutions across six states.
requirements: Students must meet clear academic benchmarks, such as earning a certain number of credits with a C or better, to receive payments
Payments are made in addition to existing aid such as Pell Grants
constraints: Scholarship amounts, duration, and benchmarks varied by state, and one site (New York) showed no significant first-year benchmark impact
target_learning_goals: Academic progress measured by credits earned, benchmark attainment, persistence, and degree completion
examples: Sites paid $1,000 per term in Louisiana, up to $1,500 in Arizona, and $300-$900 in Ohio, with benchmarks such as completing at least 6 credits with a C or better average
key_sources: Alexander Mayer, MDRC. (2014). Performance-Based Scholarships: Replication at Six Sites Using Randomized Controlled Trials. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562816

article_title: Evaluating Pedagogical Practices in Science Classrooms: A Randomized Controlled Trial Study on Teacher Virtual Professional Development with Virtual Mentoring and Coaching
citation: Lara-Alecio, R., Irby, B. J., Tong, F., Sutton-Jones, K. L., Guerrero, C. L., Tang, S., & Pang, H. (2024). Evaluating Pedagogical Practices in Science Classrooms: A Randomized Controlled Trial Study on Teacher Virtual Professional Development with Virtual Mentoring and Coaching. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 16(4), 479-494. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2024.347
title: Pedagogical Observation Protocol (POP)
description: The Pedagogical Observation Protocol (POP) is a low-inference classroom observation instrument based on the four-dimensional pedagogical theory, with "four domains: activity structure, language of instruction, language content, and communication mode" plus two later-added minor domains, physical grouping and instructional strategy. Raters code presence of practices over multiple 20-second intervals of recorded lessons. In this study POP captured fifth-grade science teachers' practices across three virtual observations, with inter-rater reliability monitored at AC1 > 0.6.
requirements: Trained raters with established and continuously monitored inter-rater reliability (Gwet's AC1 > 0.6 across rounds)
constraints: Yields non-parametric frequency data, analyzed via chi-square in this study
target_learning_goals: Evaluating pedagogical practices in science classrooms serving emergent bilingual and economically challenged students
examples: Three rounds of virtual observation (beginning, middle, end of 2017-2018) coded 13,620 twenty-second video clips from 121 teachers

article_title: The Impact of Providing Performance Feedback to Teachers and Principals. NCEE 2018-4001
citation: Garet, M.S., Wayne, A.J., Brown, S., Rickles, J., Song, M., and Manzeske, D. (2017). The Impact of Providing Performance Feedback to Teachers and Principals (NCEE 2018-4001). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Theory of action: performance feedback identifies educators needing support and signals improvement areas, leading to better practice, leadership, and achievement
description: The report's theory of action holds that performance measures provide information that "might identify educators who need support and indicate areas for improvement, leading to improved classroom practice and leadership and boosting student achievement." The intervention operationalizes this by giving educators more frequent, specific feedback with ratings and written narratives, plus self-comparison information from value-added and leadership measures, without attaching formal stakes. The study tested this chain with randomized assignment of schools within eight districts.
requirements: Feedback must be more frequent and more specific than districts' existing evaluation systems
Measures must be reliable enough to distinguish performance (overall scores, not dimension differences, in this study)
constraints: Dimension-level feedback had limited reliability for indicating specific areas of improvement
Effects on mathematics achievement were significant only in Year 1 and no reading/ELA effects were significant
target_learners: K–12 teachers and principals in district evaluation systems
target_learning_goals: Improving teaching practice and instructional leadership through data-informed feedback
examples: Exhibit 1.1 presents the study's theory of action linking feedback to practice, leadership, and achievement

article_title: Effects of Peer Tutoring on the Academic Achievement of Students in the Subject of Biology at Secondary Level
citation: Irfan Ullah, Rabia Tabassum and Muhammad Kaleem. (2018). Effects of Peer Tutoring on the Academic Achievement of Students in the Subject of Biology at Secondary Level. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 112. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8030112
title: Use peer tutoring as a supplementary, highly structured and supervised instructional technique
description: The article recommends incorporating peer tutoring alongside other teaching methodologies rather than as the principal strategy, because it "needs a highly structured supervised environment and may be conducted in controlled conditions". In the study this was operationalised through two hours of tutor orientation, thirty researcher-written lesson plans, continuous monitoring of pairs, and strict rules maintained by the researcher and laboratory attendant.
requirements: Tutors receive proper orientation about the tutoring activity before sessions
Lesson plans prepared in advance and approved by subject experts
Strict rules, discipline and supervision during tutoring sessions
constraints: The study was conducted on male students of secondary level only
The article states peer tutoring may be more fruitful as a supplementary and supporting instructional technique rather than the principal strategy
target_learners: secondary-level (10th grade) biology students, including low achievers paired with high achievers
target_learning_goals: biology achievement at the knowledge, comprehension and application levels of the cognitive domain
examples: In the study, high achievers were named tutors and low achievers tutees in the experimental group; the researcher visited each pair, intervened on academic or management problems, and discouraged passive listening by tutees.

article_title: Pre-Test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students' Academic Achievement and Permanence of Their Knowledge
citation: Kenan BAŞ, Esen DURMUŞ. (2019). Pre-test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students’ Academic Achievement and Permanence of their Knowledge. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.7n.2p.107
title: Performing-arts lesson pattern: play performance followed by teacher-led question and answer
description: A repeatable lesson structure in which a prepared play related to the lesson topic is performed at the start of class and the regular course teacher then leads discussion. As the article describes it, "In the first 20-30 minutes of each lesson (time varies by subject and play), the plays were performed by the researcher and her team, and in the remaining time, the questions were answered by the social studies teacher of the class". Plays were distributed across the unit's themes (Karagöz and Hacivat, storytelling, puppetry, village play, theater) with prepared questions given to the teacher as material.

Rehearsals done with a specialist team and teachers informed about application stages
Advance-prepared questions about the play's subject given to the course teacher as material
constraints: Performances required the researcher's team to bring equipment to each school about half an hour before lessons
Plays had to be performed simultaneously in all schools in the same week to avoid conflicts
target_learning_goals: Social studies unit content knowledge and permanence of knowledge
examples: Karagöz and Hacivat shadow play used for agriculture, animal breeding, forestry, mining, water sources and industry themes, with characters asking students for help and guest characters such as a miner and a fireman

citation: Kenan BAŞ, Esen DURMUŞ. (2019). Pre-test the Effect of Teaching Social Studies Course through Performing Arts on the Students’ Academic Achievement and Permanence of their Knowledge. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.7n.2p.107
title: Taxonomy of performing arts: traditional and contemporary branches
description: The article organizes performing arts—defined as "the general name of the art branches such as Public Storytelling, Light Comedy, Ballet, Dance, Theater" performed before a conscious community—into two categories shown in its Figure 1: Traditional and Contemporary performing arts. Traditional Turkish theater is grouped into plays performed on the stage (public storytelling, light comedy, village plays, puppetry) and games played on screen (Karagöz shadow play). Contemporary performing arts comprise theater (with genres from tragedy to absurd and epic theater), ballet-dance, music, and opera.

constraints: The taxonomy is drawn from Turkish theater historiography and dictionary definitions cited by the authors
target_learning_goals: Understanding performing-arts genres applicable to social studies teaching
examples: The study operationalized the taxonomy by using one genre per theme: Karagöz and Hacivat, storytelling, puppetry, village play, and theater across the unit's five themes

article_title: Perry Beeches Coaching Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Lord, P., Bradshaw, S., Stevens, E. and Styles, B. (2015). Perry Beeches Coaching Programme: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Perry Beeches Coaching Programme
description: A literacy catch-up programme providing academic coaching to Year 7 pupils below National Curriculum level 4c in English through one-to-one or small group tuition sessions. It was developed at Perry Beeches Academy and "is based on a one to one programme used at Match Charter School in Boston, USA". The programme did not include a pre-defined set of activities or content; coaches were intended to tailor sessions to individual pupils, drawing on starter packs and a suggested list of literacy elements including phonics, word recognition, spelling and punctuation, paired reading, and letter writing. In the trial it was intended to deliver five one-hour one-to-one sessions per fortnight over an academic year, delivered by graduate coaches integrated into schools, in addition to usual English lessons.
requirements: Graduate coaches recruited by individual schools, with training organised by each school and coaches integrated into the school to connect classroom learning with tuition
constraints: Due to its individually tailored nature, the report states a targeted programme is difficult to replicate; in practice delivery varied across schools in format, frequency, duration and coach training
target_learners: Year 7 pupils below National Curriculum level 4c in reading and/or writing at the end of Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: reading
spelling and grammar
writing attainment at the primary-secondary transition
examples: In the trial, 16 coaches across four schools were each assigned roughly 12 pupils; sessions replaced a variety of usual subject lessons from late October or early November 2013 until late June 2014.
key_sources: Lord, P., Bradshaw, S., Stevens, E. and Styles, B. (2015). Perry Beeches Coaching Programme: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581144

article_title: The Efficiency of Peer Teaching of Developing Non Verbal Communication to Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
citation: Wael Alshurman, Ihsani Alsreaa. (2015). The Efficiency of Peer Teaching of Developing Non Verbal Communication to Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.29. https://www.iiste.org
title: Peer tutoring program for non-verbal communication in children with ASD
description: A peer tutoring program in which normal peers with strong social skills act as teachers for children with autism during scheduled non-formal interaction periods. Peers were trained before each session in giving instructions, reinforcement and behavior management, and sessions ran "an average of three session per week for (25-35) minute s each session" in social situations such as the school shop, rest time and sport lessons. The method was applied for four months with 40 sessions.
requirements: Peers with outstanding social and non-verbal communication skills must be selected and trained prior to each session, with teachers supervising implementation
constraints: The study applied the program with a sample of 10 children aged 8-12 with severe autism at one qualification center
target_learners: children with autism spectrum disorder aged 8-12
target_learning_goals: non-verbal communication skills including shared attention, visual communication, imitation, listening and understanding, pointing, and understanding facial expressions and voice tones
examples: Sessions occurred during free play and social situations (going to the school shop, rest time, sport lessons), with peers trained beforehand and teachers supervising

article_title: The Efficiency of Peer Teaching of Developing Non Verbal Communication to Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
citation: Wael Alshurman, Ihsani Alsreaa. (2015). The Efficiency of Peer Teaching of Developing Non Verbal Communication to Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.29. https://www.iiste.org
title: Peer-pair role structure: peers as teachers, students with autism as lesson recipients
description: In peer tutoring sessions, students work in pairs where the socially capable peer assumes the teacher role and the student with autism is the lesson recipient. Peers are taught to initiate and sustain sharing "through modeling and lecturing accompanied with  reinforcement", targeting academic, social responses and play skills, initiating conversation, maintaining interaction, and displaying feelings. Teachers support the trained peers rather than directing the child with autism directly.
requirements: Peers must be trained in initiative and continued sharing, with teachers providing assistance and support to the trained peers
constraints: Described in the context of children with autism spectrum disorder
target_learning_goals: social interaction and non-verbal communication skills
examples: Peers reinforced visual communication, play activities, initiating conversation, offering or asking help, and maintaining social communication during sessions

article_title: The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students' Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study
citation: Alqudah, D., Bidin, A., & Md Hussin, M. A. H. (2019). The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students’ Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 12(4), 669-688. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12443a
title: Peirce's three-category semiotic sign taxonomy (iconic, index, symbol) as a basis for selecting infographic signs
description: The article applies semiotic theory to educational infographics, stating that "Semiotic signs have been classified by Charles Sanders Peirce; who adopted three main classifications of signs: iconic, index and symbol". Icons resemble the object represented (e.g., desktop screen icons); indexes indicate an object's location or relation without resembling it (e.g., smoke indicating fire); symbols carry information and alerts through a non-resembling signifier-object relationship. The study used these three categories, singly or in mutual links, when selecting semiotic forms for infographic lesson designs.
requirements: infographics must apply design principles such as color, typography, signs, icons, balance, repetition and correspondence, and have a title and complete story
constraints: the overall visual form may be effective for one purpose while other types cannot serve the wanted purpose, so the appropriate visual form must be determined
target_learning_goals: perceiving the meaning of conveyed information through visual signs
examples: Figure 1 displays the level of resemblance amongst index, icon and symbol, which the authors describe as a basic idea considered in designing infographics for the taught lessons
key_sources: Alqudah, D., Bidin, A., & Md Hussin, M. A. H. (2019). The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students’ Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 12(4), 669-688. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12443a

article_title: The Combined Effect of Instruction and Monitor in Improving Pronunciation of Potential English Teachers
citation: Qian Liu & Zunwei Fu. (2011). The Combined Effect of Instruction and Monitor in Improving Pronunciation of Potential English Teachers. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p164
title: Use peer-monitoring groups of three or four rather than pairs when learners check each other's pronunciation
description: The article presents peer-monitoring, typically organised as group work, as an activity that may promote both perceptive and productive pronunciation accuracy. Citing Celce-Murcia et al. (1996), it advises dividing learners into "groups of three or four instead of pairs", because pair-work can produce disagreement about whether the speaker erred or the listener misheard, and larger groups settle disagreements by consensus.
requirements: Learners work in groups to monitor each other's pronunciation
constraints: The group-size advice is attributed to Celce-Murcia et al. (1996) rather than tested in this study
target_learning_goals: perceptive and productive pronunciation accuracy
examples: The article recommends group peer-monitoring as one of several practices for enhancing monitor use alongside covert rehearsal and tape self-recording.
key_sources: Qian Liu & Zunwei Fu. (2011). The Combined Effect of Instruction and Monitor in Improving Pronunciation of Potential English Teachers. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p164

article_title: Use of Mobile Testing System PeLe for Developing Language Skills
citation: Titova, S. (2015). Use of mobile testing system PeLe for developing language skills. Critical CALL – Proceedings of the 2015 EUROCALL Conference, Padova, Italy. http://dx.doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2015.000387
title: PeLe mobile testing system (HiST, Norway)
description: PeLe is a mobile testing system developed at HiST (Norway) used in this study as a formative assessment tool. Students responded to in-class grammar and vocabulary tests using their smartphones or tablets over classroom Wi-Fi. The system stores each individual's responses, so "an individual student's performance can be tracked across multiple sessions", and it provides immediate feedback, interactivity and flexibility as pedagogical affordances.
requirements: Wi-Fi access in class
Handheld devices (smartphones or tablets) for student responses
constraints: The article notes more research is needed on its effects for skills beyond grammar, such as speaking, writing and listening
target_learning_goals: Grammar and vocabulary development through formative assessment with immediate feedback
examples: Used for eight formative in-class grammar and vocabulary tests from September to December 2013 in the MobiLL project's first period

article_title: Pedagogical Modeling of the Competitive Activity of Athletes in Russian Lapta
citation: Rashida G. Gabdrakhmanova and Aleksandr Y. Kostarev. (2016). Pedagogical Modeling of the Competitive Activity of Athletes in Russian Lapta. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6090-6101. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: A pedagogical model of competitive activity in Russian lapta structured into seven interrelated blocks
description: The article develops a pedagogical model of competitive activity in Russian lapta as a targeted, organized process. Its structure comprises "the following interrelated components: 1) the work -out and study session; 2) play activity; 3) internal factors that determine the functioning of the modeled object; 4) control; 5) a set of criteria for evaluating the effectiveness of training of lapta players; 6) external factors; 7) the conditions for model implementation." Quality of the model is expressed in logical interdependence of its structural elements, correspondence to implementation conditions, and flexibility for adjustments.
requirements: Implementation by coaches of a specially organized activity forming an athlete developing environment connected to the national culture of the native land
constraints: The model was developed for the specific conditions of competitive activity in Russian lapta
target_learners: lapta players of various skill levels and gender, ages 14 to 40
target_learning_goals: improvement of technical, tactical, physical and competitive performance in Russian lapta
examples: The model was implemented in a forming pedagogical experiment comparing experimental and control training groups

article_title: Using Digital Media at Home to Promote Young Children's Mathematics Learning: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Silander, M., Moorthy, S., Dominguez, X., Pasnik, S., & Llorente, C. (2016). Using Digital Media at Home to Promote Young Children's Mathematics Learning: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: PEG+CAT curated home transmedia intervention package with parent supports
description: A 12-week series of 12 approximately 30-minute opportunities for children and families to engage with PEG+CAT episodes, video clips, online games, a tablet app, and print activities across multiple devices. Materials focused on patterns, geometry, measurable attributes, ordinal numbers, and counting, plus ATL skills, and "The intervention included a series of supports for parents" covering co-viewing, math talk, and problem solving and persistence.
requirements: Families needed provided technology resources (an Android tablet and a Chromebook laptop) and supports for joint engagement with the curated content
constraints: Time and intensity of each interaction depended on the child's interest and motivation and the availability and motivation of parents
target_learners: 4- and 5-year-old children from low-income families attending preschool
target_learning_goals: early mathematics skills (patterns, geometry, measurable attributes, ordinal numbers, counting)
approaches to learning such as flexible problem solving, persistence, and productive collaboration
examples: Families were randomly assigned at the child level to receive the curated PEG+CAT experience with devices, or to continue typical home media behaviors

article_title: Study of the Effectiveness of Multi-Cultural Education on the Attitude towards National Integration of High School Students
citation: Shaheen Perveen. (2014). Study of the Effectiveness of Multi-cultural Education on the Attitude Towards National Integration of High School Students. li-manager's Journal of Psychology, Educational, Vol. 8 No. 2, August-October 2014. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Study+of+the+Effectiveness+of+Multi-cultural+Education+on+the+Attitude+towards+National+Integration%22+Perveen
title: Researcher-designed 32-hour multicultural education programme using interactive methods
description: A multicultural education programme designed and prepared by the researcher, delivered to the experimental group of high school students using interactive teaching methods. The article states lessons were prepared "using different interactive methodologies like co-operative learning, role play, debates, slogan, lecture cum discussion, poster, competition" and that "the program comprised of 32 hours". Content was developed through in-depth discussion with the literature and with colleges belonging to different cultures.
requirements: Delivered as a treatment session to an experimental group distinct from a control group
Content developed through in-depth discussion between the researchers and the available literature
constraints: The Maharashtra State syllabus does not explicitly prescribe multicultural education, per the article
target_learners: High school students in the Marathwada region of Maharashtra
target_learning_goals: Cultural literacy about different sub-cultures in India
Positive attitude towards cultural diversity and national integration
examples: The experimental group was taught the programme content while a control group from a second school received no such session

article_title: Texting Parents: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Miller, S., Davison, J., Yohanis, J., Sloan, S., Gildea, A. and Thurston, A. (2016). Texting Parents: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Parent Engagement Programme (PEP): low-cost school texting of parents about tests, homework and lesson content
description: PEP is a universal, school-based intervention in which schools text parents via their existing school information management system (SIMS, Schoolcomms or similar) about upcoming tests, missing homework, and brief lesson updates with conversational prompts sent on a three-weekly subject rotation. It is intended as "a low-cost and low-effort process". In the trial, schools sent an average of 30 texts per parent over the year; first-year cost was £7,550 per school (£7.55 per pupil), falling to £3.25 per pupil annually thereafter.
requirements: Teachers attend 1.5 days of training (one full day plus a half-day), and a member of staff is appointed as PEP project liaison officer to collate text content from subject teachers
Schools need access to suitable communication software; schools without it would need additional resources (e.g. Schoolcomms at £1,500 a year)
constraints: In this efficacy trial the delivery team sent the texts under optimal conditions; consistency of implementation varied considerably between schools
Schools could only modify text content related to conversational prompts and had to adhere to the protocol otherwise
target_learners: secondary school pupils in Years 7, 9 and 11 (Key Stages 3 and 4)
target_learning_goals: attainment in English, maths and science
school attendance
examples: In the trial, 36 English secondary schools delivered PEP from September 2014 to July 2015, with the project delivery team sending texts via Schoolcomms on the schools' behalf
key_sources: Miller, S., Davison, J., Yohanis, J., Sloan, S., Gildea, A. and Thurston, A. (2016). Texting Parents: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581121

article_title: Home Environment Quality Mediates the Effects of an Early Intervention on Children's Social-Emotional Development in Rural Pakistan
citation: Finch, J. E., Obradović, J., & Yousafzai, A. (2016). Home environment quality mediates the effects of an early intervention on children's social-emotional development in rural Pakistan. SREE Spring 2016 Conference abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: PEDS responsive stimulation intervention delivered by Lady Health Workers
description: The PEDS trial was a 2x2 factorial, community-based cluster-randomized control trial with a responsive stimulation arm and an enhanced nutrition arm. Lady Health Workers delivered an adaptation of the UNICEF and WHO Care for the Child Development package, which "promotes caregivers' sensitivity and responsiveness through developmentally appropriate play activities", via home visits and monthly group community meetings until children reached age two. Caregivers tried age-appropriate activities while workers coached them and gave feedback on interaction quality.
requirements: Delivery by trained local community women (Lady Health Workers) through home visits and group meetings integrated within existing health services
constraints: The intervention was delivered only to a birth cohort until age two; the study focuses on the responsive stimulation arm with the enhanced nutrition intervention controlled for in all models
target_learners: children from birth to age two in rural, disadvantaged communities in Sindh, Pakistan, and their primary caregivers
target_learning_goals: caregivers' sensitivity and responsiveness
children's cognitive development and school readiness
examples: The four intervention groups were control (N = 331), enhanced nutrition only (N = 311), response stimulation only (N = 354), and a combination (N = 315), all continuing to receive standard health-care services
key_sources: Finch, J. E., Obradović, J., & Yousafzai, A. (2016). Home environment quality mediates the effects of an early intervention on children's social-emotional development in rural Pakistan. SREE Spring 2016 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567225

article_title: The Effectiveness of Peer Taught Group Sessions of Physiotherapy Students within the Clinical Setting: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Scott, D. and Jelsma, J. (2014). The effectiveness of peer taught group sessions of physiotherapy students within the clinical setting: A quasi-experimental study. Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 105-117. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/9
title: Peer learning as reciprocal learning with and from each other without immediate teacher intervention
description: The article adopts Boud, Cohen, and Sampson's definition of peer learning as "the use of teaching and learning strategies in which students learn with and from each other without the immediate intervention of a teacher". It highlights "reciprocal peer learning", in which students of the same level act as both teacher and learner within a group, with emphasis on content and on the emotional support students offer each other. The article uses this framework to motivate comparing peer-led and educator-led clinical group sessions.
requirements: Students of the same academic level take turns acting as teacher and learner within a group
constraints: Some peer teachers may be poorly prepared, may have difficulty motivating students, or may be unable to control the session, and have less clinical experience than educators, per the article's background
target_learners: third-year physiotherapy students on clinical placements
target_learning_goals: clinical knowledge of paediatric health conditions
independent, self-directed learning
confidence and self-esteem of peer teachers
examples: Weekly group teaching sessions at four paediatric clinical sites were led either by a student peer or by the clinical educator, with teachers randomly assigned to health conditions
key_sources: Scott, D. and Jelsma, J. (2014). The effectiveness of peer taught group sessions of physiotherapy students within the clinical setting: A quasi-experimental study. Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 105-117. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/9

article_title: The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students' English Language Achievements
citation: İrfan Sarı, Nadir Çeliköz, Süleyman Ünal. (2017). The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students’ English Language Achievements. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.1. https://www.iiste.org
title: Use peer support as additional support alongside, not a replacement for, the teacher
description: The article frames peer support as a collaborative teaching-learning process in which a lower-level student is matched with a successful student so the lower-level student may improve "without any stress driven by an authori ty". It stresses, citing Tella (2013), that "peer support should not be considered as the replacement of the teacher but additional suppo rt to ongoing teaching process". Institutions should therefore layer organized peer support onto existing instruction rather than substituting it for teaching.
requirements: A structured matching of lower-level students with successful peers
Ongoing teacher-led instruction that the peer support supplements
constraints: Programs must be designed to prevent problems: citing Beasley (1997), the article notes "personal clashes that can take  place during peer support process and also attendance pro blems may occur"
target_learners: university-level students, particularly lower-achieving language learners
target_learning_goals: English language achievement, self-confidence, communication skills, learning responsibility
examples: The LTA program ran alongside the regular curriculum: control groups "followed their lessons as is sched uled in their curriculum" while experimental groups added weekly supervised peer-support logs
key_sources: İrfan Sarı, Nadir Çeliköz, Süleyman Ünal. (2017). The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students’ English Language Achievements. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131776

article_title: Peer Tutoring as an Improvement Strategy for School Exploitation
citation: Guerrero Flores, D. I., Urdiales Ibarra, M. E., Villarreal Treviño, M. G., Castro Campos, C., & Loredo Tejeda, A. T. (2018). Peer Tutoring as an Improvement Strategy for School Exploitation. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 953-961. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.953
title: Peer tutoring as a socio-cultural, asymmetric peer-learning mechanism grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
description: The article frames peer tutoring (PT) as a teaching and learning mechanism in which peers with similar contextual and social situations help and support one another, whose "main characteristic is learning while helping to learn within a disciplinary area." Its theoretical model rests on Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory and the zone of proximal development, whereby superior psychological processes such as language, attention and memory develop through social exchange. Pairs or small groups adopt an asymmetric tutor-tutee relationship working toward a common goal, with interaction regulated and accompanied by the teacher, and the teacher defines clear tasks with criteria of place, time, curricular content, contact format and participant roles.
requirements: A difference in attitudes and abilities between tutor and tutee, so one can guide the other in the knowledge where the tutee has difficulty
Teacher-defined clear tasks and a regulated, teacher-accompanied dynamic of interaction
constraints: Greater ease of implementation has been observed with students of the same age than at different ages, per the article's cited literature
target_learners: High school (higher secondary education) students learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in English language learning
Grammatical and communicative competence
Motivation to study
examples: In the study, tutors were 121 students scoring above 80 on the initial exam; tutees were 101 students scoring below 65; dyads were formed from a list of possible tutors to facilitate relational dynamics
key_sources: Guerrero Flores, D. I., Urdiales Ibarra, M. E., Villarreal Treviño, M. G., Castro Campos, C., & Loredo Tejeda, A. T. (2018). Peer Tutoring as an Improvement Strategy for School Exploitation. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 953-961. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.953

The author prepared the environment weekly, ensured all children participated in small and large groups, and closed each day with assessment and children's comments.

Materials and environment prepared by the instructor before each activity
Classroom teachers refrain from discussing the applications to maintain external validity

social skills
empathy
anger control
conflict resolution
cooperation

citation: Hikmet Zelyurt, )erda *|ktrk ønce. (2018). The Impact of Peaceful Life Skills Oriented Education Program on Social Adaptation and Skills of Preschool Children. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(7): 1519-1525. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.060712
title: Peace skills education should begin at early ages to build social adaptation and prevent future violence
description: The authors argue that social-emotional requirements such as recognizing emotions, developing friendships, empathy, respecting diversity, anger control and conflict resolution "should be addressed at early ages", and that education teaching children how to be peaceful is important for creating a conflict-free society. They cite literature on social skills, character, values and peace education emphasizing early starts, and report their own preschool findings as support.
requirements: Programs focusing on peace skills, activities promoting recognition of emotions and problem-solving, peer interaction, and the principle of learning by doing
constraints: Evidence base in this article is a single quasi-experimental study with one kindergarten and non-random groups

peaceful conflict resolution
empathy and cooperation

article_title: Collaborative Learning Supported by Rubrics Improves Critical Thinking
citation: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas and Sonia Olivares. (2015). Collaborative learning supported by rubrics improves critical thinking. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v15i1.12905
title: PENCRISAL Critical Thinking test
description: The PENCRISAL test is the open-format outcome measure used to assess the ARDESOS programs. It "comprises 35 situation-production problems, with an open format and is structured around 5 factors: Practical Reasoning, Deduction, Induction, Decision Making and Problem Solving", with Cronbach alpha = .632 and test-retest r = .786. It was designed by task analysis so that each problem can only be solved by a specific strategy or mechanism, allowing the mechanism to be identified in the open answers.
requirements: Open answers must be scored so the reasoning mechanism used can be identified
constraints: Reliability alpha of .632 is printed for the test
target_learning_goals: critical thinking: practical reasoning, deduction, induction, decision making, problem solving
examples: Administered one week before the start of instruction and one week after the intervention, four months between measurements
key_sources: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas and Sonia Olivares. (2015). Collaborative learning supported by rubrics improves critical thinking. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v15i1.12905

article_title: Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice?
citation: Evans, S., Steele, J., Robertson, S., & Dyer, T. (2015). Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice? Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com
title: Personalization principle: conversational, personable instructor communication supports engagement in online classrooms
description: The article invokes the personalization principle of Clark and Mayer (2011), under which personalization provides "a more conversational and personable tone that is unique to each individual instructor." It holds that successful online course designs build in opportunities for instructors to personalize the classroom, through welcome messages, announcements, grade feedback, and post titles, so the instructor appears "less machine-like and more genuine to students." The study tests one small personalization lever within this framework.
requirements: Instructors must have control over personalizable elements such as post titles, announcements, and feedback within the course design
constraints: The present study's posting-quantity result ran counter to the direction this principle would predict
target_learners: first-year undergraduate students in online courses
target_learning_goals: student engagement and participation in online discussion forums
examples: The study operationalized personalization as personalized subject headings on instructor-generated discussion posts, e.g., 'Dr. C to Penelope and Class' versus 'Re:Re:Topic3 DQ1'
key_sources: Evans, S., Steele, J., Robertson, S., & Dyer, T. (2015). Personalizing Post Titles in the Online Classroom: A Best Practice? Journal of Educators Online. https://www.thejeo.com

article_title: On the Comparative Impact of Self-Assessment and Teacher-Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation
citation: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74
title: Piloted PET reading, writing and listening sections used to homogenize participants
description: The Preliminary English Test (PET) served as the homogenization test selecting intermediate learners. The administered sample covered reading (five parts), writing (three parts) and listening (four parts); the speaking section was omitted because a qualified examiner was not available without Cambridge supervision and the study's focus was reading comprehension. After piloting with 30 students, "three items out of the 65 total items were found to be malfunctioning and were excluded", leaving 62 items plus two writing tasks scored out of 75 marks.
requirements: Pilot administration with item analysis and reliability estimates before the main administration
constraints: Speaking section not administered; only reading, writing and listening parts used
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners at a private language institute
target_learning_goals: homogenizing participants on overall language proficiency
examples: Learners scoring within one standard deviation above and below the PET mean were selected and randomly divided into two groups of 30
key_sources: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74

article_title: The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach
citation: Mohammad Mohammadipour & Sabariah MD Rashid. (2015). The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.113
title: Cambridge Preliminary English Test (PET) speaking test as pre/post proficiency measure
description: The study used "the Cambridge Preliminary English Test (PET) as a pre-post speaking test to measure freshmen university students' overall speaking proficiency". The test is conducted by two examiners with pairs of candidates in 10-12 minutes across four parts, and the interlocutor awards a global mark out of 25 on five criteria: Vocabulary, Grammar, Pronunciation, Discourse Management, and Interactive Communication. Recorded pre-test samples were rated by four raters, and inter-rater reliability was 0.85.
requirements: Two examiners (an Interlocutor and an Assessor) and pairs of candidates
Rater selection and inter-rater reliability checking
constraints: Candidates at PET level are not expected to be fully fluent or accurate speakers; the language of the test is carefully controlled
target_learning_goals: overall speaking proficiency
examples: The pre-test was administered seven days before the experiment and the post-test from 30 December 2013 over eight days

article_title: Promoting Scientific Literacy by Using ICT in Science Teaching
citation: Al-Rsa'i, M. S. (2013). Promoting Scientific Literacy by Using ICT in Science Teaching. International Education Studies, 6(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n9p175
title: PEA model for promoting scientific literacy through ICT-based constructivist science teaching
description: The PEA model is a triple learning model the study designed based on ICT and constructive learning strategy for teaching science. It depends on three requirements: "Using ICT in a way consistent with the tendencies of the Students and their attitudes", "Constructing educational content based on the constructivist theory of learning", and "Providing a social learning environment". The article presents it as a model to help teachers give students an advanced level of scientific knowledge, and expects it to include teacher and faculty training.
requirements: Using ICT in a way consistent with the tendencies of the Students and their attitudes
Constructing educational content based on the constructivist theory of learning
Providing a social learning environment
target_learning_goals: scientific literacy about science concepts
examples: The study trained instructors of the experimental group on ICT tools including e-mail, Facebook and Twitter, online conferencing, and astronomy learning sites, using planning of educational tasks and worksheets by exploratory context.
