article_title: An Analysis of the Application of Wikipedia Corpus on the Lexical Learning in the Second Language Acquisition
citation: Jing Shi. (2015). An Analysis of the Application of Wikipedia Corpus on the Lexical Learning in the Second Language Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 8(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n8p171
title: Pedagogical application of corpus linguistics as direct classroom use
description: The article frames the pedagogical application of corpus as "the direct application of corpus linguistics in the classroom setting, affecting how language is taught and learned." It argues this direct use benefits learners by exercising attention, memory, and reasoning through corpus data analysis, and by promoting autonomous learning, language awareness, and noticing of recurring language patterns that become embedded in learners' interlanguage.
requirements: Teachers need user-friendly corpus resources and consideration of teacher and learner needs for corpus pedagogy to enter mainstream practice.
constraints: The article notes corpus linguistics remains marginalized in application because many teachers lack basic training in working with corpora and feel intimidated by corpus data.
target_learners: Second language (ESL) learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: Language awareness, noticing of language patterns, and lexical acquisition through autonomous corpus data analysis
examples: The article cites the theoretical framework that concordance data, especially the KWIC format, attracts learners' attention and supports schemata construction, citing prior corpus-linguistics scholarship.
key_sources: Jing Shi. (2015). An Analysis of the Application of Wikipedia Corpus on the Lexical Learning in the Second Language Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 8(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n8p171

article_title: The Effect of Different Modes of English Captioning on EFL Learners' General Listening Comprehension: Full Text vs. Keyword Captions
citation: Sorayya Behroozizad, Sudabeh Majidi. (2015). The Effect of Different Modes of English Captioning on EFL learners' General Listening Comprehension: Full text Vs. Keyword Captions. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.115
title: PET-based listening pre-test and post-test instrumentation for captioning studies
description: The study used the listening section of the standardized Preliminary English Test (PET) as both pre-test and post-test, each consisting of 25 multiple-choice questions with a ceiling score of 25 released by Cambridge ESOL for intermediate learners. Learners listened to a conversation or monologue and answered questions. The PET reading and listening sections (60 items in total) were also used to select 45 homogeneous participants from an initial 58, excluding scores outside -1 SD to +1 SD.
requirements: Standardized intermediate-level listening test with parallel versions for pre- and post-test
constraints: Scores outside -1 SD and +1 SD on the proficiency test were excluded, reducing the sample to 45
target_learning_goals: measuring general English listening comprehension
examples: The pre-test was the listening part of the standardized PET with 25 multiple-choice questions; another PET version served as the post-test after 15 treatment sessions
key_sources: Sorayya Behroozizad, Sudabeh Majidi. (2015). The Effect of Different Modes of English Captioning on EFL learners' General Listening Comprehension: Full text Vs. Keyword Captions. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.115

article_title: Effects of Peer Education on Attitudes of Secondary School Students towards the Course of Physical Education and Sports
citation: Mustafa Karadağ, Resul Ağirtaş, Atilla Pulur. (2018). Effects of Peer Education on Attitudes of Secondary School Students Towards the Course of Physical Education and Sports. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i4a.3171
title: Use peer education in physical education to enable students to learn by teaching their peers.
description: The article describes a peer tutoring method in which "Teachers act only as observer and guide while the peer tutoring method is applied" and "Students explain basic skills and concepts included in the curriculum to each other, discuss problems". Students learn themselves while teaching their peers. The authors report this method developed class skills, increased participation by passive students, and fostered cooperation and socialization.
requirements: Peer educators must be selected and trained, with voluntary consent obtained, and the teacher must act as observer and guide.
constraints: The method was applied for four weeks with 7th-grade students in physical education; the article reports no significant attitude advantage over traditional teaching.
target_learning_goals: Attitudes toward physical education and sports
Cooperation and socialization skills
examples: Students selected as peer educators via the Peer Educator Observation Form and 'Who is this?' Test taught lessons for four weeks under teacher guidance.
key_sources: Mustafa Karadağ, Resul Ağirtaş, Atilla Pulur. (2018). Effects of Peer Education on Attitudes of Secondary School Students Towards the Course of Physical Education and Sports. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i4a.3171

article_title: The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes
citation: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274.
title: Pedagogical conditions for forming creative independence: phased creative activity, step-by-step structuring of course content, and problem tasks with linguistic situations
description: The article's conclusion enumerates three pedagogical conditions under which, it states, "the effectiveness of the development of creative independence increases": involving students in creative activity through phases such as transferring skills into a new situation and seeing a new problem in a familiar situation; structuring course content in class and extra-curricular activity according to gradual step-by-step development of creative independent cognitive activity; and organizing cognitive work with intentionally established problem tasks and linguistic situations that realize creative procedures such as analysis, synthesis, heuristic talk and associative mechanisms.
requirements: Organization of students' cognitive work must be provided with intentionally established problem tasks and linguistic situations
constraints: Conditions were tested in foreign-language (English) classes in linguistic higher education
target_learning_goals: creative independent cognitive activity
transfer of skills into new situations
experience of creative procedures
examples: The formative experiment used problem arguing statement, heuristic conversation, heuristic immersion, independent creative tasks, projects and brainstorming as methods
key_sources: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114326

article_title: Using Performance Tasks to Improve Quantitative Reasoning in an Introductory Mathematics Course
citation: Kruse, G. & Drews, D. (2013). Using Performance Tasks to Improve Quantitative Reasoning in an Introductory Mathematics Course. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 7(2), Article 19. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2013.070219
title: Pair open-ended performance tasks with explicit emphasis on the target skill as a course goal and repeated experience with its scoring rubric
description: The article's central design recommendation is that performance tasks alone are insufficient: their impact increases when the course explicitly and repeatedly emphasizes the target skill and gives students repeated experience with the rubric that operationalizes it. The authors state they "produced significant improvements in QR using a combination of performance tasks, emphasis on QR as a course goal, and explicit attention to the definition of that goal via repeated experience with the rubric that operationalizes it." Study 1 versus Study 2 results ground this recommendation.
requirements: Performance tasks modeled on ill-structured, authentic assessment formats
Explicit, repetitive emphasis on the target skill as a legitimate course goal
Repeated student experience with both general and scoring versions of the rubric
constraints: Evidence comes from a single course at one liberal arts college with non-random section assignment; gains apply most clearly to reasoning in a quantitative domain given evidence of domain specificity in critical thinking
target_learners: primarily freshman and sophomore non-majors in an introductory quantitative literacy course
target_learning_goals: quantitative reasoning as critical thinking in the mathematical domain
examples: In Study 2 the syllabus was modified to increase QR emphasis, students built and discussed a rubric for scoring snacks before the first task, graded tasks were returned with detailed rubrics and sample low/high responses, and tasks were revised to sharpen rubric-dimension focus.
key_sources: Kruse, G. & Drews, D. (2013). Using Performance Tasks to Improve Quantitative Reasoning in an Introductory Mathematics Course. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 7(2), Article 19. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2013.070219

article_title: The Effect of Peer Instruction Method on Pre-Service Teachers' Conceptual Comprehension of Methodology Course
citation: Safaa Mohammad Al-Hebaishi. (2017). The Effect of Peer Instruction Method on Pre-Service Teachers' Conceptual Comprehension of Methodology Course. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n3p70
title: Peer instruction lecture sequence: mini-lecture, individual concept-question response, peer discussion, and optional answer revision
description: The article describes a peer instruction lecture as consisting of "various mini-lectures that address key concepts", each followed by a multiple-choice concept question. Students answer individually, discuss their rationale with peers, and are then "given an opportunity to change their responses". The instructor calculates the percentage of correct responses and allocates more time to problematic concepts. In this study the sequence ran weekly for 16 weeks with questions posted on an Edmodo course page.
requirements: Students possess some prior knowledge of the materials before coming to class, supported by pre-class reading
Concept questions should be short, challenging, thought provoking, and contain sufficient ambiguity
constraints: Development of proper concept tests requires significant effort, and covering all semester material in class time is difficult
Students unaccustomed to active participation are often resistant
target_learners: post-graduate pre-service English teachers in a methodology course
target_learning_goals: conceptual comprehension of teaching methodology concepts
examples: In the study, lectures opened with a short presentation of a key concept, students responded to a conceptual multiple-choice question posted on the course page, mingled to share rationales, then revoted after a class discussion led by the instructor as guide and moderator
key_sources: Safaa Mohammad Al-Hebaishi. (2017). The Effect of Peer Instruction Method on Pre-Service Teachers' Conceptual Comprehension of Methodology Course. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n3p70

article_title: Becoming Chemists through Game-Based Inquiry Learning: The Case of "Legends of Alkhimia"
citation: Yam San Chee and Kim Chwee Daniel Tan. (2010). Becoming Chemists through Game-Based Inquiry Learning: The Case of Legends of Alkhimia. Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Volume 8, Issue 1. https://www.ejel.org
title: Performance–Play–Dialog (PPD) model of game-based learning
description: The PPD model is the article's explanatory framework for game-based learning designed around inquiry. Performance is the primary thrust, encompassing development of understanding in the subject domain and construction of self-identity; it is realized through the sub-constructs of play and dialog, which stand in dialectical relation — "3OD\ VXVWDLQV GLDORJ DQG GLDORJ LQIRUPV SOD\". The model holds that "WKH SULPDU\ WKUXVW RI OHDUQLQJ LV GULYHQ E\ SHUIRUPDQFH WKDW HQFRPSDVVHV WKH GHYHORSPHQW RI XQGHUVWDQGLQJ LQ WKH VXEMHFW GRPDLQ DQG WKH FRQVWUXFWLRQ RI VHOI-LGHQWLW\". Play is mediated by embodied engagement with a material digital game world via an avatar, while dialogism, a key Bakhtinian idea, fosters internally persuasive discourse that allows students to construct new ways of meaning. The model underpinned the design and classroom enactment of the Legends of Alkhimia curriculum.
requirements: A coherent, single, substantial digital game enacted as a full curriculum or curricular unit rather than a short embedded resource
Teacher-facilitated classroom dialog following game play, in which student voices are heard, valued, and harnessed in service of student learning
A developmental trajectory of becoming within a professional domain, instantiated through incremental game levels
constraints: The model was developed and evaluated in the domain of lower secondary school chemistry; the article states its principles are applicable to effective design of game-based learning in general but reports evidence only from chemistry
target_learning_goals: learning chemistry through inquiry
developing identity as a chemist
epistemological understanding of the nature of science
scientific argumentation and critique
examples: The curriculum instantiated the model with six levels of game play, each followed by post-gameplay learning activities and teacher-facilitated dialog, with each level targeting one focus of the inquiry cycle
key_sources: Yam San Chee and Kim Chwee Daniel Tan. (2010). Becoming Chemists through Game-Based Inquiry Learning: The Case of Legends of Alkhimia. Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Volume 8, Issue 1. https://www.ejel.org

article_title: Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test
citation: Hawthorne, K. A., Bol, L., Pribesh, S., & Suh, Y. (2015). Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test. Journal of General Education, 64(2). https://doi.org/10.1353/jge.2015.0016
title: Use personalized motivational prompts as a practical, low-cost strategy to enhance performance on low-stakes tests
description: The article recommends that low-stakes testing programs alter test instructions to include personalized motivational prompts appealing to students' sense of the test's usefulness. The authors state that "The use of personalized motivational prompts provides low-stakes testing programs with a practical, sustainable, and low-cost strategy to enhance student performance." This strategy does not require monetary incentives and can be delivered verbally and in writing by a proctor.
requirements: Prompts are delivered verbally by the proctor and in writing before test administration
constraints: The study was limited to four 100-level general education courses at one institution; additional testing in other courses and universities is needed before generalizing
It is difficult to determine if students attended to the motivational prompts
target_learners: undergraduate students in general education courses
target_learning_goals: valid demonstration of general academic competencies (critical thinking, reading, writing, mathematics) on low-stakes outcomes assessments
examples: Four intact classrooms were assigned to control, university, personal, or combined conditions; the personal condition's prompt appealed to students as individuals, and that group scored highest on the ETS PP total mean score.
key_sources: Hawthorne, K. A., Bol, L., Pribesh, S., & Suh, Y. (2015). Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test. Journal of General Education, 64(2). https://doi.org/10.1353/jge.2015.0016

article_title: Performance in an Online Introductory Course in a Hybrid Classroom Setting
citation: Aly, I. (2013). Performance in an online introductory course in a hybrid classroom setting. Canadian Journal of Higher Education, 43(2), 85-99. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103163
title: Quality of instruction and pedagogy matters more than the medium of delivery
description: The article concludes that course instruction and pedagogy are more important for student learning than the type of media delivery. It found that "students receiving only online instruction were as successful as students receiving hybrid classroom instruction", supporting the claim that robust teaching methods matter more than the delivery medium. Online instructors should therefore focus their efforts on quality in developing online courses.
requirements: Instructors must dedicate effort to quality course design and delivery regardless of medium
constraints: Findings are limited to a single introductory managerial accounting course at one university
target_learning_goals: introductory managerial accounting knowledge and skills
examples: The same instructor taught both online and hybrid sections in the same semester using identical learning outcome measurements
key_sources: Aly, I. (2013). Performance in an online introductory course in a hybrid classroom setting. Canadian Journal of Higher Education, 43(2), 85-99. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1013589

article_title: The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Ahangari, S. (2014). The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.81
title: Use paired peer correction of pronunciation to harness social interaction for pronunciation gains
description: The article describes a team frame in which pairs corrected each other's pronunciation: while one partner performed the task, the other took notes, found the correct pronunciation, and shared it. The peer-correction group outperformed the teacher-correction group, which the authors align with Vygotsky's view that learning is "a cognitive activity which takes place in social interaction".
requirements: Learners must work in pairs with one taking notes on the other's pronunciation errors and finding correct forms to share.
constraints: The article notes peer feedback may suffer from problems such as addressing surface errors and offering misleading advice, citing prior literature.
target_learning_goals: pronunciation accuracy in oral narrative production
examples: Pairs alternated performing narrative tasks and noting each other's pronunciation errors, then found and shared correct pronunciations.
key_sources: Ahangari, S. (2014). The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.81

article_title: Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience through Case Studies and Active Learning
citation: Elizabeth A. Holley. (2017). Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience Through Case Studies and Active Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/16-145.1
title: Pebble deposit acid mine drainage evaluation using released environmental baseline data
description: A course exercise in which students "conducted calculations to determine the acid-generating and acid-neutralizing potential of the rocks that host the ore at Pebble" using environmental baseline data released by Anglo American PLC. Students evaluated acid mine drainage risk and proposed other geological, environmental, and social factors to consider. The article notes this is "a unique opportunity for students to work with actual data that would not normally be available for educational use."
requirements: Access to the released Pebble environmental baseline dataset
Supplemental instructional files for the exercise
constraints: Results vary among students depending on the subset of drill-hole samples selected; some conclude the ore is acid generating, others acid neutralizing
target_learning_goals: evaluating acid mine drainage risk from geochemical data
making engineering decisions in scientific gray areas
examples: Students were asked to separate prior opinions from results generated from the dataset and to discuss sampling and statistically valid sample sizes
key_sources: Elizabeth A. Holley. (2017). Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience Through Case Studies and Active Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/16-145.1

article_title: Peer Evaluation of Team Member Effectiveness as a Formative Educational Intervention
citation: Mentzer, N., Laux, D., Zissimopoulos, A., & Richards, K. A. R. (2017). Peer evaluation of team member effectiveness as a formative educational intervention. Journal of Technology Education, 28(2), 53-77. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1144255
title: Use peer evaluation as both a formative feedback and accountability mechanism to complement cooperative learning
description: Peer evaluation of team member effectiveness should be used both to provide meaningful feedback during a project and to hold students accountable for their contributions to team work. The article recommends that educators 'consider using peer evaluation as both a feedback and accountability mechanism for students,' and suggests including both formative and summative peer evaluation in educational experiences to foster teamwork skill and improve learning success.
requirements: A reliable and valid peer evaluation instrument (e.g., CATME) is needed when results factor into student grades.
Students should receive instruction on how to give and receive feedback and interpret results.
constraints: Concerns such as collusion among team members, inflated self-ratings, and evaluation based on personal prejudices must be managed with primers and clear instructions.
target_learning_goals: teamwork skills
individual accountability in group work
examples: In the treatment semester, five cycles of formative peer evaluation were implemented, with two additional early-stage evaluations having no grade impact, allowing students to practice and discuss results.
key_sources: Mentzer, N., Laux, D., Zissimopoulos, A., & Richards, K. A. R. (2017). Peer evaluation of team member effectiveness as a formative educational intervention. Journal of Technology Education, 28(2), 53-77. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1164703

article_title: The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Erfani, S. S., & Nikbin, S. (2015). The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n4p128
title: Use peer-assisted mediation with structured feedback training within dynamic assessment to support EFL writing development.
description: The article recommends training peers to serve as mediators who provide structured feedback on writing within a dynamic assessment framework. Peers were "taught how to provide feedback on the peers' writing at the end of each session" and used a printed reciprocity rating scale as a checklist. The authors state that "EFL tutors may promote techniques of dynamic assessment through peer-assisted mediation, making the peers as mediators via teaching them how to provide feedback to remove the errors."
requirements: Peers must be trained and given a printed rating scale explaining how to rate paragraphs and provide feedback.
constraints: Evidence comes from a quasi-experimental study with intact, non-randomized classes of female intermediate EFL learners, so generalization beyond this population is limited.
target_learning_goals: EFL writing development (organization, punctuation, linking words, descriptive paragraphs)
examples: Participants were divided into pairs, switched assignments, read each other's paragraphs, identified two important errors, gave margin comments in full sentences, and negotiated problems based on the feedback.
key_sources: Erfani, S. S., & Nikbin, S. (2015). The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n4p128

article_title: The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt
citation: Ashraf Atta M. S. Salem. (2013). The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt. English Language Teaching, 6(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n7p33
title: Incorporate peer and group work and self/peer evaluation into writing classes
description: The article recommends introducing "the notion of peer and group work into writing classes instead of the traditional view of writing as an individual activity". It further recommends self and peer evaluation prior to teacher evaluation, and a student-centered environment with minimal teacher intervention during writing.
requirements: Training students to work collaboratively when writing
Self and peer evaluation introduced before teacher evaluation
constraints: Recommended on the basis of a one-group pre-post study without control comparison
target_learners: Prospective teachers of English at faculties of education
target_learning_goals: Writing skills development
Collaborative writing and evaluation practices
examples: In the workshop program, students consulted group peers and their teacher on spelling conventions and shared work in an author's chair celebration.
key_sources: Ashraf Atta M. S. Salem. (2013). The Effect of Using Writer's Workshop Approach on Developing Basic Writing Skills (Mechanics of Writing) of Prospective Teachers of English in Egypt. English Language Teaching, 6(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n7p33

article_title: Impact of clinical case discussions in anatomy on national exam performance: a 10-year longitudinal cohort study.
citation: Fang Fang, Yu Lan, Ou Yetao, Zhou Si, Ma Jun, Peng Yuntao, Liu Fang, Wang Junfeng, Xia Chunbo, Li Houzhong, Zhang Weishan, Cheng Tan, Chen Yu, Huang Yi, Li Xin, Guan Heng. (2026). Impact of clinical case discussions in anatomy on national exam performance: a 10-year longitudinal cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10288-6
title: Periodic renewal of case repository content may be important for sustaining the effectiveness of case-based instruction
description: The article concludes that the decline in the 2021 cohort's integrated performance, which coincided with the case scenarios remaining unchanged since the 2020 cohort, "suggests that periodic content renewal may be important for sustaining the improved performance observed with case-based instruction." This principle recommends regularly updating case-based learning materials to maintain pedagogical effectiveness over time.
requirements: A case-based learning intervention with a repository of case scenarios that can stagnate or be renewed over time
constraints: The article states the decline explanation remains hypothetical, as no direct evidence such as plagiarism detection data or student surveys was collected to confirm the mechanism
target_learning_goals: Integrated clinical-anatomy reasoning in foundational science courses
examples: The case scenarios in this study had remained unchanged since the 2020 cohort, and the 2021 cohort's integrated differential declined sharply to −5.34
key_sources: Fang Fang, Yu Lan, Ou Yetao, Zhou Si, Ma Jun, Peng Yuntao, Liu Fang, Wang Junfeng, Xia Chunbo, Li Houzhong, Zhang Weishan, Cheng Tan, Chen Yu, Huang Yi, Li Xin, Guan Heng. (2026). Impact of clinical case discussions in anatomy on national exam performance: a 10-year longitudinal cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10288-6

article_title: Strengthening clinical capacity in spinal muscular atrophy: Developing and implementing training on clinical outcome assessments.
citation: Osman Homira, Masnata Maria, Adamji Zainab, Rodrigue Xavier, Nguyen Cam-Tu Émilie, Slayter Jeremy, Beattie Erin, Lintern Stacey, Lochmuller Hanns, O'Connell Colleen, Gagnon Cynthia, Warman-Chardon Jodi. (2026). Strengthening clinical capacity in spinal muscular atrophy: Developing and implementing training on clinical outcome assessments. Journal of Neuromuscular Diseases. https://doi.org/10.1177/22143602261416298
title: Peer-led bilingual workshop design combining real-world evaluation videos, simulation, and multidisciplinary case discussion
description: A reusable training design in which experienced clinical evaluators (peer faculty drawn from clinical trial networks) co-develop and deliver bilingual workshops featuring "real-world evaluation videos, simulation-based learning, and multidisciplinary case discussions". Video recordings of real patient evaluations across the clinical spectrum let participants observe standardized assessments, analyze item-level performance, discuss scoring discrepancies, and reach facilitated consensus, mirroring clinical trial training practices. The article reports this format supported clarification of key uncertainties and practical knowledge translation.
requirements: Expert faculty with trial-based COA training and preceptorship experience; recruitment through clinical networks such as RQAS and NMD4C
constraints: Evaluated only on self-reported short-term familiarity and confidence gains, not objective performance or sustained practice change
target_learners: allied health clinical evaluators (PTs, OTs, nurses) in neuromuscular care
target_learning_goals: hands-on competence in administering and scoring SMA motor outcome assessments
examples: Two workshops delivered in English and French with 79 participants; consensus defined as agreement among at least 90 percent of participants
key_sources: Osman Homira, Masnata Maria, Adamji Zainab, Rodrigue Xavier, Nguyen Cam-Tu Émilie, Slayter Jeremy, Beattie Erin, Lintern Stacey, Lochmuller Hanns, O'Connell Colleen, Gagnon Cynthia, Warman-Chardon Jodi. (2026). Strengthening clinical capacity in spinal muscular atrophy: Developing and implementing training on clinical outcome assessments. Journal of Neuromuscular Diseases. https://doi.org/10.1177/22143602261416298

article_title: The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Gökduman Keleş Mine; Göçmez Sema. (2026). The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70603
title: Integrate personalised video-assisted feedback into simulation-based education as a reinforcement strategy
description: The article recommends combining simulation with individualised, video-assisted debriefing in which learners review recordings of their own performance to identify errors. It states that "personalised video‐assisted feedback in simulation‐based training improves midwifery students' knowledge, clinical skills and self‐confidence" and that "Integrating such feedback into education programmes can enhance clinical competence and preparedness for obstetric emergencies." The recommendation is grounded in the RCT findings of higher satisfaction, confidence and selected learning subdimensions.
requirements: A high-fidelity simulator with a camera system for recording performances, and a debriefing room where video review can occur
Structured debriefing time equivalent to the control condition (10 minutes) so feedback, not time on task, is the differing variable
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-university trial with second-year midwifery students; generalisability to other settings or practising clinicians is limited
Theoretical knowledge gains were not statistically significant between groups
target_learning_goals: management of bleeding during pregnancy
obstetric emergency preparedness
clinical decision-making and reflective practice
examples: Students performed a 10-minute simulated intervention on a Noella S551 mannequin; the intervention group then completed a 10-minute video-assisted debriefing while the control group completed structured self-debriefing with a reflection form.
key_sources: Gökduman Keleş Mine; Göçmez Sema. (2026). The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70603

article_title: The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Gökduman Keleş Mine; Göçmez Sema. (2026). The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70603
title: Personalised feedback as individualised, performance-specific information across cognitive, psychomotor and affective domains
description: The article defines personalised feedback in simulation as "individualised, performance‐specific information directed at a learner's cognitive, psychomotor and affective domains, with the aim of improving understanding and guiding targeted skill development". Unlike standardised group debriefing, it addresses each learner's unique errors, gaps and strengths, enabling more precise remediation and deeper clinical learning. The article uses this construct as its independent variable, operationalised through video-assisted debriefing tailored to the individual student's recorded performance.
requirements: Knowledge of each individual learner's specific performance, errors and strengths, obtained here through video recording and instructor observation
constraints: The article notes a lack of specific evidence on how personalised feedback influences long-term skill acquisition in high-risk obstetric emergencies
target_learners: nursing students preparing for critical care roles
target_learning_goals: targeted skill development
deeper clinical learning
self-awareness of performance gaps
examples: Operationalised in the trial as a 10-minute video-assisted debriefing session immediately following a recorded simulation performance.
key_sources: Gökduman Keleş Mine; Göçmez Sema. (2026). The Effect of Personalised Feedback in Simulation on Knowledge and Skills in the Management of Bleeding During Pregnancy: A Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial. Nursing in Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.70603

article_title: First Experience With Using a Simulator in Teaching Physiology of the Cardiovascular System.
citation: Mazgutova N, Mokra D, Calkovska A, Plevkova J, Biringerova Z, Mokry J. (2026). Teaching Physiology-First Experience With Using a Simulator in Teaching Physiology of the Cardiovascular System. Physiological Research. https://doi.org/10.33549/physiolres.935831
title: Alternating peer-practice and simulator small-group rotation within a single practical
description: The modified 90-minute practical split students into two subgroups: one practiced auscultation and blood pressure measurement on each other in pairs in a room without the simulator, while the other worked with the CPS Harvey in small groups of 4-8; groups then alternated. The session used a flipped-classroom design with case notes and protocols provided in advance for pre-class self-study.
requirements: Two rooms, one equipped with the simulator
Pre-class self-study materials distributed in advance
Demonstrators available to support students
constraints: Total duration limited to 90 minutes in the pilot

It informed workshop activity design (student-led discussions, scenario-based teaching, collaborative knowledge sharing) and the interpretation of knowledge and advocacy-motivation shifts, and is credited with creating a cascading effect that broadens the reach of disposal education.
requirements: Trained student ambassadors who have completed experiential engagement before facilitating peer workshops
constraints: The article notes student ambassadors reported varied confidence levels when facilitating discussions, suggesting additional training or rehearsal time may strengthen delivery consistency
target_learners: undergraduate pharmacy students (Year 1 to Year 3) attending peer-led workshops
target_learning_goals: knowledge of safe medication disposal
advocacy motivation
peer education and leadership skills
examples: Phase 2 workshop content was shaped by Phase 1 themes, with student-reported challenges incorporated into case scenarios, discussion prompts, and quiz items

article_title: Clustering of students in pre-clinical medical education and identification of academic performance profiles: does online education work for all medical students?
citation: Goudarzi Houman, Onozawa Masahiro, Ito Yoichi M., Takahashi Makoto. (2026). Clustering of students in pre-clinical medical education and identification of academic performance profiles: does online education work for all medical students? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08737-3
title: Person-centered (cluster) analysis of academic performance as a complement to variable-centered analysis for personalized education
description: The article frames person-centered analysis as a methodological framework that identifies subgroups of individuals based on how variables interrelate within people, in contrast to variable-centered analysis's "one-size-fits-all" aggregate estimates. The authors state that "person-centered analysis facilitates the development of more personalized learning" and that it "directs tailor-made education toward the students in each subgroup via a personalized education approach." They operationalize it with Ward's minimum variance hierarchical clustering on nine standardized variables and connect the resulting profiles to constructivism and self-determination theory.
requirements: A set of multiple standardized learner variables (here nine, including sex, entrance exam score, baseline skills, medical terminology, teaching style, and final exam) measured for enough participants for clustering (the authors cite a rule of thumb of more than 100).
constraints: The number of clusters was chosen by interpretability and educational relevance, an approach the authors state may introduce subjectivity or bias.
The analysis pertained to a single course at a single center, limiting generalizability to other pre-clinical medical education courses and schools.
target_learning_goals: Medical English competencies including doctor-patient interactions, medical terminology, evidence-based medicine, and scientific presentation
examples: The study clustered 321 students into four profiles differing in teaching style exposure, sex ratio, baseline skills, and final exam scores.

Clustering of students in pre-clinical medical education and identification of academic performance profiles: does online education work for all medical students? article_title: Online case-based learning to enhance pediatric endocrinology resident education.
citation: Freeman W, Kanouse A, Frank G. (2026). Online case-based learning to enhance pediatric endocrinology resident education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08517-5
title: Five self-directed online CBL modules in pediatric endocrinology with sequential questions and audiovisual feedback
description: The article describes five online case-based learning modules built in Microsoft PowerPoint and recorded with TechSmith Camtasia as interactive audiovisual files. "Clinical histories were followed by sequential probing questions requiring responses to advance", with multiple-choice and short-response formats. "Immediate feedback with animated audiovisual explanations of mandatory questions was provided for each" question, and modules ranged from 5 to 20 minutes covering growth, puberty, thyroid disorders, sexual differentiation, and calcium metabolism.
requirements: Residents need online access to the recorded audiovisual files and are encouraged to complete modules prior to or early in the rotation
constraints: Content was uniform across year of training and addressed only the five chosen pediatric endocrinology topics
target_learners: first-, second-, and third-year pediatric residents on an outpatient endocrinology elective
target_learning_goals: outpatient pediatric endocrinology concepts including growth, puberty, thyroid disorders, sexual differentiation, and calcium metabolism
examples: Figures 1 and 2 demonstrate the clinician's approach to precocious puberty with audiovisual discussion and follow-up knowledge-acquisition evaluation; Figure 3 shows feedback from the calcium module

article_title: Blended peer-led research curriculum with AI integration improves postgraduate students' academic performance and satisfaction: a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study.
citation: Natto Zuhair S. (2026). Blended peer-led research curriculum with AI integration improves postgraduate students’ academic performance and satisfaction: a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08576-2
title: Conceptual framework integrating adult learning theory and constructivist pedagogy through peer learning, AI-assisted feedback, and blended delivery
description: The study is guided by a framework grounded in adult learning theory and constructivist pedagogy in which three instructional components interact to support research literacy, critical appraisal competence, and engagement. The article states: "The framework posits that three core instructional components—peer learning, AI-assisted feedback, and blended delivery strategies (self-paced videos, in-class tasks)—interact to support students’ development of research literacy, critical appraisal competence, and learning engagement." Peer critique promotes active knowledge construction, AI feedback provides individualized iterative refinement, and blended delivery supports autonomy and flexibility.
requirements: Thoughtful integration of the components so peer critique, AI feedback, and blended delivery reinforce one another
constraints: Hypothesized to produce superior outcomes versus lecture-based instruction; measured performance differences in this pilot did not reach statistical significance
target_learning_goals: Research literacy
Critical appraisal competence
Learning engagement
examples: Reflection prompts and iterative critique tasks required students to externalize their reasoning and progressively refine understanding through authentic research problems

article_title: Empowering medical students: Peer-Led OSCE reduces anxiety and may enhance test performance.
citation: Lima Leonardo Mateus de, Favarato Maria Helena, Tibério Iolanda Fátima Lopes Calvo. (2026). Empowering medical students: Peer-Led OSCE reduces anxiety and may enhance test performance. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0340407
title: Peer-led mock OSCE intervention (student-designed and student-administered mock Objective Structured Clinical Examination)
description: A formative assessment activity in which students conceptualize and administer a mock OSCE before the summative exam. Twelve students spent four hours designing five stations with scenarios and checklists, then acted as examiners for sixteen examinee peers, with each six-minute station followed by "one additional minute for immediate feedback". A supervising professor "corrected conceptual errors without altering the structure of the stations". The element was evaluated in a randomized controlled trial against a no-intervention control group.
requirements: A supervising professor to allocate station topics and rectify content-specific inaccuracies
An online course covering OSCE history, station and checklist design, and exam organization
Station themes drawn from the semester's covered course content
constraints: The professor did not modify station structure, only inaccuracies in medical knowledge
Seven students randomized to the intervention could not attend due to academic scheduling conflicts and were reassigned to control
target_learners: Fifth-semester medical students taking their first summative OSCE
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills practice (history taking, physical examination, communication)
Familiarity with OSCE format and reduced test anxiety
examples: Mock stations covered low back pain, heart failure, trigeminal neuralgia, pleural effusion, and LGBTQIA+ health; the summative OSCE one week later used five faculty-examined stations scored 0–10

article_title: Lived experiences of peer learning to improve the professional capabilities of hospital managers: a phenomenological study.
citation: Tabatabaei Far SS, Ahmadi Marzaleh M, Moradi Farahani M, Jafari F, Sarooeyeh F. (2025). Lived experiences of peer learning to improve the professional capabilities of hospital managers: a phenomenological study. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07616-2
title: Peer learning among hospital managers operationalizes social learning and constructivist mechanisms, with mutual trust, openness, and reflective dialogue as enabling conditions
description: The article interprets managers' peer-learning experiences through social learning theory and constructivist perspectives emphasizing the social and interactive nature of learning. Managers described "observing their peers' approaches to complex managerial challenges and subsequently adapting these strategies within their own contexts," reflecting learning through imitation, reflection, and contextual adaptation. Consistent with Vygotsky's scaffolding and collaborative dialogue, peer interactions let participants construct meaning collectively and build competence. The authors add mutual trust, openness, and reflective dialogue as enabling conditions for professional growth.
requirements: Mutual trust, openness, and reflective dialogue among participants, as enabling conditions the article identifies
constraints: The authors caution that attributing improvements solely to peer learning may risk oversimplification without examining institutional culture or motivational factors
target_learning_goals: Managerial competencies such as decision-making, critical thinking, and collaborative problem-solving
examples: Managers in the study observed peers' approaches to complex managerial challenges and adapted those strategies in their own hospitals.

citation: Cevheroğlu Seda, Fırat Kılıç Hülya, Budak Vildan. (2025). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08258-5
title: PechaKucha as a concise 20×20 visual presentation format whose effects are explained by reduced cognitive load
description: The article describes PechaKucha as "a structured presentation format in which 20 slides are displayed for 20 s each, resulting in a concise, time-bound delivery", emphasizing visual storytelling over text-heavy slides. It invokes Cognitive Load Theory as the explanatory account: "The concise, visual format of PechaKucha likely reduced cognitive load, enabling students to process procedural steps in DB&C exercises more efficiently." The fast-paced, structured delivery is proposed to maintain attention and engagement during psychomotor skill instruction.
requirements: Faculty review and pilot applications of the presentation; the article states the final version was reviewed by Nursing Fundamentals faculty and piloted for clarity and feasibility.
constraints: The article notes some prior studies found no significant knowledge improvements and that the rapid pace may hinder grasping highly detailed, comprehensive content, so content suitability must be evaluated before implementation.
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skill acquisition such as deep breathing and coughing exercises
engagement and satisfaction with instruction
examples: The study delivered DB&C training as a 20-slide, approximately 7-minute PechaKucha presentation with automatic slide advance while the instructor demonstrated each procedural step.

citation: Ramos Tierle Kosloski; Cogo Silvana Bastos; Nietsche Elisabeta Albertina; Salbego Cléton; Backes Vania Marli Schubert; Adamy Edlamar Kátia; Freitas Etiane de Oliveira; Baixinho Cristina Lavareda. title: Perrenoud's formative assessment framework as the theoretical basis of IAFEE-ECS®
description: The instrument is grounded in Philippe Perrenoud's theoretical framework for formative assessment, under which "assessment is not an objective in itself, but a means of verifying whether students have acquired the necessary knowledge and, based on this, managing teaching situations". Formative assessment is characterized as "a device for individualizing the training process and differentiating interventions with each student". The framework also holds that learning is never linear, occurring through tests, trials and errors, and defends self-regulation to stimulate student self-development and self-learning.
requirements: Assessment must be analyzed as a component of a system of action, never in itself
constraints: Most teaching methods are not designed by a differentiated pedagogy resulting from formative assessment
target_learners: Nursing students in supervised curricular internship
target_learning_goals: Regulation of learning through continuous formative assessment
Student self-regulation of their own learning

article_title: On the influence of social norms on individual achievement goals.
citation: Bossert, S., Daumiller, M., Janke, S., Dresel, M., & Dickhäuser, O. (2025). On the influence of social norms on individual achievement goals. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 924–940. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12756
title: Peer achievement goals as descriptive social norms in the classroom, grounded in adolescent peer influence
description: The article proposes that classmates' achievement goals act as descriptive norms for individual students. It argues that in the classroom, classmates represent a crucial peer context, and that particularly during adolescence peers are the most important source of normative influence, with students aligning their attitudes and behaviour to peers to foster a positive self-image. Because students remain in fixed groups of classmates across subjects and over significant periods, all classmates can be frequent interaction partners and be referred to as peers. The article positions this account as complementing goal contagion explanations, which describe how people appear to catch and pursue goals implied by others' behaviours but lack a clear process; the social norms approach supplies an overarching theme that contagion research has not taken into account.
requirements: A stable peer context: students remaining in fixed groups of classmates over significant periods of their education
constraints: Operationalized as class-mean achievement goals; the article notes it could not differentiate peers by closeness, possibly underestimating the effect
target_learning_goals: Adoption and change of individual achievement goals
examples: Peer achievement goals were calculated as means of class-wise aggregated individual achievement goals and used as Level-2 predictors
key_sources: Bossert, S., Daumiller, M., Janke, S., Dresel, M., & Dickhäuser, O. (2025). On the influence of social norms on individual achievement goals. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 924–940. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12756

article_title: Perceived peer support, motivational self-regulation and academic achievement in adolescents.
citation: Villar, E., Real‐Deus, E., Martínez‐López, Z., Mayo, M. E., & Tinajero, C. (2025). Perceived peer support, motivational self‐regulation and academic achievement in adolescents. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 1325–1346. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12783
title: Consider peer support when creating a classroom climate conducive to engagement and learning
description: The article recommends that peer support be treated as a design consideration for classroom climate because peer support significantly affected motivational self-regulation and MRSs mediated the support–achievement relationship. The authors state that "peer support must be considered when the intention is to create a classroom climate conducive to engagement and learning", and that peers "seem to encourage autonomous types of regulation and address the lack of motivation in students".
requirements: Peer relationships must be available within the classroom setting for the provisions of emotional support, guidance and reassurance of worth to operate
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional and preliminary; the authors state the proposed model should be validated using longitudinal data and that directionality could not be established
target_learning_goals: motivational self-regulation
academic engagement
academic achievement
examples: In the studied sample, guidance from peers reduced work-avoidance self-talk, thereby improving achievement, and reassurance of worth positively mediated achievement via cost appraisal

Reliabilities were 0.73, 0.73, and 0.83 respectively, with CFA fit indices within acceptable thresholds.

constraints: The Hope for the Utility of University subscale was removed due to a negative factor loading before analysis

academic hope
academic engagement
examples: All three scales were completed on physical copies during 15 minutes of class time over one month

article_title: Effectiveness of video-based peer feedback in self-training for skill acquisition among surgical residents.
citation: Lu Chen, Gong Bin, Zhang Xiaochen, Wu Chengcheng, Yang Jin. (2025). Effectiveness of video-based peer feedback in self-training for skill acquisition among surgical residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08029-2
title: Pedagogical account of video-based peer feedback: cognitive alignment and reciprocal metacognitive engagement explain its effectiveness
description: The article frames VPF's benefits through two mechanisms drawn from prior literature: "the cognitive alignment between learners at similar competency levels improves feedback comprehension and implementation", and "the reciprocal nature of peer assessment promotes deeper metacognitive engagement and reflective practice". In this account, giving structured feedback on a peer's recorded performance is itself a learning act — critically evaluating others enhances one's own skill acquisition — while expert feedback remains the technical-accuracy gold standard but faces scalability and resource constraints.
requirements: Structured feedback tools (standardized checklists) to control peer leniency bias
Tasks of moderate complexity where peers share a comparable competency level
constraints: The account is presented as motivation from cited literature, not tested mechanistically in this trial
Effectiveness may be compromised when task complexity exceeds learners' peer competency level
target_learners: learners in video-based clinical skills training
target_learning_goals: clinical skill acquisition through self-training with feedback
examples: The trial operationalized the account by having VPF participants act as both trainer and trainee, scoring a randomly matched peer's video

title: PEACE-Q Br: a 33-item, nine-domain Brazilian Portuguese palliative care knowledge questionnaire for medical residents
description: The PEACE-Q Br is a translated, cross-culturally adapted version of the Japanese PEACE-Q knowledge questionnaire for assessing physicians' palliative care knowledge. The article reports that "The translated version of the instrument comprised 33 items divided into nine domains, with a content validity index of 0.95." Five Japan-specific items (2, 3, 31, 32, and 33) were replaced with new items reflecting the Brazilian healthcare context, developed by the authors and confirmed by a nine-expert committee. Domains cover philosophy of palliative care, oncological pain, opioid side effects, dyspnea, nausea and vomiting, psychological distress, delirium, communication, and palliative care in the community.

A nine-expert committee assessing conceptual, idiomatic, semantic, and experiential equivalence
A pre-test sample separate from the test-retest sample
constraints: Validated at a single institution (Santa Casa BH, Belo Horizonte); the authors state further studies are needed in different contexts
Internal consistency (KR-20 = 0.60) is lower than the original version's validation

examples: Administered to 102 medical residents at Santa Casa BH between February and May 2023, with retest after seven days

article_title: Does mental imagery make a difference in virtual reality simulation training? Results of a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Sparn Moritz B., Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Warschkow Rene, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2025). Does mental imagery make a difference in virtual reality simulation training? Results of a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy 39(10). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12012-9
title: Structured 15-minute guided PETTLEP mental imagery session on laparoscopic cholecystectomy delivered before VR simulation training
description: The intervention was a structured 15-minute guided mental imagery session delivered by an experienced laparoscopic surgeon before VRST, "based on the PETTLEP framework (Physical, Environment, Task, Timing, Learning, Emotion, and Perspective), incorporating multisensory cues". Trainees vividly imagined performing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, focusing on camera navigation, tissue handling, and dissection steps, practicing both visual and kinesthetic imagery. Technical steps followed the SAGES Safe Cholecystectomy Program and current guidelines.
requirements: An experienced laparoscopic surgeon guides the session
Content aligned with current safe-cholecystectomy guidelines and best practice
constraints: The session was short (15 minutes) and focused on procedural and safety aspects, omitting detailed rehearsal of complex psychomotor skills; the quality of the MI video was not externally validated
target_learners: novice laparoscopic surgeons with no more than three years of clinical experience
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic cholecystectomy procedural knowledge and safety-relevant surgical technique
examples: Delivered at the 2023 Davos Course to 69 MI-group participants immediately before 90 minutes of VRST, in a 2:1 randomized allocation against VRST alone
key_sources: Sparn Moritz B., Chatziisaak Dimitrios, Warschkow Rene, Schmied Bruno, Hahnloser Dieter, Bischofberger Stephan. (2025). Does mental imagery make a difference in virtual reality simulation training? Results of a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy 39(10). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12012-9

article_title: Integration of team-based learning and simulation-based learning in clinical education of infant feeding and swallowing assessment and management of speech-language pathology students: a retrospective pre-post intervention study.
citation: Kwan Connie Ching-Yin, Weir Kelly Ann, Fong Raymond, Pereira Valerie Jane, Law Thomas. (2025). Integration of team-based learning and simulation-based learning in clinical education of infant feeding and swallowing assessment and management of speech-language pathology students: a retrospective pre-post intervention study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07721-7
title: PEDS VITALS patient monitor simulator for live vital-sign display during infant simulation
description: PEDS VITALS is a computerized paediatric patient monitor simulator application used in the case simulation clinic to display the low-fidelity infant mannequin's vital signs in real time. The article states it "was used to provide the instant display of vital signs of saturation level, heart rate and respiratory rate of the low fidelity mannequin throughout the session", controlled by the instructor from a tablet device, complemented by verbal narration of clinical signs such as coughing and SpO2 readings.
requirements: An instructor controlling the monitor simulator from a separate tablet device
A low-fidelity infant mannequin whose displayed vital signs the application drives
constraints: Used within a hybrid simulation that also relied on instructor verbal narration of clinical signs
target_learning_goals: observing and interpreting infant physiological cues during feeding assessment
examples: Instructor-narrated signs paired with monitor readings, e.g. "The infant is coughing, Pulse oximetry is reading 80% SpO2."
key_sources: Kwan Connie Ching-Yin, Weir Kelly Ann, Fong Raymond, Pereira Valerie Jane, Law Thomas. (2025). Integration of team-based learning and simulation-based learning in clinical education of infant feeding and swallowing assessment and management of speech-language pathology students: a retrospective pre-post intervention study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07721-7

article_title: Evaluating the effectiveness of flight simulator training on developing perceptual-motor skills among flight cadets: a pilot study.
citation: Zhang Yang, Chen Jie, Zhong Xiao, Shao Yongcong, Fu Weiwei. (2025). Evaluating the effectiveness of flight simulator training on developing perceptual-motor skills among flight cadets: a pilot study. Scientific Reports 15, 28062. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-12929-0
title: Perceptual-motor skills theory combined with multimodal feedback and expert-template observation as an account of accelerated flight skill acquisition
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that perceptual abilities are malleable and improvable through sustained training, and that flight skills arise from the brain synthesizing "visual, auditory, and kinesthetic cues" into accurate behavioral responses. It adds a mirror-neuron account: observing actions activates the regions that execute stored movements, so "individuals learn through observation, enhancing both skill acquisition and performance". Directly providing expert behavioral templates reduces corrective attempts and reinforces the correct learning pathway. Combined with multimodal feedback, this explains why expert-action replay plus repeated practice accelerates the transition of motor skills into the automated phase.
requirements: Sustained training and exposure for perceptual abilities to improve
Expert-standard action templates presented before practice for the imitation mechanism to operate
constraints: Performance gains slow as cadets approach expert level on complex tasks such as landing and carrier landing
target_learning_goals: acquisition and automatization of perceptual-motor flight skills
key_sources: Zhang Yang, Chen Jie, Zhong Xiao, Shao Yongcong, Fu Weiwei. (2025). Evaluating the effectiveness of flight simulator training on developing perceptual-motor skills among flight cadets: a pilot study. Scientific Reports 15, 28062. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-12929-0

article_title: Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care.
citation: Wood, L., Williams, C., Luxon, L., Kumary, A., & Roth, A. (2025). Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care. Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice, 98, 553–569. https://doi.org/10.1111/papt.12575
title: Review and update competency frameworks every 5–10 years with a systematic literature search and ERG consultation
description: The article recommends that competency frameworks be treated as living documents requiring periodic review. It states "we recommend that all competency frameworks should be reviewed approximately every 5–10 years based on research lifecycles and policy development timeframes", and that a review should include a systematic search of newly published relevant literature and consultation with an Expert Reference Group to decide updates. This responds to the authors' observation that no best-practice guidelines for reviewing frameworks currently exist.
requirements: A systematic search of newly published relevant literature and establishment and consultation with an ERG during each review
constraints: No existing best-practice guidelines for reviewing and updating competency frameworks; the recommended interval is the authors' own proposal
target_learning_goals: Keeping competency frameworks aligned with current best practice
examples: The authors propose this process in the Discussion as a substitute for the absent standard review procedures
key_sources: Wood, L., Williams, C., Luxon, L., Kumary, A., & Roth, A. (2025). Developing a psychosocial competency framework for adult and older adult acute mental health inpatient care. Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice, 98, 553–569. https://doi.org/10.1111/papt.12575

article_title: Happiness training effect on primary school teachers' academic burnout and teaching effectiveness: narratives from teachers.
citation: Liu Yongmei, Xie Jian. (2025). Happiness training effect on primary school teachers’ academic burnout and teaching effectiveness: narratives from teachers. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02985-6
title: Ten-session PERMA-based happiness training workshop for primary school teachers
description: The intervention is a happiness training workshop "based on the principles of positive psychology and Seligman’s PERMA model", consisting of "10 sessions over 5 weeks", each lasting 2 hours and facilitated by a trained positive psychology coach. Sessions cover positive emotions (gratitude journaling, mindfulness), engagement and flow, positive relationships, meaning, accomplishment and goal-setting, resilience, mindfulness and stress reduction, long-term maintenance via a Happiness Action Plan, and reflection and future planning (Table 1).
requirements: A trained positive psychology coach to facilitate sessions
Sequential delivery across 5 weeks with teachers applying principles in everyday teaching
constraints: Evaluated in this study only with primary school teachers and without a control group
target_learning_goals: Reducing burnout
Enhancing well-being
Improving teaching effectiveness
examples: Session 2 used gratitude journaling about three things participants are thankful for daily plus guided mindfulness meditation; Session 6 was a goal-setting workshop on short- and long-term goals
key_sources: Liu Yongmei, Xie Jian. (2025). Happiness training effect on primary school teachers’ academic burnout and teaching effectiveness: narratives from teachers. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02985-6

article_title: Understanding the roles of grit and well-being in L2 achievement among Chinese university english learners.
citation: Li Gengchun. (2025). Understanding the roles of grit and well-being in L2 achievement among Chinese university english learners. BMC Psychology, 13, 576. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02933-4
title: Seligman's PERMA theory of well-being as the framework for L2 learner well-being
description: The article adopts Seligman's PERMA theory, which "systematically delineates the construct through five dimensions: positive emotions (P), engagement (E), relationships (R), meaning (M), and accomplishment (A)". Within L2 research the article states the PERMA model "has gained prominence as the most influential theoretical framework". The study operationalized the five elements with 15 items from the PERMA-Profiler and used them as hypothesized mediators between grit and L2 achievement. The theory grounds the study's hypothesis that grit predicts achievement through well-being.
requirements: Measurement of the five well-being elements requires a validated instrument such as the PERMA-Profiler used in this study
constraints: The article states the PERMA-Profiler is a domain-general scale, and L2 well-being may exhibit domain specificity, limiting what it can reveal about L2 learning
target_learning_goals: Second language achievement
learner well-being
examples: The study measured the five PERMA elements with 15 PERMA-Profiler items (Cronbach's α for the overall scale = 0.929) and tested them as mediators in an SEM model
key_sources: Li Gengchun. (2025). Understanding the roles of grit and well-being in L2 achievement among Chinese university english learners. BMC Psychology, 13, 576. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02933-4

article_title: Optimizing skill acquisition: the role of self-assessment during a continuous training program for laparoscopic suturing.
citation: Hillemans V, Verhoeven DJ, van de Mortel X, Bökkerink GMJ, Botden SMBI, Joosten M, de Blaauw I. (2025). Optimizing skill acquisition: the role of self-assessment during a continuous training program for laparoscopic suturing. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-11682-9
title: Use self-assessment with reflection before practice during laparoscopic suturing training, at a lower (periodic) frequency, since it yields comparable benefits to continuous use with greater efficiency
description: The article recommends incorporating self-assessment and reflection before practice into laparoscopic suturing training: participants study an assessment form beforehand and complete it afterwards. Because "a lower frequency of self-assessment and reflection before practice offered comparable benefits", the authors state it "optimizes training efficiency, and is therefore recommended". The benefit appears in instrument-use safety and efficiency parameters rather than in task time or distance.
requirements: Training must use a validated self-assessment form (the LS-CAT) studied before practice and completed afterwards
Access to a laparoscopic box trainer and instrument-tracking software for feedback data
constraints: Benefits appeared in secondary parameters (off-screen, acceleration, smoothness), not in the primary time and distance parameters
A single self-assessment use showed no immediate effect at the pre-test, and its later learning-curve impact was not investigated
target_learners: Junior doctors not yet in surgical training
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic intracorporeal suturing skill
Safe and efficient instrument handling
examples: The periodic SA group applied reflection before practice and self-assessment only at the three test moments during a two-week intensive schedule followed by three months of biweekly practice
key_sources: Hillemans V, Verhoeven DJ, van de Mortel X, Bökkerink GMJ, Botden SMBI, Joosten M, de Blaauw I. (2025). Optimizing skill acquisition: the role of self-assessment during a continuous training program for laparoscopic suturing. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-11682-9

article_title: Learning to teach by teaching your peers: exploring students' needs for training in the undergraduate medical education curriculum.
citation: George SS, Bonnevier A, Stenfors T, Kenne E. (2025). Learning to teach by teaching your peers: exploring students’ needs for training in the undergraduate medical education curriculum. BMC Medical Education 25(1):414. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07022-z
title: Design peer-teacher training that combines a theoretical base with contextualized practical teaching experience and feedback
description: The article recommends that peer teaching in undergraduate medical education be supported by training combining a theoretical base in evidence-based pedagogy with contextualized, realistic practical teaching experiences accompanied by feedback. Students stated that "a training program to include a theoretical base and to learn by contextualized practical experiences with feedback" is what they want. Implementation should consider timing, the subject area taught, and proper training for peer teachers.
requirements: Time allocated in the schedule for peer teaching and training
Quality assurance mechanisms such as formative feedback and assessment of peer teachers
Clear guidelines for the peer teaching assignment
constraints: Students held mixed opinions about making peer teaching mandatory; concerns included unmotivated teachers lowering quality for peer learners and curriculum overload
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students acting as peer teachers
target_learning_goals: Teaching skills
Communication and supervision skills
Evidence-based understanding of how people learn
examples: Students suggested role play, shadowing a professional, interactive small group teaching, and having senior students supervise junior peers in clinical skills as practice with feedback
key_sources: George SS, Bonnevier A, Stenfors T, Kenne E. (2025). Learning to teach by teaching your peers: exploring students’ needs for training in the undergraduate medical education curriculum. BMC Medical Education 25(1):414. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07022-z

article_title: The application effectiveness of the "One Case to the End" teaching model based on BOPPPS in pediatric nursing: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Xiao Xuejun, Xie Ying, Zhao Xiangfeng, Dai Xiaohong, Liang Feng, Wang Wanchao, Zhang Xianhua. (2025). The application effectiveness of the “One Case to the End” teaching model based on BOPPPS in pediatric nursing: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07073-2
title: Clinical case library of over 30 cases in three pediatric nursing modules
description: A curated set of real clinical cases built by the course supervisor with pediatric clinical teachers, containing "Over 30 clinical cases have been collected" from the NICU and pediatric wards, categorized into three modules: Home Health Care and Nursing for Children, Nursing Care for Common Pediatric Diseases, and Nursing for Pediatric Critical Illnesses. Each case includes clinical data and tiered questions for theoretical and laboratory classes; the same cases were used for both to guarantee coherence of knowledge.
requirements: Common diseases from the past three years with 2–4 typical diseases per system and complete clinical data, reviewed by the course coordinator
target_learning_goals: applying pediatric nursing theory in realistic clinical scenarios
examples: Demonstration cases include a 1-month-old well-child visit, a 2-year-old malnutrition case, and a febrile-seizure case, each with theory-class and laboratory-class question sets.
