article_title: pECGreview: Assessment of a Novel Tool to Evaluate the Accuracy of Pediatric ECG Interpretation Skills.
citation: Jacquemyn Xander, Guerrier Karine, Harvey Evan, Tackett Sean, Kutty Shelby, Wetzel Glenn T. (2024). pECGreview: Assessment of a Novel Tool to Evaluate the Accuracy of Pediatric ECG Interpretation Skills. Pediatric Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00246-024-03556-z
title: pECGreview: a web-based, ECG-of-the-week training program with commit-then-feedback design and a large multicenter interpretation database
description: pECGreview is a web-based, ECG-of-the-week style program hosted on REDCap that presents a weekly pediatric ECG with brief clinical history and asks participants to "commit to a specific interpretation of each week's pECG" before receiving the official interpretation and teaching points. Since April 2019, 31 pediatric cardiology fellowship training centers and 630 participants have enrolled, mostly in local reading groups with a facilitator. It has generated the first reported large-scale database of repeated pediatric ECG interpretations by physicians at multiple training stages.
requirements: Participants submit free-text interpretations and a required Severity score; a local facilitator is available to provide feedback in most enrollment settings
constraints: Participants are not required to submit interpretations, so the cohort is variable for each ECG; the ECG-of-the-week format tests interpretation outside a true clinical context
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of pediatric electrocardiograms, including dysrhythmia recognition
examples: Response data from 19 ECGs interpreted between 1/29/22 and 6/25/22 were analyzed, yielding 1460 completed responses from 192 participants
key_sources: Jacquemyn Xander, Guerrier Karine, Harvey Evan, Tackett Sean, Kutty Shelby, Wetzel Glenn T. (2024). pECGreview: Assessment of a Novel Tool to Evaluate the Accuracy of Pediatric ECG Interpretation Skills. Pediatric Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00246-024-03556-z

article_title: Juxtaposing pedagogical paradigms: the efficacy of peer-assisted learning (PAL) versus faculty-assisted learning (FAL) in the refinement of surgical proficiency.
citation: Vijayan Santhosh Thekkoot, Kattuparambil Jithin Joshy, Mani Praveen Thichur, Chirukandath Ravindran, Antony Manoj. (2025). Juxtaposing pedagogical paradigms: the efficacy of peer-assisted learning (PAL) versus faculty-assisted learning (FAL) in the refinement of surgical proficiency. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11846272/
title: Peyton's four-step approach as a structured framework for psychomotor skill acquisition
description: Peyton's four-step approach is a structured method for teaching psychomotor skills comprising four sequential stages: "Demonstration ‑faculty/peer teacher demonstrates suturing techniques on a mannequin at normal pace without any comments", deconstruction where the tutor repeats the procedure describing all necessary steps, comprehension where the teacher repeats the procedure following the trainee's instructions while others watch, and performance where the trainee performs while others watch and then receives feedback. The article describes it as "the gold standard for teaching psychomotor skills" and applies it identically in both PAL and FAL conditions, noting its ideal implementation requires a 1:1 teacher-to-student ratio that is rarely feasible.
requirements: A structured framework that fosters effective skill acquisition through demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension, and performance stages
constraints: Its ideal implementation requires a 1:1 teacher-to-student ratio, which is rarely feasible due to faculty shortages and increasing educator workload
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students learning psychomotor surgical skills
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill acquisition such as suturing techniques
examples: The study used Peyton's four-step approach to teach interrupted, vertical mattress, and continuous suturing with 2-0 silk on a mannequin (Opsys 3-layer suture practice pad OP-25)
key_sources: Vijayan Santhosh Thekkoot, Kattuparambil Jithin Joshy, Mani Praveen Thichur, Chirukandath Ravindran, Antony Manoj. (2025). Juxtaposing pedagogical paradigms: the efficacy of peer-assisted learning (PAL) versus faculty-assisted learning (FAL) in the refinement of surgical proficiency. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11846272/

article_title: Development and Implementation of a Pediatric Pulmonary-Focused Active Learning Curriculum.
citation: Vaziri Sanaz MD, Neemuchwala Fatima MD, Lim Janet MD, Chan Marilynn MD. (2024). Development and Implementation of a Pediatric Pulmonary–Focused Active Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11470
title: Four interactive case-based e-learning modules on pediatric pulmonary topics built in Articulate Rise 360
description: The article describes four case-based, interactive e-learning modules on asthma, chronic cough, tracheostomy, and obstructive sleep apnea, created in the Articulate Rise 360 platform, which was chosen for its "user-friendly interface and wide range of interactive features including quizzes, simulations, and scenarios". Each case follows a virtual patient from chief complaint through history, exam, differential, workup, and treatment, with videos, flashcards, audio clips, and continue-button dividers controlling navigation. Modules were published on the UCSF Learning Center website and distributed by email for self-paced completion during the elective.
requirements: Faculty-recorded expert videos and interactive elements (quizzes, flashcards, audio clips) to maintain engagement
Access via an institutional learning website with credentials so completion status can be monitored
constraints: Each module required a 2-week creation period by a single developer, including revision time from feedback
target_learners: medical students on a pediatric pulmonology elective
target_learning_goals: diagnosing common childhood pulmonary conditions
managing chronic cough, asthma, OSA, and tracheostomy care
proper inhaler technique (metered dose, dry powder, redihalers)
examples: Cases included Alexa, a 7-year-old with asthma; Adam, a 13-month-old with tracheostomy and ventilator dependence; Matteo, a 5-year-old with protracted bacterial bronchitis; and Sean, a 6-year-old with sleep apnea
key_sources: Vaziri Sanaz MD, Neemuchwala Fatima MD, Lim Janet MD, Chan Marilynn MD. (2024). Development and Implementation of a Pediatric Pulmonary–Focused Active Learning Curriculum. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11470

article_title: Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice.
citation: Smith Christopher J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory MD, Wardian Jana PhD, MSW, Sahak Khalid MD. (2024). Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11476
title: Peyton's four-step model for skills training integrated into Gagne's framework
description: Peyton's four-step model is an evidence-based approach to teaching clinical skills with four steps: demonstration (teacher performs without explanation), deconstruction (teacher performs while explaining each step), reconstruction (teacher performs while the learner explains each step), and performance (learner performs and describes the skill). The workshop integrated it into Gagne's framework to give more detailed instruction for the learning-guidance and learner-performance steps, and a cited meta-analysis found students trained with Peyton's model "had higher skills performance scores and required less time to complete the procedure than students receiving traditional teaching methods."
requirements: Teacher models the procedure across the demonstration, deconstruction, and reconstruction steps before learner performance
target_learning_goals: acquisition and teaching of procedural (psychomotor) skills
examples: The workshop didactic described Peyton's four-step model within the context of Gagne's model, and participants answered a knowledge question about it
key_sources: Smith Christopher J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory MD, Wardian Jana PhD, MSW, Sahak Khalid MD. (2024). Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11476

article_title: Flipped classroom-based application of Peyton's four-step approach in standardized training of ultrasound residents for thyroid and cervical lymph node zoning.
citation: Wang Jiajia, Zhan Yunyun, Sun Biyun, Bi Yu, Li Rubing, Jiang Fan, Peng Mei. (2024). Flipped classroom-based application of Peyton’s four-step approach in standardized training of ultrasound residents for thyroid and cervical lymph node zoning. PeerJ. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.18633
title: Peyton's four-step approach as a staged clinical skills teaching model
description: Peyton's four-step approach is a skill-teaching method comprising four structured stages: "demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension, and performance". The instructor first performs the scan without theoretical explanation, then lectures while repeating scans, then has trainees recite the procedure while the instructor scans and corrects errors, and finally trainees perform independently. The article applies it to ultrasound scanning of the thyroid and cervical lymph nodes and reports it as aligned with human cognitive learning, particularly through the comprehension stage's self-assessment via guiding others.
requirements: Instructors assigned to the method completed at least three consecutive months of training in Peyton's four-step approach for US teaching before teaching activities began
constraints: Its application in ultrasound skills education is described as relatively limited, suggesting the necessity of further exploration and validation in this specialized domain
target_learners: ultrasound resident trainees in standardized residency training
target_learning_goals: ultrasound skill operation
anatomical localization of cervical lymph node zones
ultrasound image interpretation
examples: In the observation group, weeks 2, 3, and 4 centered on the four stages of demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension, and performance to enhance skill development
key_sources: Wang Jiajia, Zhan Yunyun, Sun Biyun, Bi Yu, Li Rubing, Jiang Fan, Peng Mei. (2024). Flipped classroom-based application of Peyton’s four-step approach in standardized training of ultrasound residents for thyroid and cervical lymph node zoning. PeerJ. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.18633

article_title: Does an aptitude for surgery exist and can we predict it? An experimental study.
citation: Ruchay Zino, Julian Pape, Julia-Sophie Cordt, Carolina Kerres, Sebastian Siehl, Karina Jansone, Johannes Ackermann, Veronika Guenther, Liselotte Mettler, Leila Allahqoli, Nicolai Maass, Frauke Nees, Ibrahim Alkatout. (2024). Does an aptitude for surgery exist and can we predict it? An experimental study. International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000001577
title: Incorporate personality traits and motivation into surgical training curricula
description: The article argues that surgical training curricula should extend beyond technical skill components to include individual traits. As stated: "Our results highlight the importance of incorporating additional factors such as personality traits and motivation in future training curricula". The authors suggest curriculum advancement may include individual adjustment, such as intensified simulator or virtual reality training before in vivo surgery when personality factors like neuroticism are prominent, and evaluation of psychomotor skill levels during medical school.
requirements: Existing training curricula with technical skill components that can be extended with trait assessment
constraints: The authors note there is inconsistent evidence of skill transfer between conventional and robotic training methods, and further research is needed on interrelationships of training techniques
target_learning_goals: surgical training performance
selection and allocation of suited trainees
examples: The authors propose a checkup of psychomotor skills levels within medical school or training curricula, and training of specific psychomotor skills outside the operation theater for individuals low in these skills

article_title: Be prepared! Impact of structured video-assisted coaching on performance in a simulated bleeding exercise during laparoscopic surgery.
citation: Chatziisaak D, Sparn M, Krstic D, Bauci G, Warschkow R, Brunner W, Schmied B, Hahnloser D, Bischofberger S. (2024). Be prepared! Impact of structured video-assisted coaching on performance in a simulated bleeding exercise during laparoscopic surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11173-3
title: Perfused porcine bleeding simulation exercise with tablet-recorded video assessment
description: A simulation exercise in which trainees face simulated emergency bleeding during laparoscopy using "perfused porcine aorta/kidney specimens that exhibited arterial hemorrhage from a lumbar artery" in box trainers with the P.O.P Pulsating Organ Perfusion system. Participants had 5 minutes to control the bleeding; all exercises were recorded via a tablet with a prototype web-based application for cloud upload and later blinded GOALS assessment. Bleeding location varied per exercise.
requirements: Perfused porcine organ specimens, a full laparoscopy unit with hemostasis instruments, box trainers, and a video recording/upload application for later assessment
constraints: Bleeding location varied for each exercise; participants were unaware of the task at the first exercise
target_learners: advanced surgical trainees in a colorectal surgery module
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic hemostasis and emergency bleeding management under stress
examples: Used across four sequences on two days at the 40th Annual Davos Course, each participant operating once as surgeon and once as assistant
key_sources: Chatziisaak D, Sparn M, Krstic D, Bauci G, Warschkow R, Brunner W, Schmied B, Hahnloser D, Bischofberger S. (2024). Be prepared! Impact of structured video-assisted coaching on performance in a simulated bleeding exercise during laparoscopic surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11173-3

article_title: Effects of undergraduate ultrasound education on cross-sectional image understanding and visual-spatial ability - a prospective study.
citation: Weimer Johannes, Ruppert Johannes, Vieth Thomas, Weinmann-Menke Julia, Buggenhagen Holger, Künzel Julian, Rink Maximilian, Lorenz Liv, Merkel Daniel, Ille Carlotta, Yang Yang, Müller Lukas, Kloeckner Roman, Weimer Andreas. title: Peer-tutored 15-hour undergraduate ultrasound course based on DEGUM curricula with hands-on practice in groups of five
description: A voluntary extracurricular ultrasound course for third-year medical students, developed "based on the current national resident course curricula of the German Society for Ultrasound in Medicine (DEGUM)". It comprises 20 teaching units of 45 min each (15 h) over 10 weeks, emphasizing abdominal sonography with some head and neck content. Students practised examinations on each other in groups of 5 taught by 1 peer tutor, with weekly review of theoretical principles and a final practical ultrasound exam.
requirements: Groups of 5 participants taught by 1 peer tutor with access to ultrasound devices for hands-on practice
constraints: The course was voluntary and extracurricular; emphasis was on abdominal sonography with only some head and neck sonography
target_learning_goals: Practical and theoretical ultrasound competencies

Radiological cross-sectional image understanding
examples: Students practised ultrasound examinations on each other in groups of 5 taught by 1 peer tutor over 10 weekly 90-min sessions, with a practical ultrasound exam in the last session

article_title: Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method.
citation: Zhang Dandan, Wang Xiaoxue, Chen Xueting, Lou Yingze, Zhou Xin, Zhang Kai. (2024). Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05851-y
title: Small-group rotation with peer scoring and feedback in the comprehension step of skills training
description: A lesson-level design pattern for the comprehension phase of procedural skills teaching: residents work in small teams and rotate through the roles of reciting the procedural steps, demonstrating the operation, and observing with a scoring sheet, with immediate feedback from peers and the supervising physician at each stage. The article describes "dividing each batch of 12 to 16 residents into four groups of 3 to 4 people each, with one instructing physician for every two groups", ensuring each resident completes a recitation, a demonstration, and one to two scoring observations per procedure.
requirements: Teams of 3 to 4 residents with rotation through recitation, demonstration, and scoring-observer roles
One instructing physician for every two groups
A scoring sheet used by the observing resident to provide checks, reminders, and noted issues
Immediate feedback from the supervising physician and team members on problems or deficiencies
constraints: Described and evaluated in the context of OB-GYN basic skill training with batches of 12 to 16 residents
target_learning_goals: procedural skill mastery
peer feedback and evaluation skills
metacognitive reflection on strengths and weaknesses
examples: In the RP group's comprehension step, resident A recited each procedural step, resident B demonstrated the operation, and residents C or D oversaw with the scoring sheet before the group rotated roles
key_sources: Zhang Dandan, Wang Xiaoxue, Chen Xueting, Lou Yingze, Zhou Xin, Zhang Kai. (2024). Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05851-y

article_title: Modelling the associations between academic engagement, study process and grit on academic achievement of physical education and sport university students.
citation: Tannoubi Amayra, Quansah Frank, Magouri Iteb, Chalghaf Nasr, Bonsaksen Tore, Srem-Sai Medina, Hagan John Elvis, Handrianto Ciptro, Azaiez Fairouz, Bragazzi Nicola Luigi. (2023). Modelling the associations between academic engagement, study process and grit on academic achievement of physical education and sport university students. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-023-01454-2
title: Arabic-language instrument battery: PE-SPQ, PE-Grit and A-USEI for PES students
description: The study used three contextually appropriate Arabic scales: the 20-item Physical Education-Study Process Questionnaire (deep/surface × theory/practice tasks), the 16-item PE-Grit (physical and academic interest and effort), and the 15-item A-USEI (behavioral, cognitive, emotional engagement). Reliabilities were strong: "The McDonald internal consistency indices across all four PE-SPQ components ranged from 0.86 to 0.94", with CFA fit indices also reported for each scale.
requirements: Contextually appropriate measurement scales validated with the target population (Arabic-language versions validated with university students).
target_learners: Physical education and sport university students
target_learning_goals: Measuring study processes, grit and academic engagement in higher education research
examples: PE-SPQ Cronbach's α ranged from 0.73 to 0.90 in this sample; PE-Grit CFA showed CFI = 0.96 and TLI = 0.95; A-USEI α ranged 0.77–0.82.

article_title: Virtual reality vs. physical models in surgical skills training. An update of the evidence.
citation: Chahal Baldev, Aydin Abdullatif, Ahmed Kamran. (2023). Virtual reality vs. physical models in surgical skills training. An update of the evidence. Current Opinion in Urology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MOU.0000000000001145
title: Perfused 3D-printed organ phantoms for urological procedural simulation
description: Perfused 3D-printed simulators are physical models built from patient-specific or hydrogel-based organ phantoms, validated across a range of urological procedures including prostate enucleation and pyeloplasty. The review states "3D printed organ phantoms have been validated for prostate enucleation procedures" and concludes that perfused 3D-printed models "may soon be superseded" cadavers as the gold-standard modality at substantially lower cost, incorporating anatomical variation and intraoperative complications. Unlike VR, they inadequately simulate morcellation.
requirements: 3D printing and perfusion capability; procedure-specific phantom design
constraints: Inadequate simulation of morcellation compared with VR simulators, as stated for prostate enucleation phantoms
target_learners: urology trainees learning endourological, laparoscopic and reconstructive procedures
target_learning_goals: procedural simulation incorporating anatomical variation and intraoperative complications
examples: 3D-printed pyeloplasty models demonstrated construct validity, with expert laparoscopic surgeons completing the procedure in significantly shorter time than novices
key_sources: Chahal Baldev, Aydin Abdullatif, Ahmed Kamran. (2023). Virtual reality vs. physical models in surgical skills training. An update of the evidence. Current Opinion in Urology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MOU.0000000000001145

article_title: Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications.
citation: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384
title: PEMDAS pediatric sedation complication simulation cases with full appendix toolkit (cases, patient triage set, critical actions checklist, equipment list, debriefing materials, evaluation, didactic)
description: Two simulation cases for learners in the pediatric emergency department: case 1, a 12-year-old with shoulder dislocation requiring propofol sedation who develops apnea and hypotension, and case 2, a forearm fracture under ketamine with laryngospasm, hypersalivation, and hypoxia. Learner actions include that participants "demonstrated how to take a presedation history, perform a presedation exam, assess American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classification, prepare the room for sedation, perform a time-out, and appropriately dose and redose two common sedation medications." Appendices A-H supply the cases, three triage patients, a critical actions checklist, equipment list, X-ray images, PEARLS debriefing materials, an evaluation form, and a PowerPoint, so instructors "would have access to all potential resources needed to carry out the session in their own setting."
requirements: A high-fidelity adolescent mannequin and a simulation lab or in-situ ED room, with appropriate equipment, simulated medications, and personal protective equipment per the Appendix D checklist
constraints: Limitations include the inability to portray typical medication side effects, such as nystagmus and hypersalivation, with a high-fidelity mannequin
Cases were designed for providers working in a pediatric emergency department but the authors state they can be tailored to any training background of learner providing sedation
target_learning_goals: Indications and contraindications of ED procedural sedation with propofol and ketamine
ASA classification and patient selection for ED sedation
informed verbal consent, assent, presedation history and exam
sedation room setup and equipment selection
dosing and redosing of sedation medications
management of propofol and ketamine complications
examples: Case 2 requires learners to select the appropriate sedation candidate from three patients with differing histories, physical exams, and ASA classifications
In case 2 the team performed jaw thrust with laryngospasm notch pressure, activated a code response, and administered succinylcholine
key_sources: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384

article_title: Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications.
citation: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384
title: PEARLS debriefing framework with three educational strategies (learner self-assessment, focused discussion, directive feedback)
description: The article uses the Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS) framework to structure post-simulation debriefing. As the authors describe it, "Through PEARLS' three broad educational strategies (fostering learner self-assessment, facilitation of a focused discussion, and information provided via directive feedback) and its blended approach, debriefing was interactive and collaborative." Debriefing was conducted "immediately following both simulations in a safe environment" using Appendix F materials modeled after the PEARLS approach. In this publication PEARLS supplies the debrief structure for reviewing missed learning objectives and answering learner questions after each sedation complication case.
requirements: A debriefing guide or materials (Appendix F) to aid discussion
A facilitator experienced in simulation to lead the debrief immediately after the cases
constraints: Allotted debriefing time was around 40 minutes per simulation
target_learners: advanced practice providers participating in sedation simulation
target_learning_goals: reflective learning after simulated sedation complications
self-assessment of critical actions
consolidating missed learning objectives
examples: Debriefing sessions were instructed and led by PEM providers with experience in simulation, using the PEARLS-based Appendix F materials

article_title: Learning with our peers: peer-led versus instructor-led debriefing for simulated crises, a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Jaffrelot M, Boet S, Floch Y, Garg N, Dubois D, Laparra V, Touffet L, Bould MD. (2024). Learning with our peers: peer-led versus instructor-led debriefing for simulated crises, a randomized controlled trial. Korean J Anesthesiol. https://doi.org/10.4097/kja.23317
title: Use peer-led debriefing as a feasible, lower-cost alternative to instructor-led debriefing in simulation-based crisis training
description: The article proposes that trainees can facilitate debriefing after simulated crisis scenarios, replacing or supplementing the expert instructor. Peer debriefers used a structured form covering "actions observed," "use of good judgement," and "exploring and closing the gaps observed." The authors argue "The peer debriefing model is a feasible alternative to the traditional, costlier instructor model," since instructor time is the main recurrent cost of simulation.
requirements: Peer debriefers need orientation and a structured debriefing form derived from best-practice guides; debriefing sessions were limited to 20 minutes.
constraints: The study was not statistically powered to conclude equivalence with instructor debriefing; findings come from a single center with fourth- and fifth-year medical students and may not generalize to residents.
target_learners: undergraduate medical students (fourth and fifth year)
target_learning_goals: non-technical crisis resource management skills such as leadership, communication, and situational awareness
examples: Peer debriefers observed two scenarios and facilitated 20-minute debriefings using a three-part structured form; their debriefees improved as much as instructor-debriefed controls.
key_sources: Jaffrelot M, Boet S, Floch Y, Garg N, Dubois D, Laparra V, Touffet L, Bould MD. (2024). Learning with our peers: peer-led versus instructor-led debriefing for simulated crises, a randomized controlled trial. Korean J Anesthesiol. https://doi.org/10.4097/kja.23317

article_title: The PEST (Pathology, Epidemiology, Severity, Treatment) approach to optimizing antimicrobial therapy.
citation: Davar Kusha, Vijayan Tara. (2023). The PEST (Pathology, Epidemiology, Severity, Treatment) approach to optimizing antimicrobial therapy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04286-1
title: The PEST model: a four-step structured cognitive tool (pathology, epidemiology, severity, treatment) for therapeutic reasoning in empiric antibiotic selection
description: The PEST model is a structured cognitive reasoning tool, described by the authors as an "instructions at test" intervention, that guides prescribers through four checklist questions: pathology (suspected pathogens), epidemiology (local resistance patterns from institutional antibiograms), severity (syndrome and host driven), and treatment (route, dosing, interactions). The article presents it as "a four-step approach to therapeutic reasoning and choosing an appropriate antimicrobial regimen for a given infectious disease syndrome." It is taught alongside case-based vignettes in small-group noon-conference sessions and doubles as a scoring rubric for therapeutic reasoning, awarding points when learners use at least three of the four criteria.
requirements: Learners need access to institutional antibiograms to apply the epidemiology step as the article describes
Delivery in the article pairs the checklist with clinical vignette-style cases and group discussion
constraints: The rubric was not previously validated, as the article states
Meta-analyses cited by the authors suggest cognitive reasoning tools provide only modest improvement in diagnostic accuracy
target_learning_goals: Therapeutic reasoning for empiric antimicrobial selection
Appropriate antibiotic prescribing and antimicrobial stewardship
examples: Two one-hour noon-conference sessions at UCLA RRMC and GLA VAHS combining a PEST overview, group work on vignette-style questions, and use of the institutional antibiogram
key_sources: Davar Kusha, Vijayan Tara. (2023). The PEST (Pathology, Epidemiology, Severity, Treatment) approach to optimizing antimicrobial therapy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04286-1

article_title: The Effects of an E-learning Module on Medical Trainees Rotating on a Perioperative Medicine Clinical Service.
citation: Wegner Lauren E. MS, Shiffermiller Jason F. MD, MPH, Vokoun Chad W. MD, O'Rourke Michael J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory J. MD. (2023). The Effects of an E-learning Module on Medical Trainees Rotating on a Perioperative Medicine Clinical Service. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11325
title: Interactive 1-hour perioperative medicine e-learning module built on Articulate Storyline 360
description: An interactive, approximately 1-hour e-module created on the Articulate Storyline 360 platform and hosted on Canvas, mapped to six educational objectives. Content design utilized "brief audiovisual didactics with a variety of embedded interactive elements such as drag-and-drop surgical risk categorization and case-based clinical decision prompts", frequent self-assessment quizzes with immediate feedback, and a single case vignette revisited at multiple points to place objectives in clinical context. It was offered as an elective self-directed learning experience during rotations.
requirements: Content based on published evidence and, where available, consensus guidelines
Mapped to six educational objectives
Designed to require approximately 1 hour to complete
constraints: Content was not presented in any other formal learning experience during the perioperative medicine rotation
target_learners: residents (PGY ≥ 2) in internal medicine, anesthesiology, neurology, and physical medicine and rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: preoperative risk assessment
selection of lab and ancillary testing
cardiac stress testing modalities
management of high-risk perioperative medications
common postoperative complications
examples: Offered to trainees on perioperative medicine rotations between July 2018 and March 2021 at three participating institutions; 67 of 75 participants reported completing more than 75% of the content

article_title: Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning.
citation: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249
title: PeerWise online cooperative question-authoring platform
description: PeerWise is an online application in which students build a bank of multiple-choice questions for peers and cycle through authoring, answering, and discussion. "PeerWise is an online application designed to facilitate students in creating a bank of MCQs for their peers and supporting cycles of question authoring, answering, and discussion." Students rate peers' questions on a five-point scale, which correlates well with expert ratings, and the system tracks how each question is answered so distractor effectiveness can be empirically assessed.
requirements: Student participation sustained over a teaching semester to build the shared question bank
constraints: The peer question-rating scheme is a sparse form of feedback that may be suboptimal for improving question quality, especially in large early-year cohorts with variable abilities
target_learners: higher education students, including large early-year undergraduate cohorts
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of course content; question quality
examples: In this study 712 students used PeerWise for course credit; the median number of questions answered in step 2 was 51, with a long tail up to 489.
key_sources: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249

article_title: Relationships between Perfectionism, Extra Training and Academic Performance in Chinese Collegiate Athletes: Mediating Role of Achievement Motivation.
citation: Han Chengjiang, Li Feng, Lian Bizhen, Vencúrik Tomas, Liang Wei. (2022). Relationships between Perfectionism, Extra Training and Academic Performance in Chinese Collegiate Athletes: Mediating Role of Achievement Motivation. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph191710764
title: Multidimensional perfectionism: perfectionistic concerns versus perfectionistic strivings
description: The article adopts the contemporary consensus conceptualizing perfectionism as a multidimensional, multifaceted trait with two higher-order dimensions. Perfectionistic concerns capture "concern over mistakes, feelings of discrepancy between one's expectations and performance, and negative reactions to imperfection (doubts about action)", while perfectionistic strivings capture self-oriented striving for perfection and setting exceedingly high standards. The study operationalizes this with five MPS-F facets (concern over mistake, doubts about action, personal standard, organization, parental expectation) and shows the facets relate differently to extra training and GPA.
requirements: Perfectionism must be measured at the facet level, since the facets show distinct patterns of relationships with outcomes
constraints: The authors state research on the specific facets within each dimension is limited and facet–outcome relationships are complex and ambiguous
target_learning_goals: understanding personality and motivation influences on training and academic performance
examples: The study measured the five facets with the Chinese Version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (31 items, 5-point Likert) in wave one of the two-wave survey
key_sources: Han Chengjiang, Li Feng, Lian Bizhen, Vencúrik Tomas, Liang Wei. (2022). Relationships between Perfectionism, Extra Training and Academic Performance in Chinese Collegiate Athletes: Mediating Role of Achievement Motivation. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph191710764

article_title: An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case-based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education.
citation: Lundegren N, Jönsson A, Lindberg P. (2021). An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case‐based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education. European Journal of Dental Education, 25(4), 649-656. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12642
title: Peer-assessed written assignments as substitute and ongoing literacy activity
description: Peer-assessed assignments are a component of the upgraded Malmö model serving two functions. When a student cannot attend the mandatory seminar, they complete "a written assignment dealing with the questions and discussions that took place in the seminar," which is read and reviewed by a student peer. In addition, peer- and teacher-reviewed assignments are given continuously throughout the programme to promote academic literacy and a research-based process for learning, with topics predefined by lecturers or based on students' own questions or interests. The article cites studies indicating peer assessment can improve learning and is sometimes as effective as lecturer assessment.
requirements: A student peer available to read and review the assignment
target_learning_goals: academic literacy
self-assessment skills
independent thinking and writing
examples: Students absent from seminars receive a written assignment on the seminar questions, reviewed by a peer
key_sources: Lundegren N, Jönsson A, Lindberg P. (2021). An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case‐based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education. European Journal of Dental Education, 25(4), 649-656. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12642

article_title: Does a Person-Environment-Fit Promote the Academic Achievement of Hearing-Impaired Students in Malaysian Polytechnics? The Mediating Effects of Satisfaction and Adjustment.
citation: Azizan Che’ Rozaniza, Roslan Samsilah, Abdullah Maria Chong, Asimiran Soaib, Zaremohzzabieh Zeinab, Ahrari Seyedali, Tchounwou Paul B. (2021). Does a Person-Environment-Fit Promote the Academic Achievement of Hearing-Impaired Students in Malaysian Polytechnics? The Mediating Effects of Satisfaction and Adjustment. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182413381
title: Person-Environment (P-E) fit theory as a model of inclusion for hearing-impaired students
description: P-E fit theory holds that well-being and productivity result from interactions between people and their environments, with excellent fits promoting "emotions of control, self-confidence, and contentment". The article applies the theory's three constructs — personality-major fit, demands-abilities fit, and needs-supplies fit — to hearing-impaired students in Malaysian polytechnics, concluding it is "a possible model of inclusion for hearing-impaired students". Personality-major fit draws on Holland's RIASEC typology of six personality and environment types.
requirements: Assessment of fit requires measuring students' interests, abilities, and needs against the demands and supplies of the academic environment, as done with the Graphic-Assisted Personality-Major Congruence Instrument and fit questionnaires.
constraints: The article notes the study's cross-sectional design and that P-E fit is a continuous process developing with students' maturity and experience, so longitudinal work is needed.
target_learners: Hearing-impaired students in tertiary technical and vocational education
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
adjustment to the academic environment
satisfaction with the course of study
examples: Survey of 195 hearing-impaired students across five Malaysian polytechnics offering the Special Skills Certificate program, analysed with PLS-SEM.
key_sources: Azizan Che’ Rozaniza, Roslan Samsilah, Abdullah Maria Chong, Asimiran Soaib, Zaremohzzabieh Zeinab, Ahrari Seyedali, Tchounwou Paul B. (2021). Does a Person-Environment-Fit Promote the Academic Achievement of Hearing-Impaired Students in Malaysian Polytechnics? The Mediating Effects of Satisfaction and Adjustment.
